projects.fullMarkdown:
# Ara: A 1-GHz+ Scalable and Energy-Efficient RISC-V Vector Processor With Multiprecision Floating-Point Support in 22-nm FD-SOI

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Matheus Cavalcante; Fabian Schuiki; Florian Zaruba; Michael Schaffner; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich; Google (Schaffner); University of Bologna (Benini) |
| Venue | IEEE Transactions on Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) Systems |
| Venue type | journal |
| Year | 2020 |
| Volume / issue / pages | Vol. 28, No. 2, pp. 530-543 |
| Paper DOI | [10.1109/TVLSI.2019.2950087](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVLSI.2019.2950087) |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00478 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/ara |
| Keywords | RISC-V, vector processor, SIMD, 22FDX, energy efficiency |
| Open access | IEEE + arXiv preprint |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Corresponding: matheusd@iis.ee.ethz.ch.

## TL;DR

- Ara is a scalable RISC-V vector unit (RVV draft 0.5) tightly coupled to Ariane/CVA6, built from identical 64-bit lanes with local VRF, ALU/MUL/FPU, VLSU, and SLDU.
- 16-lane instance: >1 GHz typical 22FDX, up to 33 DP-GFLOPS, 97% FPU util on 256x256 DP MATMUL, up to 41 DP-GFLOPS/W.
- Four-lane P&R macro 1.125 mm x 1.000 mm; ~575 kGE per lane; vector-side area ~2.46 MGE excluding scalar core; ~2.5x energy efficiency vs Ariane alone on comparable integer GEMM.

## Problem statement

Data-parallel workloads need energy-efficient programmable datapaths that amortize instruction fetch better than multicore scalar or short SIMT warps; open RISC-V vector microarchitecture at advanced CMOS with measured scalability was lacking.

## Motivation

Implement and characterize a lane-scalable open RISC-V vector coprocessor in GF 22FDX, quantifying FPU utilization, memory-bound kernels, and PPA as lane count grows from 2 to 16.

## Prior art

ARM SVE; RISC-V RVV drafts; Hwacha (Berkeley, ST 28 nm, ~64 DP-GFLOPS / ~40 DP-GFLOPS/W claimed); packed-SIMD DSP extensions; GPU SIMT.

## Category of work

Primary: `circuit-design`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: Vector coprocessor microarchitecture + 22 nm P&R/power (SCORE architecture: Ara).

## Method / approach

**Coupling (Fig. 1).** Ariane RV64GC issues vector commands via lightweight scoreboard port; Ara main sequencer dispatches to N lanes; memory port width W bits.

**Lane (Figs. 1b, 2).** Lane sequencer (up to 8 in-flight vector ops), 16 KiB VRF (8 banks), operand queues, integer ALU/MUL, FPU (open IEEE FPU), commit. SLDU for inter-lane permutes; VLSU for vector memory.

**ISA.** RVV 0.5 draft; FP64/32/16 mixed precision via FPU.

**Physical.** Synth/P&R 2/4/8/16 lanes in 22FDX; detailed four-lane macro.

## Experimental setup

- Technology: GF 22FDX FD-SOI; typical TT/0.80 V/25 C for headline GHz/GFLOPS.
- Kernels: DP MATMUL, AXPY, CONV2D across n and lane counts; FPU vs VLSU utilization traces.
- Power: post-layout switching activity with Ariane+Ara vs Ariane-only.

## Results summary

- MATMUL 256x256, 16 lanes: 97% FPU util; 2-lane 98%.
- Peak: 33 DP-GFLOPS, 41 DP-GFLOPS/W, >1 GHz.
- MATMUL 4.27 DP-FLOP/cycle at 16 lanes (~80% of peak issue); 2-lane 0.65 DP-FLOP/cycle.
- CONV2D: 3.73 DP-FLOP/cycle (fewer lanes better for short vectors).
- Ara FPU util up to 66% higher than comparable Hwacha open RTL on authors' comparison setup.
- Four-lane: 575 kGE/lane, vector unit 2.46 MGE (lanes 93%); Ariane without caches ~524 kGE ~ one lane.
- Integer 256x256 GEMM energy: four-lane Ara much higher throughput; Ariane-only 17 GOPS/W with caches 46% of power.
- 16-lane clock ~17% lower than 2-lane due to VLSU packing path.

## Contributions

- Open lane-scalable RVV 0.5 vector unit coupled to Ariane.
- 22FDX implementation and kernel scaling study (util vs n vs lanes).
- Energy comparison vs scalar Ariane and literature vector units.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Identical-lane scaling with local VRF banks plus slim global VLSU/SLDU keeps non-lane area ~7% at four lanes.
- Analysis: Quantifies short-vector / in-order scalar issue as the limiter of 16-lane FPU util, not lane datapath.

## Limitations and future work

- RVV 0.5 (not frozen 1.0); Ara2/AraXL are later SCORE-relevant follow-ons.
- Power-gating per lane not implemented (area/timing cost).
- Memory interface / in-order Ariane issue limits wide-lane short kernels.
- IEEE journal PDF (user download); arXiv:1906.00478 is the preprint twin.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Open 22 nm RVV datapath with lane sweep vs Hwacha's less complete public RTL comparison.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: RVV 1.0 compliance, multi-core Ara, HBM/SoC integration (Occamy/Cheshire hosts).

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE Ara vs AraXL vs Spatz as three RVV scaling styles in one registry table.
- Analysis: Pair Ara lanes with Cheshire host instead of Ariane-only coprocessor port.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Strong PPA + utilization evidence for SCORE Ara row.
- Analysis: Open-source intent with Ariane/CVA6 ecosystem.

### Cons

- Analysis: Draft vector spec; later Ara2 is the RVV 1.0 design.
- Analysis: Kernel set is LA/DSP, not full SoC Linux workloads on the vector path.

- Pass 0: IEEE PDF; 10 figure captions (no Fig. 3 in detector); 3 tables; extra figure candidates added manually for strict validation.

- Page 1: Title, authors, abstract (97%, 33 GFLOPS, 41 GFLOPS/W), DOI 10.1109/TVLSI.2019.2950087, intro VNB/vector motivation.
- Page 2: Open-source claim; Figs 1-2 architecture; Ariane coupling start.
- Page 3: Ariane changes, sequencer, memory interface.
- Page 4: Lane sequencer, VRF banks, queues, execution units.
- Page 5: FPU, VLSU/SLDU, programming/ISA notes.
- Page 6: Fig. 4 MATMUL utilization; kernel methodology.
- Page 7: Fig. 5 performance; CONV/AXPY discussion.
- Page 8: Fig. 6 kernels vs lanes; Table I P&R comparison start.
- Page 9: Fig. 7 layout; Tables II-III; frequency vs lanes.
- Page 10: Fig. 8 area; power vs Ariane; Hwacha energy scaling.
- Page 11: Discussion/scalability of issue path; conclusion start.
- Page 12: Figs 9-11 pipeline and 32x32 util; remaining discussion.
- Page 13: References.
- Page 14: References end / IEEE footer.

### Pass 3 accuracy audit:

- Verified: 16-lane 97% FPU, 33 DP-GFLOPS, 41 DP-GFLOPS/W, >1 GHz TT 0.80 V.
- Verified: 16 KiB VRF/lane, 8 banks, 575 kGE/lane, 2.46 MGE four-lane vector side, 1.125 mm x 1.000 mm macro.
- Verified: Ariane ~524 kGE without caches; 17 GOPS/W Ariane integer GEMM; 2.5x efficiency vs Ariane.
- Verified: DOI and 22FDX technology.
- Checked: Fig. 3 not in unique_figure_numbers; analysis headings match detector set 1,2,4-11.

All listed figures: `a_manual` caption-aligned clips with `b_manual` alternate rect.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# AraXL: A Physically Scalable, Ultra-Wide RISC-V Vector Processor Design for Fast and Efficient Computation on Long Vectors

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Navaneeth Kunhi Purayil; Matteo Perotti; Tim Fischer; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich; University of Bologna (Benini) |
| Venue | DATE 2025 / arXiv:2501.10301 |
| Venue type | conference preprint |
| Year | 2025 |
| Volume / issue / pages | DATE DOI 10.23919/DATE64628.2025.10992880 |
| Paper DOI | [10.23919/DATE64628.2025.10992880](https://doi.org/10.23919/DATE64628.2025.10992880) |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10301 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/AraXL |
| Keywords | RISC-V V 1.0, long vectors, Ara2, physical scalability |
| Open access | arXiv |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- AraXL modularizes Ara2 into a hierarchical cluster of vector lanes with distributed GLSU and RINGI, targeting up to 64 lanes and the RVV 1.0 max 64 Kibit/vreg.
- 22 nm 64-lane instance: 146 GFLOPs peak on dense kernels (>99% FPU util), 40.1 GFLOPs/W at 1.15 GHz TT/0.8 V; only 3.8x the area of a 16-lane instance.
- Addresses wire-dominated physical limits that stopped prior Ara2/Vitruvius+ scaling beyond ~8-16 lanes.

## Problem statement

Long-vector RVV needs huge VRF + many FPUs, but lumped interconnects make >16-lane physical design inefficient.

## Motivation

Reach RVV-legal maximum VLEN and tens of lanes with a physically hierarchical Ara2-based architecture.

## Prior art

Ara/Ara2; Vitruvius+; Arm SVE/SVE2 (A64FX, Graviton4); NEC TSUBASA; Spatz compact vectors.

## Category of work

Primary: `circuit-design`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture AraXL.

## Method / approach

**Cluster.** Hierarchical Ara2-like lane groups; Global LSU; Ring Interface for reshuffles/reductions; MASKU distribution.

**ISA.** RISC-V V 1.0 long vectors up to 64 Kibit/vreg; up to 64 DP FPUs.

**Physical.** 22 nm P&R; 16-lane floorplan focus; scale area to 64 lanes; latency-tolerance experiments.

## Experimental setup

- TT/0.8 V, 1.15 GHz class; weak scaling and injected memory/request/ring latency sweeps.
- Benchmarks parameterized in Table I; SoA PPA Table III.

## Results summary

- 64-lane: 146 GFLOPs, >99% FPU util on compute-intensive kernels; 40.1 GFLOPs/W.
- Area scales to only 3.8x a 16-lane instance at 64 lanes.
- Latency-tolerance experiments show long vectors absorb memory/NoC stalls better than short Ara2 configs.
- Open AraXL based on Ara2.

## Contributions

- Physically scalable AraXL architecture to 64 lanes / max VLEN.
- 22 nm PPA and latency study.
- Comparison vs Ara2 and SoA laned vectors.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Hierarchical GLSU/RINGI replace lumped SLDU as the scaling bottleneck.
- Analysis: Quantifies that area need not grow linearly with lane count when interconnect is distributed.

## Limitations and future work

- Short DATE-style paper (7 pages); limited full-app evaluation.
- Pass 0 missing Fig. 6 caption in unique set.
- Depends on Ara2 lane microarchitecture assumptions.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: First open path toward RVV max VLEN with many lanes.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Silicon bring-up, sparse kernels, and host-SoC integration (Occamy-class).

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE Ara vs AraXL scaling table (lanes, VLEN, GFLOPs/W).
- Analysis: Pair AraXL with Cheshire/Occamy hosts for survey system diagrams.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Direct SCORE AraXL primary; clear link to Ara2 lineage.
- Analysis: Physical scalability evidence is the survey-relevant claim.

### Cons

- Analysis: Brief conference format.
- Analysis: Dense-kernel focused peaks.

digestSections.tl;dr:
- AraXL modularizes Ara2 into a hierarchical cluster of vector lanes with distributed GLSU and RINGI, targeting up to 64 lanes and the RVV 1.0 max 64 Kibit/vreg.
- 22 nm 64-lane instance: 146 GFLOPs peak on dense kernels (>99% FPU util), 40.1 GFLOPs/W at 1.15 GHz TT/0.8 V; only 3.8x the area of a 16-lane instance.
- Addresses wire-dominated physical limits that stopped prior Ara2/Vitruvius+ scaling beyond ~8-16 lanes.
digestSections.problem statement: Long-vector RVV needs huge VRF + many FPUs, but lumped interconnects make >16-lane physical design inefficient.
digestSections.motivation: Reach RVV-legal maximum VLEN and tens of lanes with a physically hierarchical Ara2-based architecture.
digestSections.prior art: Ara/Ara2; Vitruvius+; Arm SVE/SVE2 (A64FX, Graviton4); NEC TSUBASA; Spatz compact vectors.
digestSections.category of work:
Primary: `circuit-design`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture AraXL.
digestSections.method / approach:
**Cluster.** Hierarchical Ara2-like lane groups; Global LSU; Ring Interface for reshuffles/reductions; MASKU distribution.

**ISA.** RISC-V V 1.0 long vectors up to 64 Kibit/vreg; up to 64 DP FPUs.

**Physical.** 22 nm P&R; 16-lane floorplan focus; scale area to 64 lanes; latency-tolerance experiments.
digestSections.experimental setup:
- TT/0.8 V, 1.15 GHz class; weak scaling and injected memory/request/ring latency sweeps.
- Benchmarks parameterized in Table I; SoA PPA Table III.
digestSections.results summary:
- 64-lane: 146 GFLOPs, >99% FPU util on compute-intensive kernels; 40.1 GFLOPs/W.
- Area scales to only 3.8x a 16-lane instance at 64 lanes.
- Latency-tolerance experiments show long vectors absorb memory/NoC stalls better than short Ara2 configs.
- Open AraXL based on Ara2.
digestSections.contributions:
- Physically scalable AraXL architecture to 64 lanes / max VLEN.
- 22 nm PPA and latency study.
- Comparison vs Ara2 and SoA laned vectors.
digestSections.innovations:
- Analysis: Hierarchical GLSU/RINGI replace lumped SLDU as the scaling bottleneck.
- Analysis: Quantifies that area need not grow linearly with lane count when interconnect is distributed.
digestSections.limitations and future work:
- Short DATE-style paper (7 pages); limited full-app evaluation.
- Pass 0 missing Fig. 6 caption in unique set.
- Depends on Ara2 lane microarchitecture assumptions.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Silicon bring-up, sparse kernels, and host-SoC integration (Occamy-class).

- Analysis: SCORE Ara vs AraXL scaling table (lanes, VLEN, GFLOPs/W).

projects.fullMarkdown:
# A Reliable, Time-Predictable Heterogeneous SoC for AI-Enhanced Mixed-Criticality Edge Applications

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Angelo Garofalo; Alessandro Ottaviano; Matteo Perotti; Thomas Benz; Yvan Tortorella; Robert Balas; Michael Rogenmoser; Chi Zhang; Luca Bertaccini; Nils Wistoff; Maicol Ciani; Cyril Koenig; Mattia Sinigaglia; Luca Valente; Paul Scheffler; Manuel Eggimann; Matheus Cavalcante; Francesco Restuccia; Alessandro Biondi; Francesco Conti; Frank K. Gurkaynak; Davide Rossi; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich (D-ITET); University of Bologna (DEI); UCSD; Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna |
| Venue | arXiv preprint (IEEE-style brief format) |
| Venue type | preprint |
| Year | 2025 |
| Paper DOI | not found |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18953 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/carfield |
| Keywords | Heterogeneous mixed-critical SoC, time-predictable SoC, hardware acceleration, fault tolerant hardware, RISC-V |
| Open access | arXiv + open-source RTL (liberal license) |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Corresponding: {agarofalo,aottaviano}@ethz.ch. Funding: HORIZON CHIPS-JU TRISTAN (101095947) and ISOLDE (101112274).

## TL;DR

- Carfield is a 16 nm Intel FinFET heterogeneous RISC-V SoC for AI-enhanced mixed-criticality edge workloads under a 1.2 W envelope at 0.8 V.
- Software-configurable TSU, DPLLC, and DCSPM hardware IPs partition interconnect and memory for bounded WCET at zero performance overhead when idle.
- Dual-core RVV vector cluster hits 121.8 GFLOPS (FP8) at 1.1 TFLOPS/W; 12-core AMR integer cluster hits 304.9 GOPS at 1.6 TOPS/W with runtime lockstep redundancy.

## Problem statement

Near-sensor zonal controllers for automotive, space, and robotics must run AI-enhanced perception alongside hard real-time control within roughly 2 W, with reliable execution and bounded worst-case latency when heterogeneous initiators share interconnect and memory.

## Motivation

Prior heterogeneous SoCs achieve freedom-from-interference mainly in software (large overhead) or address only interconnect QoS; mission-critical AI needs silicon-proven predictability plus compact, dependable accelerators without sacrificing programmability.

## Prior art

NXP i.MXRT1170 crossover MCUs; ST Stellar automotive MCU; Renesas ISSCC'19 virtualized flash MCU; Valente et al. TCAS-I nano-UAV SoC; edge AI processors (JSSCC'23, JSSCC'22, ISSCC'24); Cheshire host platform; AXI-ICRT and AXI-REALM traffic regulation research.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`, `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture Carfield.

## Method / approach

**Domains (Fig. 1).** SECD (HWRoT), SAFED (triple lockstep RV32 + ECC SPM + 6-cycle CLIC), HOSTD (Cheshire-extended dual RV64GCH with H-extension and vCLIC), vector cluster, AMR cluster, 1 MiB L2 DCSPM, DPLLC + HyperBUS HyperRAM, 64b AXI4.

**Predictability IPs (Fig. 2).** TSU per initiator (GBS burst splitter, write buffer, TRU budget); DCSPM bank partitioning via aliased addresses; DPLLC set-based spatial partitions with selective flush.

**Vector cluster.** Two RVZve64d VLEN=512 RVVUs + scalar cores + DMA; 2 KiB latch VRF per engine; 16-bank 1024b/cyc L1 SPM; FP8-FP64 mixed precision including sdotp.

**AMR cluster (Fig. 3).** 12 RV32IMFC cores, 256 KiB ECC L1 SPM, custom SIMD sdotp (2b-16b), runtime INDIP/DLM/TLM with HFR (24-cycle recovery).

## Experimental setup

- Intel 16 nm FinFET silicon; 0.6-1.1 V; nominal 0.8 V / 1.2 W budget; standalone PCB (Fig. 4).
- V/F/P sweeps and perf vs energy efficiency for MatMul/FFT kernels on both clusters (Fig. 5).
- Interference scenarios: HOSTD TCT on HyperRAM vs DMA; AMR TCT vs vector MatMul on shared AXI/DCSPM (Fig. 6).
- Room temperature 25 C measurements; 2 OP = 1 MAC convention.

## Results summary

- AMR: up to 304.9 GOPS (2bx2b MatMul), 161.4 GOPS in DLM; 1.6 TOPS/W peak efficiency at 0.6 V / 300 MHz.
- Vector: 122 GFLOPS FP8 MatMul at 1.1 V / 1 GHz; 1.1 TFLOPS/W at 0.6 V / 250 MHz; 97.9% FPU util on edge MatMuls.
- Unregulated HyperRAM interference degrades TCT latency 225x; TSU + DPLLC partitioning recovers to 75% of isolated performance.
- AMR-vs-vector DCSPM conflict drops AMR perf 12.2x; TSU + aliased DCSPM paths restore 95% isolated (R-E4).
- 6-cycle CV32RT interrupt latency; only surveyed SoC with HW cache partitioning, predictable comm, and dynamic SPM (Fig. 7).
- AMR/vector clusters lead SoA edge AI and FP accelerators on area/energy metrics (Fig. 8).

## Contributions

- End-to-end time-predictable MCT execution via TSU, DPLLC, and DCSPM at zero idle overhead.
- 1.07 TFLOPS/W / 107 GFLOPS/mm2 dual-core RV vector cluster for FP mixed-precision DSP.
- 1.61 TOPS/W / 260.7 GOPS/mm2 12-core AMR cluster with runtime adaptive modular redundancy.
- Open-source synthesizable RTL release for extension and benchmarking.

## Innovations

- Analysis: First holistic silicon-proven MCS combining safety domains, HW resource partitioning, and leading-edge programmable accelerators under 1.2 W.
- Analysis: HFR + AMR mode switching (82-183 cycles) trades 1.89x-2.85x perf for DLM/TLM reliability without cluster reboot.
- Analysis: Aliased DCSPM addressing creates interference-free memory paths at zero extra latency vs software-only isolation.

## Limitations and future work

- Brief format; long-form journal version may expand OS/hypervisor integration details.
- Benchmarks emphasize MatMul/FFT; broader robotics stack validation not shown.
- Comparison tables mix COTS datasheets and literature with scaled estimates (marked in Fig. 8).
- No multi-chiplet or HBM integration story in this work.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: ST/NXP/Renesas MCS prototypes lack combined HW memory partitioning + dual accelerator classes at this power class.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Formal WCET tooling tied to TSU/DPLLC configs, Occamy/Cheshire host coupling, and ISO 26262 software stack evidence remain open.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE Carfield row pairing predictability IPs with Cheshire HOSTD and Spatz/MemPool accelerator baselines.
- Analysis: Co-simulate hypervisor-driven DPLLC partition policies under realistic automotive sensor fusion traces.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Strong SCORE primary for mixed-criticality + open RTL with measured interference mitigation.
- Analysis: Dual accelerator story (FP vector + integer AMR) covers DSP and mission-critical AI in one die.

### Cons

- Analysis: Preprint without peer-reviewed DOI yet.
- Analysis: Predictability demos are controlled lab scenarios; full application WCET certification path not established.

## Benchmarks and tables

No formal numbered tables in PDF (`table_caption_count: 0`). Comparison data appear as Fig. 7 (heterogeneous MCS SoC comparison) and Fig. 8 (edge AI / vector accelerator comparison) — reproduced as figure embeds below.

digestSections.tl;dr:
- Carfield is a 16 nm Intel FinFET heterogeneous RISC-V SoC for AI-enhanced mixed-criticality edge workloads under a 1.2 W envelope at 0.8 V.
- Software-configurable TSU, DPLLC, and DCSPM hardware IPs partition interconnect and memory for bounded WCET at zero performance overhead when idle.
- Dual-core RVV vector cluster hits 121.8 GFLOPS (FP8) at 1.1 TFLOPS/W; 12-core AMR integer cluster hits 304.9 GOPS at 1.6 TOPS/W with runtime lockstep redundancy.
digestSections.problem statement: Near-sensor zonal controllers for automotive, space, and robotics must run AI-enhanced perception alongside hard real-time control within roughly 2 W, with reliable execution and bounded worst-case latency when heterogeneous initiators share interconnect and memory.
digestSections.motivation: Prior heterogeneous SoCs achieve freedom-from-interference mainly in software (large overhead) or address only interconnect QoS; mission-critical AI needs silicon-proven predictability plus compact, dependable accelerators without sacrificing programmability.
digestSections.prior art: NXP i.MXRT1170 crossover MCUs; ST Stellar automotive MCU; Renesas ISSCC'19 virtualized flash MCU; Valente et al. TCAS-I nano-UAV SoC; edge AI processors (JSSCC'23, JSSCC'22, ISSCC'24); Cheshire host platform; AXI-ICRT and AXI-REALM traffic regulation research.
digestSections.category of work:
Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`, `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture Carfield.
digestSections.method / approach:
**Domains (Fig. 1).** SECD (HWRoT), SAFED (triple lockstep RV32 + ECC SPM + 6-cycle CLIC), HOSTD (Cheshire-extended dual RV64GCH with H-extension and vCLIC), vector cluster, AMR cluster, 1 MiB L2 DCSPM, DPLLC + HyperBUS HyperRAM, 64b AXI4.

**Predictability IPs (Fig. 2).** TSU per initiator (GBS burst splitter, write buffer, TRU budget); DCSPM bank partitioning via aliased addresses; DPLLC set-based spatial partitions with selective flush.

**Vector cluster.** Two RVZve64d VLEN=512 RVVUs + scalar cores + DMA; 2 KiB latch VRF per engine; 16-bank 1024b/cyc L1 SPM; FP8-FP64 mixed precision including sdotp.

**AMR cluster (Fig. 3).** 12 RV32IMFC cores, 256 KiB ECC L1 SPM, custom SIMD sdotp (2b-16b), runtime INDIP/DLM/TLM with HFR (24-cycle recovery).
digestSections.experimental setup:
- Intel 16 nm FinFET silicon; 0.6-1.1 V; nominal 0.8 V / 1.2 W budget; standalone PCB (Fig. 4).
- V/F/P sweeps and perf vs energy efficiency for MatMul/FFT kernels on both clusters (Fig. 5).
- Interference scenarios: HOSTD TCT on HyperRAM vs DMA; AMR TCT vs vector MatMul on shared AXI/DCSPM (Fig. 6).
- Room temperature 25 C measurements; 2 OP = 1 MAC convention.
digestSections.results summary:
- AMR: up to 304.9 GOPS (2bx2b MatMul), 161.4 GOPS in DLM; 1.6 TOPS/W peak efficiency at 0.6 V / 300 MHz.
- Vector: 122 GFLOPS FP8 MatMul at 1.1 V / 1 GHz; 1.1 TFLOPS/W at 0.6 V / 250 MHz; 97.9% FPU util on edge MatMuls.
- Unregulated HyperRAM interference degrades TCT latency 225x; TSU + DPLLC partitioning recovers to 75% of isolated performance.
- AMR-vs-vector DCSPM conflict drops AMR perf 12.2x; TSU + aliased DCSPM paths restore 95% isolated (R-E4).
- 6-cycle CV32RT interrupt latency; only surveyed SoC with HW cache partitioning, predictable comm, and dynamic SPM (Fig. 7).
- AMR/vector clusters lead SoA edge AI and FP accelerators on area/energy metrics (Fig. 8).
digestSections.contributions:
- End-to-end time-predictable MCT execution via TSU, DPLLC, and DCSPM at zero idle overhead.
- 1.07 TFLOPS/W / 107 GFLOPS/mm2 dual-core RV vector cluster for FP mixed-precision DSP.
- 1.61 TOPS/W / 260.7 GOPS/mm2 12-core AMR cluster with runtime adaptive modular redundancy.
- Open-source synthesizable RTL release for extension and benchmarking.
digestSections.innovations:
- Analysis: First holistic silicon-proven MCS combining safety domains, HW resource partitioning, and leading-edge programmable accelerators under 1.2 W.
- Analysis: HFR + AMR mode switching (82-183 cycles) trades 1.89x-2.85x perf for DLM/TLM reliability without cluster reboot.
- Analysis: Aliased DCSPM addressing creates interference-free memory paths at zero extra latency vs software-only isolation.
digestSections.limitations and future work:
- Brief format; long-form journal version may expand OS/hypervisor integration details.
- Benchmarks emphasize MatMul/FFT; broader robotics stack validation not shown.
- Comparison tables mix COTS datasheets and literature with scaled estimates (marked in Fig. 8).
- No multi-chiplet or HBM integration story in this work.
digestSections.research opportunity:
**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: ST/NXP/Renesas MCS prototypes lack combined HW memory partitioning + dual accelerator classes at this power class.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Formal WCET tooling tied to TSU/DPLLC configs, Occamy/Cheshire host coupling, and ISO 26262 software stack evidence remain open.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE Carfield row pairing predictability IPs with Cheshire HOSTD and Spatz/MemPool accelerator baselines.
- Analysis: Co-simulate hypervisor-driven DPLLC partition policies under realistic automotive sensor fusion traces.
digestSections.pros and cons:
### Pros

- Analysis: Strong SCORE primary for mixed-criticality + open RTL with measured interference mitigation.
- Analysis: Dual accelerator story (FP vector + integer AMR) covers DSP and mission-critical AI in one die.

### Cons

- Analysis: Preprint without peer-reviewed DOI yet.
- Analysis: Predictability demos are controlled lab scenarios; full application WCET certification path not established.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Cheshire: A Lightweight, Linux-Capable RISC-V Host Platform for Domain-Specific Accelerator Plug-In

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Alessandro Ottaviano; Thomas Benz; Paul Scheffler; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich; University of Bologna (Benini) |
| Venue | IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems II: Express Briefs (TCAS-II) |
| Venue type | journal |
| Year | 2023 |
| Volume / issue / pages | Vol. 70, No. 10 (5 pages); arXiv:2305.04760v2 |
| Paper DOI | [10.1109/TCSII.2023.3312019](https://doi.org/10.1109/TCSII.2023.3312019) |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04760 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/cheshire |
| Keywords | RISC-V, Linux, RPC DRAM, heterogeneous computing, DSA host, open-source SoC |
| Open access | arXiv preprint; RTL open-source (SolderPad) |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Corresponding: {aottaviano,tbenz,paulsc,lbenini}@iis.ethz.ch. Funding: ECSEL FRACTAL, HORIZON TRISTAN.

## TL;DR

- Cheshire is a modular RV64GC Linux-capable host SoC platform for plugging in domain-specific accelerators via configurable AXI4 ports, DMA, and optional D2D link.
- First taped-out open-source fully digital RPC DRAM interface: 22 switching IOs, 3.5 kGE PHY, 750 MB/s peak at 200 MHz, 250 pJ/B measured on silicon.
- Silicon demonstrator Neo (TSMC 65 nm, 6.4 mm2) runs up to 325 MHz at 1.2 V under 300 mW on data-intensive workloads.

## Problem statement

Extreme-edge IoT and TinyML need heterogeneous SoCs pairing efficient accelerators with application-class hosts that run Linux, but prior tinyML hosts use weak 32-bit managers (e.g., HyperRAM-limited HULK-V) or lack reusable DSA attachment interfaces.

## Motivation

Minimize area and energy of the Linux-capable host while maximizing resources for DSAs/PMCAs; provide low-pin-count DRAM bandwidth beyond HyperRAM without LPDDR integration cost.

## Prior art

Compares mobile/HPC heterogeneous SoCs (Raspberry Pi Zero, NVIDIA Orin, HiFive, ESP, OpenPiton BYOC), tinyML SoCs (Kraken, Vega), HULK-V HyperRAM host, HyperBus/HyperRAM academic implementations, LiteDRAM RPC PHY (FPGA-only), and transprecision DDR3 controller baseline [25].

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Open-source Linux host platform + silicon-measured RPC DRAM subsystem for heterogeneous SoC integration.

## Method / approach

**Platform (Fig. 1).** CVA6 RV64GC host, AXI4 crossbar (configurable manager/subordinate DSA ports), LLC configurable per-way as scratchpad, modular DMA, Regbus demux for simple peripherals, JTAG debug, INTC, UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO/VGA, digital D2D link, SoC control port, boot ROM (7.2 KiB with LTO).

**RPC DRAM (Figs. 2-5 in paper).** Technology-independent digital PHY + controller with NSRRP frontend; command/timing FSMs; 256-bit RPC word; AXI4 frontend with read/write buffering and 2 KiB burst splitter; ZQ cal and refresh manager.

**Neo demonstrator (Fig. 6).** 128 KiB SPM, 64b data / 48b addr, 32 KiB L1 I/D caches, 8 KiB RPC read/write buffers, on-chip FLL; no DSA ports in this chip.

## Experimental setup

- RTL simulation for RPC utilization (Fig. 8); DMA-programmed burst sweeps 8 B to 8 KiB+.
- Neo taped out TSMC 65 nm (9 metal), Synopsys DC 2019.03, Cadence Innovus 2019.10, 200 MHz target SS 125 C low-VT.
- Bring-up PCB (Fig. 7) with 32 MiB RPC DRAM (EM6GA16LBXA-12H), ATE or standalone, UART/VGA.
- Power scenarios: WFI, NOP loop, 2MM (double-precision matrix multiply with tiles in SPM), MEM (DMA write bursts).

## Results summary

- RPC bus utilization approaches peak for bursts >= 2 KiB; reads ~1.3x higher utilization than writes (Fig. 8).
- Peak throughput Theta = alpha * 800 MB/s at 200 MHz DDR on 16b DB; Gamma ~ 250 pJ/B on MEM writes (worst-case buffering).
- Area: CVA6 dominates; RPC controller <= 7.6%; crossbar grows 3.6% to 10.6% with eight DSA port pairs (Fig. 9 in paper).
- PHY/manager/FSM only 3.5 kGE (~1% of RPC block); controller 6.3% area and 33% beachfront vs 65 nm DDR3 controller [25].
- Neo: up to 325 MHz at 1.2 V, < 300 mW total on 2MM; CORE dominates power (~69% of MEM at 200 MHz); RPC IO power 45% lower than DDR3 high-load baseline [25].

## Contributions

- Minimal customizable RV64GC Linux host with AXI4 + D2D for DSA co-integration.
- First synthesizable open-source fully digital RPC DRAM interface characterized in taped-out SoC.
- Agile memory: 8-cycle 32 B RPC access path; runtime LLC-to-SPM configuration.
- Neo silicon demonstrator with measured power, bandwidth, and area data.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Open-source RPC DRAM PHY/controller at 3.5 kGE enables HyperRAM-class pin count with DDR3-level efficiency claims vs HyperBus academic baselines.
- Analysis: LLC ways selectable as SPM at runtime decouple host working set from accelerator memory domains without separate memory controllers.
- Analysis: Regbus attachment pattern reduces crossbar area for lightweight peripherals while preserving Linux driver compatibility.

## Limitations and future work

- Neo ships without integrated DSA ports; heterogeneous end-to-end not demonstrated on this chip.
- RPC interface lacks Deep Power Down; RAM idle power present in all benchmarks.
- AXI4 QoS-based transfer prioritization planned but not implemented (FCFS across IDs).
- AXI frontend buffers over-provisioned in Neo; future area reduction possible.
- Single CVA6 host only in this brief; multi-core coherent hosts noted as future integration path.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: HULK-V and Vega show PULP-class heterogeneity but lack Cheshire's reusable AXI plug-in + open RPC DRAM characterization for Linux-capable 64-bit hosts.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: DSA-attached Neo variant, chiplet D2D + Occamy-class accelerator coupling, and OS-visible DMA vs coherent accelerator sharing not evaluated.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE registry row for Cheshire/Neo: document AXI manager/subordinate counts, RPC vs LPDDR trade study rubric.
- Analysis: Co-integrate Cheshire with Snitch or Ara accelerator generators using same AXI port template for reproducible heterogeneous FPGA demos.
- Analysis: Compare Cheshire DMA offload vs CVA6 memcpy for TinyML host-accelerator staging on shared RPC DRAM.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Complete open RTL (Cheshire + rpc_dram controller) with silicon validation.
- Analysis: RPC DRAM energy/area numbers directly comparable to survey memory-interface dimension.
- Analysis: FPGA Genesys II implementation enables pre-silicon heterogeneous prototyping.

### Cons

- Analysis: 5-page brief limits software/Linux bring-up detail and DSA case studies.
- Analysis: Demonstrator lacks on-chip accelerator; heterogeneous claims are architectural not measured end-to-end.
- Analysis: TSMC 65 nm single-site results; technology scaling not explored.

## Benchmarks and tables

No numbered tables in the TCAS-II brief. Key quantitative results appear in Figs. 8-11 (RPC utilization, area breakdowns, power). Silicon headline metrics: Neo 6.4 mm2, up to 325 MHz at 1.2 V, <300 mW, RPC 750 MB/s @200 MHz, 250 pJ/B, PHY 3.5 kGE.

![Figure 11](./figures/figure_11.png)

digestSections.tl;dr:
- Cheshire is a modular RV64GC Linux-capable host SoC platform for plugging in domain-specific accelerators via configurable AXI4 ports, DMA, and optional D2D link.
- First taped-out open-source fully digital RPC DRAM interface: 22 switching IOs, 3.5 kGE PHY, 750 MB/s peak at 200 MHz, 250 pJ/B measured on silicon.
- Silicon demonstrator Neo (TSMC 65 nm, 6.4 mm2) runs up to 325 MHz at 1.2 V under 300 mW on data-intensive workloads.
digestSections.problem statement: Extreme-edge IoT and TinyML need heterogeneous SoCs pairing efficient accelerators with application-class hosts that run Linux, but prior tinyML hosts use weak 32-bit managers (e.g., HyperRAM-limited HULK-V) or lack reusable DSA attachment interfaces.
digestSections.motivation: Minimize area and energy of the Linux-capable host while maximizing resources for DSAs/PMCAs; provide low-pin-count DRAM bandwidth beyond HyperRAM without LPDDR integration cost.
digestSections.prior art: Compares mobile/HPC heterogeneous SoCs (Raspberry Pi Zero, NVIDIA Orin, HiFive, ESP, OpenPiton BYOC), tinyML SoCs (Kraken, Vega), HULK-V HyperRAM host, HyperBus/HyperRAM academic implementations, LiteDRAM RPC PHY (FPGA-only), and transprecision DDR3 controller baseline [25].
digestSections.category of work:
Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Open-source Linux host platform + silicon-measured RPC DRAM subsystem for heterogeneous SoC integration.
digestSections.method / approach:
**Platform (Fig. 1).** CVA6 RV64GC host, AXI4 crossbar (configurable manager/subordinate DSA ports), LLC configurable per-way as scratchpad, modular DMA, Regbus demux for simple peripherals, JTAG debug, INTC, UART/SPI/I2C/GPIO/VGA, digital D2D link, SoC control port, boot ROM (7.2 KiB with LTO).

**RPC DRAM (Figs. 2-5 in paper).** Technology-independent digital PHY + controller with NSRRP frontend; command/timing FSMs; 256-bit RPC word; AXI4 frontend with read/write buffering and 2 KiB burst splitter; ZQ cal and refresh manager.

**Neo demonstrator (Fig. 6).** 128 KiB SPM, 64b data / 48b addr, 32 KiB L1 I/D caches, 8 KiB RPC read/write buffers, on-chip FLL; no DSA ports in this chip.
digestSections.experimental setup:
- RTL simulation for RPC utilization (Fig. 8); DMA-programmed burst sweeps 8 B to 8 KiB+.
- Neo taped out TSMC 65 nm (9 metal), Synopsys DC 2019.03, Cadence Innovus 2019.10, 200 MHz target SS 125 C low-VT.
- Bring-up PCB (Fig. 7) with 32 MiB RPC DRAM (EM6GA16LBXA-12H), ATE or standalone, UART/VGA.
- Power scenarios: WFI, NOP loop, 2MM (double-precision matrix multiply with tiles in SPM), MEM (DMA write bursts).
digestSections.results summary:
- RPC bus utilization approaches peak for bursts >= 2 KiB; reads ~1.3x higher utilization than writes (Fig. 8).
- Peak throughput Theta = alpha * 800 MB/s at 200 MHz DDR on 16b DB; Gamma ~ 250 pJ/B on MEM writes (worst-case buffering).
- Area: CVA6 dominates; RPC controller <= 7.6%; crossbar grows 3.6% to 10.6% with eight DSA port pairs (Fig. 9 in paper).
- PHY/manager/FSM only 3.5 kGE (~1% of RPC block); controller 6.3% area and 33% beachfront vs 65 nm DDR3 controller [25].
- Neo: up to 325 MHz at 1.2 V, < 300 mW total on 2MM; CORE dominates power (~69% of MEM at 200 MHz); RPC IO power 45% lower than DDR3 high-load baseline [25].
digestSections.contributions:
- Minimal customizable RV64GC Linux host with AXI4 + D2D for DSA co-integration.
- First synthesizable open-source fully digital RPC DRAM interface characterized in taped-out SoC.
- Agile memory: 8-cycle 32 B RPC access path; runtime LLC-to-SPM configuration.
- Neo silicon demonstrator with measured power, bandwidth, and area data.
digestSections.innovations:
- Analysis: Open-source RPC DRAM PHY/controller at 3.5 kGE enables HyperRAM-class pin count with DDR3-level efficiency claims vs HyperBus academic baselines.
- Analysis: LLC ways selectable as SPM at runtime decouple host working set from accelerator memory domains without separate memory controllers.
- Analysis: Regbus attachment pattern reduces crossbar area for lightweight peripherals while preserving Linux driver compatibility.
digestSections.limitations and future work:
- Neo ships without integrated DSA ports; heterogeneous end-to-end not demonstrated on this chip.
- RPC interface lacks Deep Power Down; RAM idle power present in all benchmarks.
- AXI4 QoS-based transfer prioritization planned but not implemented (FCFS across IDs).
- AXI frontend buffers over-provisioned in Neo; future area reduction possible.
- Single CVA6 host only in this brief; multi-core coherent hosts noted as future integration path.
digestSections.research opportunity:
**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: HULK-V and Vega show PULP-class heterogeneity but lack Cheshire's reusable AXI plug-in + open RPC DRAM characterization for Linux-capable 64-bit hosts.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: DSA-attached Neo variant, chiplet D2D + Occamy-class accelerator coupling, and OS-visible DMA vs coherent accelerator sharing not evaluated.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE registry row for Cheshire/Neo: document AXI manager/subordinate counts, RPC vs LPDDR trade study rubric.
- Analysis: Co-integrate Cheshire with Snitch or Ara accelerator generators using same AXI port template for reproducible heterogeneous FPGA demos.
- Analysis: Compare Cheshire DMA offload vs CVA6 memcpy for TinyML host-accelerator staging on shared RPC DRAM.
digestSections.pros and cons:
### Pros

- Analysis: Complete open RTL (Cheshire + rpc_dram controller) with silicon validation.
- Analysis: RPC DRAM energy/area numbers directly comparable to survey memory-interface dimension.
- Analysis: FPGA Genesys II implementation enables pre-silicon heterogeneous prototyping.

### Cons

- Analysis: 5-page brief limits software/Linux bring-up detail and DSA case studies.
- Analysis: Demonstrator lacks on-chip accelerator; heterogeneous claims are architectural not measured end-to-end.
- Analysis: TSMC 65 nm single-site results; technology scaling not explored.
digestSections.benchmarks and tables: No numbered tables in the TCAS-II brief. Key quantitative results appear in Figs. 8-11 (RPC utilization, area breakdowns, power). Silicon headline metrics: Neo 6.4 mm2, up to 325 MHz at 1.2 V, <300 mW, RPC 750 MB/s @200 MHz, 250 pJ/B, PHY 3.5 kGE.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Basilisk: A 34 mm² End-to-End Open-Source 64-bit Linux-Capable RISC-V SoC in 130nm BiCMOS

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Philippe Sauter; Thomas Benz; Paul Scheffler; Martin Povišer; Frank K. Gürkaynak; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich; University of Bologna |
| Venue | arXiv preprint |
| Venue type | preprint |
| Year | 2025 |
| Volume / issue / pages | 2 pages |
| Paper DOI | Not assigned (preprint) |
| arXiv | arXiv:2505.10060v1 [cs.AR], 15 May 2025 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/cheshire-ihp130-o |
| Keywords | Open-source EDA, Linux-capable SoC, RISC-V, silicon measurements |
| Open access | Yes |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- Reports first silicon of Basilisk, the largest claimed end-to-end open-source SoC (~2.7 MGE, 34 mm² in IHP130).
- 64-bit RV64GC Linux host with HyperRAM, USB 1.1, VGA, and 62 Mb/s C2C link; open Yosys-Slang frontend and tuned ORFS flow.
- Post-synthesis: 77 MHz, 1.1 MGE std cells; fabricated chip runs 62 MHz @ 1.2 V and 102 MHz @ 1.64 V.
- FP64 GEMM peak energy efficiency 18.9 MFLOP/s/W at 0.88 V; Table I shows 4.8x larger std-cell complexity vs next open 130 nm design.
- Die area reduced 12% (39 to 34 mm²) via OpenROAD tuning; complexity-normalized flow runtime competitive with smaller open chips.

## Problem statement

End-to-end open-source EDA (OSEDA) has proven viable on small designs but not yet on industry-grade Linux-capable SoCs. Closing the QoR and silicon-validation gap for multi-MGE open flows is necessary to make open silicon credible for application-class workloads.

## Motivation

Chips Acts and supply-chain diversification push more designers toward reproducible, auditable flows. Basilisk silicon data test whether recent Yosys/OpenROAD improvements (also described in arXiv:2406.15107) survive fabrication and measurement.

## Prior art

Open 130 nm tapeouts include HEP, Ghazi, Ibtida, GreenRio, and MLEM -- mostly microcontrollers on SKY130 or IHP130. Cheshire/CVA6 provide the open host platform. Prior Basilisk flow paper focused on QoR; this work adds silicon, shmoo, and cross-chip comparison.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`
Note: Silicon bring-up and benchmarking of an end-to-end OSEDA Linux-capable SoC.

## Method / approach

Same Cheshire/CVA6 architecture as the flow paper with updated specs: 124 MB/s HyperRAM, 473 MB/s LLC, four-way 16 KiB L1 caches, 12 Mb/s USB 1.1, 62 Mb/s C2C. Implementation uses Yosys-Slang SV frontend, MUX/LMS synthesis tuning, and ORFS placement/routing tweaks (routing blockages near power straps, congestion-aware global settings).

Silicon validation uses a custom evaluation board, DUTCTL orchestration, and 48x48 FP64 GEMM sweeps over voltage/frequency (Shmoo, Fig. 3).

## Experimental setup

- Fabrication: IHP SG13G2 open 130 nm BiCMOS; 34.4 mm² die, 1140 kGE std cells (2700 kGE chip complexity reported).
- Measurement: 25 C ambient; core voltage 0.84-1.64 V; frequency sweep; FP64 GEMM energy efficiency annotation on Fig. 3.
- Comparison: Table I vs MLEM, HEP, Ghazi, Ibtida, GreenRio on area, complexity, synthesis/impl time, PDK, application-class flag.

## Results summary

Silicon reaches 62 MHz at nominal 1.2 V (51 logic levels) and 102 MHz at 1.64 V. Peak FP64 GEMM efficiency 18.9 MFLOP/s/W at 0.88 V / 10 MHz. Average leakage 437 uW across ten packaged parts. Normalized synthesis 110 min/MGE and P&R 21 h/MGE beat GreenRio; only MLEM (flow reuse) is faster. Basilisk is the sole application-class entry in Table I with 4.8x std-cell complexity vs next largest.

## Contributions

- First silicon characterization of a multi-MGE end-to-end open Linux-capable SoC.
- Quantified open-flow QoR (1.6x area, 2.3x timing) with measured clock and energy efficiency.
- Table I positioning against open 130 nm peers on complexity, speed, and normalized EDA runtime.
- Evidence that tuned OSEDA flow ports to MLEM microcontroller with best normalized runtime.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Bridges prior QoR-only Basilisk flow paper with packaged-chip measurements and board infrastructure.
- Analysis: Technology-normalized 51 LL vs 46 LL for commercial Cheshire-based design cited as competitive implementation depth.

## Limitations and future work

2-page format limits architectural and flow detail (see companion flow paper). Fig. 4-5 die/board photos not auto-extracted in Pass 0. Some Table I cells are marked unavailable for third-party designs. Ultra-low-voltage efficiency measured on GEMM microbenchmark, not full Linux workload.

## Research opportunity

- Analysis: Publish Linux boot time and peripheral driver validation alongside GEMM shmoo for system-level energy stories.
- Analysis: Correlate open-flow DRC/congestion fixes with on-die hotspot IR-drop measurements on the evaluation board.
- Analysis: Extend Table I as living benchmark for open 130 nm application-class vs MCU tapeouts in the corpus.
- Analysis: Integrate silicon RoT (OpenTitan blocks) and re-measure security-overhead vs efficiency.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Rare measured silicon proof point for OSEDA at Linux-capable scale.
- Clear Table I showing complexity leadership among open 130 nm chips.
- Documents portable flow benefits via MLEM reuse and normalized runtime metrics.

### Cons

- Very compressed publication; relies on external flow paper for methodology depth.
- Peak 102 MHz still modest for application processors; efficiency metric is kernel-specific.
- Analysis: capture_tables.py failed on Table I -- manual transcription required.

## Benchmarks and tables

### Table I: Comparison to other open 130 nm designs implemented with open flows.

Source page 2.  
Clip: [PNG](./tables/table_i.png) | Draft: [table_i.md](./tables/table_i.md) (manual transcription)

digestSections.tl;dr:
- Reports first silicon of Basilisk, the largest claimed end-to-end open-source SoC (~2.7 MGE, 34 mm² in IHP130).
- 64-bit RV64GC Linux host with HyperRAM, USB 1.1, VGA, and 62 Mb/s C2C link; open Yosys-Slang frontend and tuned ORFS flow.
- Post-synthesis: 77 MHz, 1.1 MGE std cells; fabricated chip runs 62 MHz @ 1.2 V and 102 MHz @ 1.64 V.
- FP64 GEMM peak energy efficiency 18.9 MFLOP/s/W at 0.88 V; Table I shows 4.8x larger std-cell complexity vs next open 130 nm design.
- Die area reduced 12% (39 to 34 mm²) via OpenROAD tuning; complexity-normalized flow runtime competitive with smaller open chips.
digestSections.problem statement: End-to-end open-source EDA (OSEDA) has proven viable on small designs but not yet on industry-grade Linux-capable SoCs. Closing the QoR and silicon-validation gap for multi-MGE open flows is necessary to make open silicon credible for application-class workloads.
digestSections.motivation: Chips Acts and supply-chain diversification push more designers toward reproducible, auditable flows. Basilisk silicon data test whether recent Yosys/OpenROAD improvements (also described in arXiv:2406.15107) survive fabrication and measurement.
digestSections.prior art: Open 130 nm tapeouts include HEP, Ghazi, Ibtida, GreenRio, and MLEM -- mostly microcontrollers on SKY130 or IHP130. Cheshire/CVA6 provide the open host platform. Prior Basilisk flow paper focused on QoR; this work adds silicon, shmoo, and cross-chip comparison.
digestSections.category of work:
Primary: `system-architecture`
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`
Note: Silicon bring-up and benchmarking of an end-to-end OSEDA Linux-capable SoC.
digestSections.method / approach:
Same Cheshire/CVA6 architecture as the flow paper with updated specs: 124 MB/s HyperRAM, 473 MB/s LLC, four-way 16 KiB L1 caches, 12 Mb/s USB 1.1, 62 Mb/s C2C. Implementation uses Yosys-Slang SV frontend, MUX/LMS synthesis tuning, and ORFS placement/routing tweaks (routing blockages near power straps, congestion-aware global settings).

Silicon validation uses a custom evaluation board, DUTCTL orchestration, and 48x48 FP64 GEMM sweeps over voltage/frequency (Shmoo, Fig. 3).
digestSections.experimental setup:
- Fabrication: IHP SG13G2 open 130 nm BiCMOS; 34.4 mm² die, 1140 kGE std cells (2700 kGE chip complexity reported).
- Measurement: 25 C ambient; core voltage 0.84-1.64 V; frequency sweep; FP64 GEMM energy efficiency annotation on Fig. 3.
- Comparison: Table I vs MLEM, HEP, Ghazi, Ibtida, GreenRio on area, complexity, synthesis/impl time, PDK, application-class flag.
digestSections.results summary: Silicon reaches 62 MHz at nominal 1.2 V (51 logic levels) and 102 MHz at 1.64 V. Peak FP64 GEMM efficiency 18.9 MFLOP/s/W at 0.88 V / 10 MHz. Average leakage 437 uW across ten packaged parts. Normalized synthesis 110 min/MGE and P&R 21 h/MGE beat GreenRio; only MLEM (flow reuse) is faster. Basilisk is the sole application-class entry in Table I with 4.8x std-cell complexity vs next largest.
digestSections.contributions:
- First silicon characterization of a multi-MGE end-to-end open Linux-capable SoC.
- Quantified open-flow QoR (1.6x area, 2.3x timing) with measured clock and energy efficiency.
- Table I positioning against open 130 nm peers on complexity, speed, and normalized EDA runtime.
- Evidence that tuned OSEDA flow ports to MLEM microcontroller with best normalized runtime.
digestSections.innovations:
- Analysis: Bridges prior QoR-only Basilisk flow paper with packaged-chip measurements and board infrastructure.
- Analysis: Technology-normalized 51 LL vs 46 LL for commercial Cheshire-based design cited as competitive implementation depth.
digestSections.limitations and future work: 2-page format limits architectural and flow detail (see companion flow paper). Fig. 4-5 die/board photos not auto-extracted in Pass 0. Some Table I cells are marked unavailable for third-party designs. Ultra-low-voltage efficiency measured on GEMM microbenchmark, not full Linux workload.
digestSections.research opportunity:
- Analysis: Publish Linux boot time and peripheral driver validation alongside GEMM shmoo for system-level energy stories.
- Analysis: Correlate open-flow DRC/congestion fixes with on-die hotspot IR-drop measurements on the evaluation board.
- Analysis: Extend Table I as living benchmark for open 130 nm application-class vs MCU tapeouts in the corpus.
- Analysis: Integrate silicon RoT (OpenTitan blocks) and re-measure security-overhead vs efficiency.
digestSections.pros and cons:
### Pros

- Rare measured silicon proof point for OSEDA at Linux-capable scale.
- Clear Table I showing complexity leadership among open 130 nm chips.
- Documents portable flow benefits via MLEM reuse and normalized runtime metrics.

### Cons

- Very compressed publication; relies on external flow paper for methodology depth.
- Peak 102 MHz still modest for application processors; efficiency metric is kernel-specific.
- Analysis: capture_tables.py failed on Table I -- manual transcription required.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# CHIMERA: A Flexible and Scalable 3.1 TOPS/W AI-MCU with Transformer Accelerator and 563 Gb/s Shared-L2 Memory Subsystem with QoS Guarantees

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Lorenzo Leone; Philip Wiese; Gamze Islamoglu; Michael Rogenmoser; Davide Rossi; Francesco Conti; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich; University of Bologna; Chips-IT |
| Venue | arXiv preprint |
| Venue type | preprint |
| Year | 2026 |
| Paper DOI | not found |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02358 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/chimera |
| Keywords | AI-MCU, transformer accelerator, shared L2, QoS, TinyML |
| Open access | arXiv + open RTL release tag CONVOLVE-TO |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- Chimera is a 22 nm FDX AI-MCU with nine RV32IMA cores plus a transformer acceleration cluster (TAC), shared L2 memory island (563 Gb/s), and QoS-aware L2 for latency-critical traffic.
- Peak 3.1 TOPS/W and 281 GOPS/mm²; up to 16× latency reduction vs conventional L2 under contention; 34-cycle worst-case L2 access.
- Targets ultra-low-power edge transformer inference with multi-cluster scalability.

## Problem statement

TinyML AI-MCUs must run evolving attention-based models under hundred-of-mW budgets while scaling L2 bandwidth and guaranteeing worst-case latency for host/cluster control traffic.

## Motivation

Single-cluster shared-L1 designs do not scale to multi-cluster TinyML; Chimera co-designs TAC, high-bandwidth L2 island, and QoS isolation for heterogeneous workloads.

## Prior art

PULP/OpenHW clusters; attention accelerators; multi-cluster L2 bandwidth studies; QoS memory architectures for embedded AI.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`, `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture Chimera.

## Method / approach

**Innovation A — TAC (Fig. 2b).** Transformer accelerator with 16 PEs, 64-way dot products, double-buffered weights, on-the-fly softmax, ReLU/GeLU activation unit; tightly coupled to RV32IMA cluster via TCDM.

**Innovation B — L2 island (Fig. 2a).** 256 KiB L2 memory island; 563 Gbit/s peak; logarithmic low-latency interconnect; multi-cluster shared workspace support.

**Innovation C — QoS L2.** Latency-critical host/cluster control traffic isolated from bulk DMA; 34-cycle WCET; up to 16× latency reduction vs baseline.

**SoC integration.** Host domain (boot ROM, peripherals, debug); cluster domains with clock gating and AXI CDC; HyperBus external memory path.

## Experimental setup

- Technology: 22 nm FDX (GlobalFoundries).
- Silicon implementation and post-layout characterization (per paper).
- Transformer and multi-cluster workload scheduling experiments.

## Results summary

- 3.1 TOPS/W peak energy efficiency; 281 GOPS/mm² area efficiency.
- 1.37× higher energy efficiency vs SoA SoCs; up to 100× area efficiency vs some SoA platforms.
- 563 Gb/s aggregate L2 bandwidth; QoS reduces latency up to 16×.
- Comparable energy efficiency to standalone accelerators with up to 1.8× area efficiency.

## Contributions

- End-to-end AI-MCU combining programmable RV32 cluster, TAC, and QoS L2 for transformers at the edge.
- Open-source Chimera release (GitHub tag CONVOLVE-TO).
- Measured efficiency leadership vs published SoA AI-MCUs/accelerators.

## Innovations

- Co-designed TAC + shared-L2 island + QoS for multi-cluster TinyML under strict power/area envelopes.

## Limitations and future work

- arXiv preprint (2026 listing in PDF); long-form journal metrics may evolve.
- Benchmark suite focused on transformer-class kernels; broader OS/host integration not emphasized in brief.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Few open AI-MCUs publish QoS L2 WCET alongside TOPS/W at sub-W scale.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Multi-die Chimera scaling, formal WCET proofs, and SCORE cross-benchmarks with MemPool/Snitch remain open.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Compare Chimera L2 QoS policies against Carfield/Cheshire host domains in SCORE MCS surveys.
- Analysis: Map TAC programming model to upstream transformer operator churn (Fig. 1a trend).

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Strong SCORE Track A primary for PULP AI-MCU with silicon-class metrics.
- Analysis: Clear three-pillar architecture story (TAC, bandwidth, QoS).

### Cons

- Analysis: Preprint without stable DOI at digest time.
- Analysis: Multi-cluster evaluation complexity may limit reproducibility without released RTL snapshot parity.

## Benchmarks and tables

### Table I: Comparison with State-of-the-Art (SoA)

*Page 4. Chimera vs transformer accelerators and AI-MCUs (Ayaka, EVA, TinyVers, etc.). Key row: Chimera 22 nm, 3.19 mm², 550 MHz, 896 GOPS peak @ 600 mW, GP-host/prog-accel ✓/✓, L2 aggregate bandwidth 563 Gb/s.*

### Table II: Full network evaluation derived from silicon measurements

*Page 4. Energy per inference on transformer workloads from silicon-derived network evaluation (values in extracted text).*

## Figures

![Figure 1](./figures/figure_01.png)

### Figure 2: Chimera SoC and TAC architecture

![Figure 2](./figures/figure_02.png)

# Croc: An End-to-End Open-Source Extensible RISC-V MCU Platform to Democratize Silicon

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Phillippe Sauter; Thomas Benz; Paul Scheffler; Hannah Pochert; Luisa Wüthrich; Martin Povišer; Beat Muheim; Frank K. Gürkaynak; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich (Integrated Systems Laboratory); University of Bologna |
| Venue | RISC-V Summit Europe 2025 (Paris); arXiv preprint |
| Venue type | conference + preprint |
| Year | 2025 |
| Paper DOI | not found |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05090 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/croc |
| Keywords | RISC-V MCU, open-source EDA, education, silicon democratization, IHP 130 nm |
| Open access | arXiv + Creative Commons teaching materials |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Corresponding: phsauter@iis.ee.ethz.ch. Funding: SwissChips Initiative; German BMBF FMD-QNC (16ME0831).

## TL;DR

- Croc is a minimal extensible open-source RISC-V MCU platform (CVE2/Ibex-based) for hands-on VLSI teaching and innovation with a documented Yosys/OpenROAD/IHP 130 nm flow.
- MLEM demonstrator tapeout (Nov 2024) by two bachelor students in eight weeks: 5 mm2, 350 kGE, 80 MHz @ 1.2 V, NeoPixel + UART extensions.
- ETH VLSI2 course (spring 2025) adopts Croc for up to 80 students, 40 ASIC layouts, and five student SoC tapeouts.

## Problem statement

Chips Acts aim to grow the VLSI talent pipeline, but most university courses teach theory or FPGA emulation without end-to-end access to PDKs, EDA tools, and silicon-proven RTL needed for real ASIC design.

## Motivation

Provide a production-ready, industry-aligned MCU platform small enough for students to implement fully on open 130 nm PDKs, lowering the barrier from classroom to tapeout and commercial RISC-V MCU products.

## Prior art

Edu4Chip / Didactic-SoC (Kactus2, IP-XACT, no synthesis flow); Basilisk/IWLS 2024 open EDA flow; Ibex/CVE2 cores; IHP open PDK; IIC-OSIC-TOOLS container; FPGA verification on Digilent Genesys 2.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: SCORE architecture CROC.

## Method / approach

**Croc domain (Fig. 1a).** OpenHW CVE2 RV32I(EMC) core, OBI crossbar, tightly coupled I/D SRAM banks (1 IPC ideal), GPIO/UART/timer/debug, single-cycle interconnect.

**User domain.** Loosely coupled port for student accelerators, peripherals, or experimental RV cores.

**EDA flow.** Yosys with yosys-slang SV frontend; OpenROAD backend; Verilator simulation; IIC-OSIC-TOOLS Docker; optional Genesys 2 FPGA flow.

**MLEM extension.** Optimized UART + NeoPixel controller in user domain; full physical design by two students.

## Experimental setup

- Target: IHP SG13G2 open 130 nm PDK via IIC-OSIC-TOOLS.
- MLEM: 5 mm2 die, 350 kGE, 56% global density; 48 IO pads (12 Croc, 36 user: NeoPixel/UART/26 GPIO).
- Implementation on 6th-gen Intel Core i7: under 1 h runtime, under 8 GiB RAM.
- Spring 2025 VLSI2 course scale: 80 students, 40 layouts, up to 5 tapeouts planned.

## Results summary

- MLEM taped out successfully in eight weeks validating Croc flow viability.
- 80 MHz top clock (58 logic levels) at 1.2 V typical conditions.
- Teaching materials and exercises released under Creative Commons (vlsi.ethz.ch).
- Platform uses silicon-proven SV IPs from commercial/industry-supported repos vs generated Didactic-SoC code.

## Contributions

- Education-focused extensible ASIC platform with minimal production-ready RISC-V MCU.
- Streamlined documented OS synthesis/implementation flow (yosys-slang + OpenROAD).
- Successful IHP 130 nm MLEM demonstrator tapeout proving educational end-to-end path.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Bridges Edu4Chip-scale cohort teaching with a complete tapeout-proven EDA pipeline on industry CVE2 RTL.
- Analysis: User/Croc domain split lets students modify interconnect or ISA extensions while keeping a debuggable known-good MCU core.
- Analysis: MLEM shows two-student team can close PD in eight weeks on laptop-class hardware.

## Limitations and future work

- Two-page summit abstract; limited silicon measurement data in this document (MLEM bring-up ongoing at writing).
- Focused on MCU scale, not Linux-capable host SoCs (contrast Basilisk/Cheshire).
- Course outcomes (2025 tapeout yield) reported as plans, not completed results in this PDF.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Didactic-SoC lacks synthesis/implementation flow; Basilisk targets multi-million-gate Linux SoCs beyond single-student MCU scope.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Security-focused Croc variants, multi-project wafer automation, and formal equivalence between FPGA and ASIC flows not evaluated.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE CROC row vs Cheshire/Basilisk for teaching ladder (MCU -> host SoC).
- Analysis: Template user-domain plugins (crypto, tinyML) with shared Croc verification harness.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Strong SCORE entry for open educational MCU platform with proven 130 nm tapeout.
- Analysis: Single-repo RTL + software + docs lowers onboarding vs multi-tool generated platforms.

### Cons

- Analysis: Short conference paper; limited PPA characterization vs research silicon briefs.
- Analysis: IHP 130 nm node differs from advanced FDX/FinFET PULP research chips.

## Benchmarks and tables

No numbered tables or auto-detected figure captions in audit manifest (`figure_caption_count: 0`; PDF uses "Figure 1:" colon style on page 2). Key metrics summarized in Results; Fig. 1 embed below.

## Figures

### Figure 1: (a) Architecture Croc, (b) MLEM's layout.

![Figure 1](./figures/figure_01.png)

## Reproducibility

|----------|----------------|
| RTL + flow | https://github.com/pulp-platform/croc |
| yosys-slang | https://github.com/povik/yosys-slang |
| PDK/tools | IHP SG13G2 + IIC-OSIC-TOOLS |
| MLEM gallery | https://asic.ethz.ch/2024/MLEM.html |
| Course material | https://vlsi.ethz.ch (CC license) |

## References

2. H.R.4346 CHIPS and Science Act. URL: congress.gov -- `[unresolved]`
3. India semiconductor investment news. URL: spectrum.ieee.org -- `[unresolved]`

# The Cost of Application-Class Processing: Energy and Performance Analysis of a Linux-ready 1.7GHz 64bit RISC-V Core in 22nm FDSOI Technology

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Florian Zaruba; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich |
| Venue | IEEE Transactions on Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) Systems (IEEE-style author manuscript on arXiv) |
| Venue type | journal preprint |
| Year | 2019 |
| Volume / issue / pages | IEEE TVLSI 27(11):2629-2640 (published); arXiv:1904.05442v1 (this PDF) |
| Paper DOI | [10.1109/TVLSI.2019.2926114](https://doi.org/10.1109/TVLSI.2019.2926114) |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.05442 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/ariane (now CVA6 / OpenHW) |
| Keywords | RISC-V, application-class, Linux, energy breakdown, 22FDX |
| Open access | arXiv manuscript |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

SCORE maps this core to **CVA6**. Primary architecture paper for the Ariane/CVA6 lineage.

## TL;DR

- Ariane is a 6-stage single-issue in-order RV64GC Linux-capable core, taped out in GF 22FDX; silicon up to 1.7 GHz and up to 40 Gop/sW.
- Energy breakdown (silicon-calibrated post-layout) shows caches/translation dominate; actual ALU compute can be <1% of instruction energy on mixed code.
- Open-sourced (GitHub ariane/CVA6); compared to on-die MCU-class core and literature application-class RISC-V.

## Problem statement

Linux-capable RISC-V cores were scarce relative to MCU cores; the energy cost of TLB/PTW, caches, privileged modes, and atomics versus MCU-class RISC-V was not quantified on silicon.

## Motivation

Build a competitive in-order 64-bit application-class core, tape out in 22 nm, and attribute energy per ISA/microarchitectural feature to guide heterogeneous SoCs.

## Prior art

Open MCU cores (PULP, PicoRV32); BOOM/Rocket application class; ARM-class Linux cores; Mr. Wolf / Quentin on same 22FDX family.

## Category of work

Primary: `circuit-design`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: Foundational CVA6/Ariane silicon energy study.

## Method / approach

**Microarchitecture.** Six handshake-coupled stages; scoreboard around execute; branch prediction with light predecode; hardware PTW + TLBs; 6 FUs including IEEE FPU; RISC-V debug.

**Silicon.** Ariane coreplex separately supplyable; 16 kB I-cache in taped-out instance (paper); on-die small RISC-V core for comparison.

**Analysis.** Static binary characterization (Table I); post-layout power per unit; FBB/voltage sweeps.

## Experimental setup

- GF 22 FDX tapeout; frequency from ~220 MHz (min SRAM-limited ~0.5 V) to 1.7 GHz.
- Mixed instruction power (Fig. 3); energy per op class (Table III); 16-bit 5x5 conv (Table IV).
- DMIPS: up to 1.65 DMIPS/MHz.

## Results summary

- 1.7 GHz, 40 Gop/sW peak efficiency.
- Caches account for up to 27% of instruction energy; compute FU share <1% on mixed workload cited.
- RF/scoreboard overheads quantified (e.g., ~12 kGE / 5.7% RF related in one comparison).
- vs 32-bit MCU on same die: MCU much lower pJ/op; Ariane pays for OS support and 64-bit caches.
- vs 40 nm 10 pJ class small core scaled to 22 nm vs Ariane 51.8 pJ in authors' comparison.
- Open-source release Feb 2019 with Linux image.

## Contributions

- Ariane RV64GC implementation and 22 nm silicon.
- Per-unit energy/PPA analysis of application-class features.
- Open RTL + Linux bring-up artifacts.

## Innovations

- Analysis: First detailed silicon-calibrated energy split of Linux-ready RISC-V application-class vs MCU-class on the same 22FDX SoC story.
- Analysis: Argues ISA extensions (packed SIMD) beat deeper OoO for compute efficiency on this in-order baseline.

## Limitations and future work

- arXiv v1 manuscript (April 2019); published TVLSI pagination 27(11).
- In-order only; CVA6 later gained virtualization (separate 2023 TVLSI paper the user also downloaded).
- Fig. 1-2 architecture diagrams not in Pass 0 unique figure list (detector found Figs 3-6 only).

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Quantifies OS-support tax that SCORE Linux SoCs (Cheshire, Occamy host) inherit from CVA6.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Multicore/coherence, hypervisor, and 12 nm Occamy-class integration not in this 2019 study.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Use Table III energy classes as CVA6 baseline in survey core tables next to Ibex/Zero-riscy MCU numbers.
- Analysis: Cite Cheshire Neo as CVA6-in-SoC silicon follow-on.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Direct silicon + open RTL for the SCORE CVA6 row.
- Analysis: Energy breakdown is more useful than peak GHz alone.

### Cons

- Analysis: 2019 in-order snapshot; OpenHW CVA6 has since evolved.
- Analysis: Mixed-workload energy depends on benchmark mix (Table I static analysis).

## Benchmarks and tables

### Table I: RISC-V static binary analysis

*Page 2. Instruction-class mix used to motivate energy attribution.*

### Table II: Architectural design choices for silicon implementation

*Page 5. Cache/TLB/pipeline parameters of the taped-out instance.*

### Table III: Energy per operation class [pJ], leakage [mW]

digestSections.tl;dr:
- Ariane is a 6-stage single-issue in-order RV64GC Linux-capable core, taped out in GF 22FDX; silicon up to 1.7 GHz and up to 40 Gop/sW.

digestSections.problem statement: Linux-capable RISC-V cores were scarce relative to MCU cores; the energy cost of TLB/PTW, caches, privileged modes, and atomics versus MCU-class RISC-V was not quantified on silicon.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Gemmini: Enabling Systematic Deep-Learning Architecture Evaluation via Full-Stack Integration

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Hasan Genc, Seah Kim, Alon Amid, Ameer Haj-Ali, Vighnesh Iyer, Pranav Prakash, Jerry Zhao, Daniel Grubb, Harrison Liew, Howard Mao, Albert Ou, Colin Schmidt, Samuel Steffl, John Wright, Ion Stoica, Jonathan Ragan-Kelley, Krste Asanovic, Borivoje Nikolic, Yakun Sophia Shao |
| Affiliations | UC Berkeley; MIT (Ragan-Kelley) |
| Venue | arXiv preprint (v3 posted 9 Jul 2021) |
| Venue type | preprint |
| Year | 2021 (arXiv v3); original submission 2019 |
| Volume / issue / pages | arXiv:1911.09925v3 |
| Paper DOI | |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.09925 |
| URL | https://github.com/ucb-bar/gemmini |
| Keywords | DNN accelerator generator, full-stack, RISC-V, Chipyard, FireSim, systolic array, virtual memory, SoC integration |
| Open access | arXiv + open-source generator |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Corresponding email: hngenc@berkeley.edu. Funding: DARPA RTML FA8650-20-2-7006.

## TL;DR

- Gemmini is an open-source full-stack generator producing configurable DNN accelerators plus software and Linux-capable SoC integration in the RISC-V/Chipyard ecosystem.
- Hardware template: two-level spatial array (systolic or vector MAC trees), scratchpad/accumulator SRAMs, DMA/TLB, optional im2col/pooling/ReLU peripherals; RoCC-attached to host CPU.
- Unlike prior generators focused on standalone accelerators, Gemmini supports ONNX push-button flow, C APIs, virtual memory without special drivers, and multi-core/multi-accelerator Chipyard SoCs evaluated on FireSim.
- Evaluated on ResNet50, AlexNet, SqueezeNet, MobileNetV2, BERT with Rocket/BOOM hosts; up to 2670x speedup vs in-order Rocket on ResNet50 with on-chip im2col.
- Case studies: private vs shared TLB sizing with filter registers; scratchpad vs L2 partitioning for single- vs dual-core ResNet50 (BigL2 +8% dual-core).

## Problem statement

DNN accelerator research often evaluates accelerators in isolation, missing SoC resource contention, OS overheads, programming-stack inefficiencies, and host-accelerator partitioning effects that dominate real deployments (industry reports cite up to 77% time on CPU even with accelerators). Existing hardware generators (VTA, MAGNet, PolySA, etc.) emphasize accelerator RTL but lack flexible spatial templates, multi-level software, virtual memory, and full Linux SoC integration needed for systematic cross-stack architecture evaluation.

## Motivation

Deep learning drives demand for specialized accelerators from edge to cloud, but designing and validating them with realistic software stacks is expensive. Parameterized generators improve productivity, yet comparing systolic vs vector arrays, dataflows, host CPU choices, TLB schemes, and shared-cache partitioning requires a platform that boots Linux, runs FireSim cycle-exact full-system simulation, and synthesizes ASIC instances. Gemmini targets co-design of accelerator microarchitecture, system memory hierarchy, and translation hardware with measurable end-to-end DNN workload impact.

## Prior art

Compares accelerator generators and platforms in Table I vs NVDLA, VTA, PolySA, DNNBuilder, MAGNet, DNNWeaver, MAERI. Related DNN accelerators include TPU/systolic, NVDLA vector, Eyeriss v2, ShiDianNao, ScaleDeep, Brainwave, sparsity and in-memory designs. Software stacks: TVM (VTA), Caffe-centric flows, custom compilers. System integration prior work: Chipyard [26], FireSim [27], NeuMMU [28] and Cong et al. [29] on accelerator address translation. Industry holistic ML system papers from Facebook/HPCA cited for CPU-side overhead motivation.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Full-stack open DNN accelerator generator with SoC/Linux integration for ML architecture research, not a single fixed ASIC.

## Method / approach

**Architectural template (Fig. 1).** RoCC-attached accelerator with DMA engine, local TLB, banked scratchpad SRAM, transposer, two-level spatial array, accumulator SRAM, bitshift/ReLU, dependency management, optional matrix-scalar multiplier, pooling engine, im2col block; RoCC PTW path for page walks.

**Two-level spatial array (Figs. 2-3).** Tiles of combinational PE MAC arrays connected by pipeline registers between tiles; configurable weight- or output-stationary dataflow per PE. Supports TPU-like pipelined systolic meshes and NVDLA-like combinational vector reduction trees. Synthesis example (256 PEs): systolic 1.89 GHz max vs vector 0.69 GHz; systolic 1.8x area and 3.0x power vs vector at 500 MHz (120K vs 67K um2).

**Programming support.** High-level ONNX push-button flow mapping kernels to accelerator; low-level C/C++ APIs with per-configuration generated header (array dimensions, dataflows, optional blocks). Runtime tile-size heuristics for DRAM/L2/scratchpad staging; manual tile override available. Virtual memory in RTL enables TLB profiling (Fig. 4 miss rates 20-30% on DNN tiles vs CPU benchmarks).

**System integration (Chipyard).** Configurable Rocket in-order to BOOM OoO hosts; multi-CPU/multi-accelerator; shared L2 and bus widths; Fig. 5 dual-core dual-Gemmini example. Full Linux stack exposed non-deterministic deadlock and permission bugs not seen baremetal.

**Evaluation flow.** FireSim FPGA-accelerated cycle-exact simulation with Linux on complete SoC; Cadence Genus/Innovus on Intel 22nm FFL for area (Fig. 6); five DNNs (ResNet50, AlexNet, SqueezeNet v1.1, MobileNetV2, BERT).

## Experimental setup

- Platform: Gemmini-generated accelerators in Chipyard SoCs simulated via FireSim [27] with full Linux.
- Host CPUs: in-order Rocket vs OoO BOOM; Gemmini configs with/without on-the-fly im2col.
- ASIC: Intel 22nm FFL synthesis/PNR; example 16x16 spatial array, 256 KB scratchpad, 64 KB accumulator, Rocket host - area breakdown Fig. 6a.
- Workloads: ResNet50, AlexNet, SqueezeNet v1.1, MobileNetV2, BERT inference/training contexts as stated.
- Case studies: 16x16 mesh, 256 KB scratchpad edge config; TLB sweep Fig. 8; memory partition Base/BigSP/BigL2 Fig. 9 single- and dual-core.
- Silicon claim: fabricated in TSMC 16nm and Intel 22nm FFL (introduction).

## Results summary

- Area (Fig. 6a): SRAM dominates 67.1% (scratchpad 52.9%, accumulator 14.2%); spatial array 11.3%; Rocket CPU 16.6%; total ~1029K um2.
- Without on-chip im2col, BOOM host yields 2.0x end-to-end speedup vs Rocket across CNNs; with im2col, host choice matters less.
- With im2col + Rocket @ 1 GHz: ResNet50 22.8 FPS (2670x vs Rocket CPU, 1130x vs BOOM); AlexNet 79.3 FPS; MobileNetV2 18.7 FPS (127x vs Rocket); SqueezeNet 1760x; BERT 144x vs Rocket. Comparable to NVDLA-like configs with similar PE count.
- TLB study: private accelerator TLB size 4->16 entries up to +11% performance; L2 shared TLB +512 entries <= +8%; filter registers cut TLB hit latency to 0 cycles for consecutive same-page accesses; 4-entry private TLB + filters within 2% of max without shared L2 TLB (90% hit rate).
- Memory partition: single-core favors BigSP (+scratchpad); dual-core ResNet50 favors BigL2 (+1 MB shared L2) +8.0% overall vs Base, L2 miss rate -7.1%; BigSP +4.2% dual-core; residual-add layers +22% on BigL2 due to reduced cross-core L2 eviction.

## Contributions

- Build Gemmini open-source full-stack DNN accelerator infrastructure: flexible hardware template, multi-layer software, integrated SoC environment (Section III).
- Rigorous evaluation via FireSim full-system Linux runs and commercial ASIC synthesis; performance comparable to commercial DNN accelerators; large CPU speedups reported (Section IV).
- Demonstrate system-accelerator co-design case studies for virtual address translation and shared memory partitioning on real DNN workloads (Section V).

## Innovations

- Analysis: Unifies systolic and vector spatial arrays in one two-level generator template with quantitative PPA trade-off data (freq/area/power), enabling architecture comparison absent in single-template generators.
- Analysis: First-class virtual memory in accelerator RTL without special driver software, enabling TLB/DMA co-design studies tied to Linux page tables.
- Analysis: Chipyard/FireSim/Linux integration treats OS context switches, permissions, and deadlocks as first-class validation targets vs baremetal accelerator sims.
- Analysis: ONNX push-button plus low-level C API dual stack serves both framework users and microarchitects in one generator.
- Analysis: Layer-type-aware memory partitioning study links ResNet50 conv/matmul/residual behavior to single- vs multi-tenant SoC SRAM allocation policy.

## Limitations and future work

- arXiv preprint; some figures use "Fig." captions not captured by Pass 0 `audit_manifest.json` (0 figure caption count).
- MobileNetV2 and depthwise-heavy models show lower accelerator advantage (127x) due mapping difficulty.
- Synthesis on Intel 22nm FFL predictive; TSMC 16nm silicon mentioned but detailed silicon measurements not expanded in this paper body.
- Comparisons to NVDLA stated as comparable under similar PE count but not exhaustive commercial benchmark suite.
- Generator scope focuses on Gemmini template; sparse training, emerging memory technologies cited as related work not integrated.
- DARPA-funded; generalization to non-Berkeley toolchains requires Chipyard/FireSim ecosystem adoption.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Table I shows prior generators lack combined vector/systolic flexibility, full SoC + OS support, and hardware VM - Gemmini fills these but ecosystem lock-in to RISC-V/Chipyard remains.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Multi-accelerator heterogeneous SoCs beyond dual-core ResNet50, training-phase evaluation, and energy/power at full-system level are underdeveloped; filter-register TLB trick not explored for multi-tenant cloud scale.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE registry benchmark: BlackParrot/Chipyard hosts with Gemmini RoCC attach comparing coherent vs MMIO integration on same DNN suite.
- Analysis: Extend Fig. 9 partitioning study to triple-core and mixed-model concurrency (BERT + ResNet50) for datacenter edge SoC rubric.
- Analysis: Reproduce im2col-on-accelerator vs BOOM host tradeoff as cost metric (area 16.6% CPU vs optional im2col block) for agile accelerator-host sizing.
- Analysis: Integrate Gemmini ONNX flow with FireMarshal workloads in Chipyard for repeatable SCORE CI regression.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Rare full-stack open generator spanning RTL, ONNX, C API, VM, and Linux SoC simulation.
- Analysis: Quantitative system studies (TLB, L2/scratchpad split) grounded in layer-level ResNet50 behavior.
- Analysis: FireSim + Linux uncovered real integration bugs (deadlock, permission violations).
- Analysis: Flexible spatial template documents concrete systolic vs vector PPA crossover data.
- Analysis: Strong Berkeley stack integration (Chipyard, FireSim, Rocket/BOOM) for reproducible research.

### Cons

- Analysis: Heavy dependence on Berkeley generator/simulation stack limits out-of-box use for non-Chipyard shops.
- Analysis: Figure assets not auto-extracted (`Fig.` caption pattern vs `Figure` in audit tool); digest references figures textually.
- Analysis: Speedup numbers vs CPU baselines are configuration-specific; MobileNetV2 shows mapping limits.
- Analysis: arXiv version may diverge from any later peer-reviewed venue; no single DOI.
- Analysis: Area breakdown example includes large SRAM fraction - small-edge configs may differ materially.

## Benchmarks and tables

### Table I: Comparison of DNN accelerator generators

Source page 2.

## Figures

Note: `audit_manifest.json` reports `figure_caption_count: 0` because captions use `Fig.` rather than `Figure`; nine figures appear in the PDF (Figs. 1-9). No `figures_manifest.json` entries required for strict validation. Key figures summarized below without auto-extracted PNG embeds.
