digestSections.tl;dr:
- Gemmini is an open-source full-stack generator producing configurable DNN accelerators plus software and Linux-capable SoC integration in the RISC-V/Chipyard ecosystem.
- Hardware template: two-level spatial array (systolic or vector MAC trees), scratchpad/accumulator SRAMs, DMA/TLB, optional im2col/pooling/ReLU peripherals; RoCC-attached to host CPU.
- Unlike prior generators focused on standalone accelerators, Gemmini supports ONNX push-button flow, C APIs, virtual memory without special drivers, and multi-core/multi-accelerator Chipyard SoCs evaluated on FireSim.
- Evaluated on ResNet50, AlexNet, SqueezeNet, MobileNetV2, BERT with Rocket/BOOM hosts; up to 2670x speedup vs in-order Rocket on ResNet50 with on-chip im2col.
- Case studies: private vs shared TLB sizing with filter registers; scratchpad vs L2 partitioning for single- vs dual-core ResNet50 (BigL2 +8% dual-core).
digestSections.problem statement: DNN accelerator research often evaluates accelerators in isolation, missing SoC resource contention, OS overheads, programming-stack inefficiencies, and host-accelerator partitioning effects that dominate real deployments (industry reports cite up to 77% time on CPU even with accelerators). Existing hardware generators (VTA, MAGNet, PolySA, etc.) emphasize accelerator RTL but lack flexible spatial templates, multi-level software, virtual memory, and full Linux SoC integration needed for systematic cross-stack architecture evaluation.
digestSections.motivation: Deep learning drives demand for specialized accelerators from edge to cloud, but designing and validating them with realistic software stacks is expensive. Parameterized generators improve productivity, yet comparing systolic vs vector arrays, dataflows, host CPU choices, TLB schemes, and shared-cache partitioning requires a platform that boots Linux, runs FireSim cycle-exact full-system simulation, and synthesizes ASIC instances. Gemmini targets co-design of accelerator microarchitecture, system memory hierarchy, and translation hardware with measurable end-to-end DNN workload impact.
digestSections.prior art: Compares accelerator generators and platforms in Table I vs NVDLA, VTA, PolySA, DNNBuilder, MAGNet, DNNWeaver, MAERI. Related DNN accelerators include TPU/systolic, NVDLA vector, Eyeriss v2, ShiDianNao, ScaleDeep, Brainwave, sparsity and in-memory designs. Software stacks: TVM (VTA), Caffe-centric flows, custom compilers. System integration prior work: Chipyard [26], FireSim [27], NeuMMU [28] and Cong et al. [29] on accelerator address translation. Industry holistic ML system papers from Facebook/HPCA cited for CPU-side overhead motivation.
digestSections.category of work:
Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Full-stack open DNN accelerator generator with SoC/Linux integration for ML architecture research, not a single fixed ASIC.
digestSections.method / approach:
**Architectural template (Fig. 1).** RoCC-attached accelerator with DMA engine, local TLB, banked scratchpad SRAM, transposer, two-level spatial array, accumulator SRAM, bitshift/ReLU, dependency management, optional matrix-scalar multiplier, pooling engine, im2col block; RoCC PTW path for page walks.

**Two-level spatial array (Figs. 2-3).** Tiles of combinational PE MAC arrays connected by pipeline registers between tiles; configurable weight- or output-stationary dataflow per PE. Supports TPU-like pipelined systolic meshes and NVDLA-like combinational vector reduction trees. Synthesis example (256 PEs): systolic 1.89 GHz max vs vector 0.69 GHz; systolic 1.8x area and 3.0x power vs vector at 500 MHz (120K vs 67K um2).

**Programming support.** High-level ONNX push-button flow mapping kernels to accelerator; low-level C/C++ APIs with per-configuration generated header (array dimensions, dataflows, optional blocks). Runtime tile-size heuristics for DRAM/L2/scratchpad staging; manual tile override available. Virtual memory in RTL enables TLB profiling (Fig. 4 miss rates 20-30% on DNN tiles vs CPU benchmarks).

**System integration (Chipyard).** Configurable Rocket in-order to BOOM OoO hosts; multi-CPU/multi-accelerator; shared L2 and bus widths; Fig. 5 dual-core dual-Gemmini example. Full Linux stack exposed non-deterministic deadlock and permission bugs not seen baremetal.

**Evaluation flow.** FireSim FPGA-accelerated cycle-exact simulation with Linux on complete SoC; Cadence Genus/Innovus on Intel 22nm FFL for area (Fig. 6); five DNNs (ResNet50, AlexNet, SqueezeNet v1.1, MobileNetV2, BERT).
digestSections.experimental setup:
- Platform: Gemmini-generated accelerators in Chipyard SoCs simulated via FireSim [27] with full Linux.
- Host CPUs: in-order Rocket vs OoO BOOM; Gemmini configs with/without on-the-fly im2col.
- ASIC: Intel 22nm FFL synthesis/PNR; example 16x16 spatial array, 256 KB scratchpad, 64 KB accumulator, Rocket host - area breakdown Fig. 6a.
- Workloads: ResNet50, AlexNet, SqueezeNet v1.1, MobileNetV2, BERT inference/training contexts as stated.
- Case studies: 16x16 mesh, 256 KB scratchpad edge config; TLB sweep Fig. 8; memory partition Base/BigSP/BigL2 Fig. 9 single- and dual-core.
- Silicon claim: fabricated in TSMC 16nm and Intel 22nm FFL (introduction).
digestSections.results summary:
- Area (Fig. 6a): SRAM dominates 67.1% (scratchpad 52.9%, accumulator 14.2%); spatial array 11.3%; Rocket CPU 16.6%; total ~1029K um2.
- Without on-chip im2col, BOOM host yields 2.0x end-to-end speedup vs Rocket across CNNs; with im2col, host choice matters less.
- With im2col + Rocket @ 1 GHz: ResNet50 22.8 FPS (2670x vs Rocket CPU, 1130x vs BOOM); AlexNet 79.3 FPS; MobileNetV2 18.7 FPS (127x vs Rocket); SqueezeNet 1760x; BERT 144x vs Rocket. Comparable to NVDLA-like configs with similar PE count.
- TLB study: private accelerator TLB size 4->16 entries up to +11% performance; L2 shared TLB +512 entries <= +8%; filter registers cut TLB hit latency to 0 cycles for consecutive same-page accesses; 4-entry private TLB + filters within 2% of max without shared L2 TLB (90% hit rate).
- Memory partition: single-core favors BigSP (+scratchpad); dual-core ResNet50 favors BigL2 (+1 MB shared L2) +8.0% overall vs Base, L2 miss rate -7.1%; BigSP +4.2% dual-core; residual-add layers +22% on BigL2 due to reduced cross-core L2 eviction.
digestSections.contributions:
- Build Gemmini open-source full-stack DNN accelerator infrastructure: flexible hardware template, multi-layer software, integrated SoC environment (Section III).
- Rigorous evaluation via FireSim full-system Linux runs and commercial ASIC synthesis; performance comparable to commercial DNN accelerators; large CPU speedups reported (Section IV).
- Demonstrate system-accelerator co-design case studies for virtual address translation and shared memory partitioning on real DNN workloads (Section V).
digestSections.innovations:
- Analysis: Unifies systolic and vector spatial arrays in one two-level generator template with quantitative PPA trade-off data (freq/area/power), enabling architecture comparison absent in single-template generators.
- Analysis: First-class virtual memory in accelerator RTL without special driver software, enabling TLB/DMA co-design studies tied to Linux page tables.
- Analysis: Chipyard/FireSim/Linux integration treats OS context switches, permissions, and deadlocks as first-class validation targets vs baremetal accelerator sims.
- Analysis: ONNX push-button plus low-level C API dual stack serves both framework users and microarchitects in one generator.
- Analysis: Layer-type-aware memory partitioning study links ResNet50 conv/matmul/residual behavior to single- vs multi-tenant SoC SRAM allocation policy.
digestSections.limitations and future work:
- arXiv preprint; some figures use "Fig." captions not captured by Pass 0 `audit_manifest.json` (0 figure caption count).
- MobileNetV2 and depthwise-heavy models show lower accelerator advantage (127x) due mapping difficulty.
- Synthesis on Intel 22nm FFL predictive; TSMC 16nm silicon mentioned but detailed silicon measurements not expanded in this paper body.
- Comparisons to NVDLA stated as comparable under similar PE count but not exhaustive commercial benchmark suite.
- Generator scope focuses on Gemmini template; sparse training, emerging memory technologies cited as related work not integrated.
- DARPA-funded; generalization to non-Berkeley toolchains requires Chipyard/FireSim ecosystem adoption.
digestSections.research opportunity:
**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Table I shows prior generators lack combined vector/systolic flexibility, full SoC + OS support, and hardware VM - Gemmini fills these but ecosystem lock-in to RISC-V/Chipyard remains.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Multi-accelerator heterogeneous SoCs beyond dual-core ResNet50, training-phase evaluation, and energy/power at full-system level are underdeveloped; filter-register TLB trick not explored for multi-tenant cloud scale.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE registry benchmark: BlackParrot/Chipyard hosts with Gemmini RoCC attach comparing coherent vs MMIO integration on same DNN suite.
- Analysis: Extend Fig. 9 partitioning study to triple-core and mixed-model concurrency (BERT + ResNet50) for datacenter edge SoC rubric.
- Analysis: Reproduce im2col-on-accelerator vs BOOM host tradeoff as cost metric (area 16.6% CPU vs optional im2col block) for agile accelerator-host sizing.
- Analysis: Integrate Gemmini ONNX flow with FireMarshal workloads in Chipyard for repeatable SCORE CI regression.
digestSections.pros and cons:
### Pros

- Analysis: Rare full-stack open generator spanning RTL, ONNX, C API, VM, and Linux SoC simulation.
- Analysis: Quantitative system studies (TLB, L2/scratchpad split) grounded in layer-level ResNet50 behavior.
- Analysis: FireSim + Linux uncovered real integration bugs (deadlock, permission violations).
- Analysis: Flexible spatial template documents concrete systolic vs vector PPA crossover data.
- Analysis: Strong Berkeley stack integration (Chipyard, FireSim, Rocket/BOOM) for reproducible research.

### Cons

- Analysis: Heavy dependence on Berkeley generator/simulation stack limits out-of-box use for non-Chipyard shops.
- Analysis: Figure assets not auto-extracted (`Fig.` caption pattern vs `Figure` in audit tool); digest references figures textually.
- Analysis: Speedup numbers vs CPU baselines are configuration-specific; MobileNetV2 shows mapping limits.
- Analysis: arXiv version may diverge from any later peer-reviewed venue; no single DOI.
- Analysis: Area breakdown example includes large SRAM fraction - small-edge configs may differ materially.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# HEROv2: Full-Stack Open-Source Research Platform for Heterogeneous Computing

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Andreas Kurth; Bjorn Forsberg; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich (Integrated Systems Laboratory) |
| Venue | arXiv preprint |
| Venue type | preprint |
| Year | 2022 |
| Volume / issue / pages | arXiv:2201.03861v1, 14 pages |
| Paper DOI | Not assigned (preprint) |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03861 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/hero |
| Keywords | heterogeneous computing, RISC-V accelerator, OpenMP offloading, FPGA research platform, LLVM |
| Open access | Yes (arXiv + permissive open-source stack) |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- HEROv2 is a full-stack FPGA research platform coupling a 64-bit ARMv8 or RV64 host with 32-bit RISC-V accelerator clusters, shared virtual memory via hybrid IOMMU, and OpenMP 4.5 offloading.
- Open LLVM toolchain + runtime + API (AutoDMA) can tile loops and infer DMA transfers, reaching up to 4.4x speedup vs unmodified OpenMP and ~85% of handwritten tiling (2.6x more LOC).
- Four case studies span applications, compiler AutoDMA, interconnect data-width, and custom ISA (Xpulpv2) on the mature Aurora (Cortex-A53 + 8x CV32E40P) configuration.

## Problem statement

Heterogeneous computers pairing general-purpose hosts with domain-specific manycore accelerators are hard to evaluate accurately: simulators trade speed for fidelity, and prior platforms lack mixed data models (64-bit host / 32-bit accelerator), full software stacks, or open customizable interconnects.

## Motivation

Provide a working open prototype that runs real applications and benchmarks on RTL-mapped accelerators with a complete programming stack, enabling collaborative full-stack research from applications through microarchitecture.

## Prior art

HEROv1 (same data model only); FPGA accelerator + host platforms [15]-[18]; OpenPiton; ESP; FireSim-class simulators; OpenMP/HSA offloading models; PULP CV32E40P and Snitch accelerator cores.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Full-stack open heterogeneous research platform (FPGA RTL + LLVM + runtime), not a single taped-out ASIC paper.

## Method / approach

**Hardware (Fig. 1 in paper).** Hard-macro ARMv8 Cortex-A (Zynq UltraScale+) or soft CVA6 RV64 host; accelerator clusters of 4-16 RV32 cores (CV32E40P or Snitch) with SPM, DMA, hybrid IOMMU/TLB sharing host page tables; open AXI-class on-chip network; shared DDR/HBM.

**Toolchain (Fig. 2).** LLVM-based mixed-ISA, mixed-data-model compiler with OpenMP 4.5 offloading; AutoDMA automatic tiling and DMA inference for software-managed SPM.

**Runtime (Fig. 3).** Host OpenMP plugin + device offload manager; teams/parallel on clusters; VMM library for TLB miss handling; HAL for DMA/mailbox; Linux device driver.

**API.** hero_lN_malloc/free/capacity; host2dev/dev2host memcpy (blocking/async, 1D/2D); performance counters.

**Configs (Table 1).** Aurora (mature: A53 + 8x CV32E40P @50 MHz PL); Blizzard (MLT accelerator); Cyclone (RV64 host + multi-cluster, in development).

## Experimental setup

- Primary eval: Aurora on Xilinx ZU9EG — 4x Cortex-A53 @1.2 GHz, 8x CV32E40P RV32IMAFCXpulpv2, 128 KiB L1 SPM, hybrid IOMMU, 4 GiB DDR4 (up to 19.2 GB/s), PL @50 MHz.
- PL utilization: 98.1% CLBs (87.7% PMCA, 10.4% IOMMU); Vivado 2019.2.
- Kernels: PolyBench-style and Darknet workloads (2mm, 3mm, atax, bicg, conv2d, covar, darknet, gemm, etc.) with OpenMP offload.
- Case studies: handwritten vs AutoDMA tiling; 8-thread parallel speedup; interconnect 32/64/128-bit; Xpulpv2 custom instructions.

## Results summary

- AutoDMA: up to 4.4x vs original OpenMP on local memory; typically within ~15% of handwritten DMA (handwritten needs 2.6x LOC / 1.8x cyclomatic complexity).
- High spatial-locality kernels achieve ~85% of handwritten speedup; column-wise kernels (covar, atax) see only marginal AutoDMA gains but still up to ~20% over baseline OpenMP.
- 8 accelerator threads: substantial parallel speedups (Fig. 5); interconnect width scales DMA bandwidth roughly linearly (Fig. 8 in paper).
- Custom Xpulpv2 instructions further accelerate DSP-style kernels (Fig. 9).
- Platform enables system-level experiments (data width, ISA) without rewriting the full software stack.

## Contributions

- Resolve HEROv1 limitations: mixed 64/32-bit data models, customizable open on-chip network, full OpenMP + LLVM stack.
- Demonstrate four quantitative full-stack case studies on real FPGA RTL.
- AutoDMA compiler feature that makes software-managed SPM nearly as programmable as hardware caches for spatially local codes.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Hybrid software-managed IOMMU lets 32-bit accelerators share 64-bit host virtual addresses with low TLB hit overhead (~3 cycles remote) without full hardware SMMU.
- Analysis: AutoDMA closes the programmability gap of SPM hierarchies while keeping expert manual tiling as an opt-out for last percent.
- Analysis: Single open platform spans application, toolchain, system architecture, and microarchitecture evaluation with the same binaries.

## Limitations and future work

- Aurora host is closed hard-macro Cortex-A53; fully open soft host (Cyclone/CVA6) still in development.
- FPGA frequency (50 MHz) limits absolute performance vs ASIC; relative speedups remain the primary metric.
- AutoDMA weak on non-contiguous column-wise access; no automatic loop reordering/polyhedral rewrite.
- Blizzard/Cyclone configs not fully evaluated in this paper.
- Fig. 1 architecture overview referenced but not captured as a numbered caption in Pass 0 audit (caption set starts at Fig. 2).

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: HEROv1 and simulator-centric stacks lack mixed-width shared VM + open RTL interconnect customization in one package.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: ASIC tapeout of HEROv2-class host+accelerator, energy measurements, and multi-accelerator contention under Linux not reported.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE registry: link HERO Aurora/Blizzard configs to Cheshire host + Snitch/CV32 accelerators for cross-platform comparison.
- Analysis: Reuse AutoDMA evaluation suite as a survey benchmark for software-managed vs coherent accelerator memory.
- Analysis: Port same OpenMP kernels to Chipyard/FireSim and ESP to calibrate FPGA-prototype vs simulation fidelity.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Rare complete open heterogeneous stack (RTL + LLVM + OpenMP + API) with GitHub pulp-platform/hero.
- Analysis: Quantitative compiler vs handwritten tiling evidence with LOC complexity metrics.
- Analysis: Configurable interconnect and ISA case studies show platform research utility.

### Cons

- Analysis: Primary results on FPGA soft accelerator @50 MHz, not silicon PPA.
- Analysis: Mature config still uses proprietary ARM hard host.
- Analysis: AutoDMA limitations on irregular access patterns remain.

## Benchmarks and tables

Primary evaluation uses PolyBench-style and Darknet kernels on Aurora (Table 1 configs; Table 2 kernels). AutoDMA reaches up to 4.4x vs unmodified OpenMP and ~85% of handwritten tiling. Table 3 compares FPGA emulation platforms.

Detailed table transcriptions follow the Figures section.

## Figures

### Figure 2: Overview of HEROv2 heterogeneous toolchain and compilers.

![Figure 2](./figures/figure_02.png)

*Page 4. Host and device compilation flows for mixed-ISA OpenMP offload.*

### Figure 3: HEROv2 runtime stack integrating host OS and accelerator offload.

![Figure 3](./figures/figure_03.png)

*Page 5. Host OpenMP plugin, mailbox, device offload manager, VMM, and HAL layers.*

### Figure 4: Speed-up on local memory with handwritten tiling and DMA.

![Figure 4](./figures/figure_04.png)

*Page 7. Handwritten DMA/tiling speedups across evaluated kernels.*

### Figure 5: Speed-up with 8 accelerator threads vs single thread.

![Figure 5](./figures/figure_05.png)

*Page 8. Parallel scaling on the octa-core CV32E40P accelerator.*

### Figure 6: Code complexity of handwritten tiling/DMA vs AutoDMA.

![Figure 6](./figures/figure_06.png)

*Page 8. LOC and complexity overhead of manual vs compiler-managed data movement.*

### Figure 7: Speed-up with compiler-generated tiling and DMA (AutoDMA).

![Figure 7](./figures/figure_07.png)

*Page 9. AutoDMA achieves up to 4.4x; typically near handwritten for contiguous kernels.*

### Figure 9: Speed-up with custom instructions (Xpulpv2).

![Figure 9](./figures/figure_09.png)

*Page 10. ISA extension impact on accelerator kernels.*

## Tables

### Table 1: HEROv2 target platforms and configurations (Aurora / Blizzard / Cyclone).

| Config | Host | Accel | Mem | Carrier | Status |
|--------|------|-------|-----|---------|--------|
| Aurora | 4x Cortex-A53 ARMv8 | 8x CV32E40P Xpulpv2 | 4 GiB DDR4 | ZU9EG @50 MHz | mature |
| Blizzard | shared Aurora host | 8x MLT RV32 + SSR/FREP | shared | ZU9EG | in development |
| Cyclone | soft CVA6 RV64GC | multi-cluster Snitch-class | 8 GiB HBM2E | VU37P @25 MHz | in development |

*Page 6. Table transcribed from PDF text (Pass 0 table capture incomplete for multi-column layout).*

### Table 2: Evaluated kernels and applications (selected).

| Kernel | Computation class | Space | Compute |
|--------|-------------------|-------|---------|
| 2mm / gemm / darknet | matrix multiply style | N2 | N3 |
| atax / bicg | transpose/mv variants | N2 | N2 |
| conv2d | 3x3 convolution | N2 | N2 |
| covar | covariance | N2 | N3 |

*Page 7. Complexity columns from paper Table 2.*

### Table 3: Comparison of computer emulation systems on programmable logic (summary).

Paper Table 3 contrasts HEROv2 vs related FPGA emulation/research platforms on FAME taxonomy, emulation focus, host/accelerator openness, and software stack completeness (page 12). Full cell-level transcription deferred; used for related-work positioning only.

## Reproducibility

| Artifact | Link / status |
|----------|----------------|
| Code | https://github.com/pulp-platform/hero |
| Hardware | Open SystemVerilog RTL components (PULP stack) |
| FPGA | Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ ZU9EG (Aurora) |
| Tools | LLVM-based heterogeneous compiler; Vivado 2019.2 |

## References

1. A. Kurth et al., HERO (HEROv1), 2019. DOI: [10.1145/3295816.3295821](https://doi.org/10.1145/3295816.3295821) -- `[resolved]`
2. F. Zaruba and L. Benini, CVA6, IEEE TVLSI 2019. DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Slow and Steady Wins the Race? A Comparison of Ultra-Low-Power RISC-V Cores for Internet-of-Things Applications

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Pasquale Davide Schiavone; Francesco Conti; Davide Rossi; Michael Gautschi; Antonio Pullini; Eric Flamand; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich / PULP Platform contributors |
| Venue | PATMOS 2017 |
| Venue type | conference |
| Year | 2017 |
| Volume / issue / pages | 8 pages |
| Paper DOI | [10.1109/PATMOS.2017.8106976](https://doi.org/10.1109/PATMOS.2017.8106976) |
| URL | PULPino / Zero-riscy lineage (Ibex); open-source release announced for summer 2017 |
| Keywords | RISC-V, ultra-low-power, IoT cores, Zero-riscy, Micro-riscy, energy efficiency |
| Open access | IEEE Xplore (authorized); cores later open-sourced as Zero-riscy / Ibex lineage |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Funding: SNSF 162524 (MicroLearn).

## TL;DR

- Introduces Zero-riscy (RVC32IM, 18.9 kGE) and Micro-riscy (RVC32E, 11.6 kGE) and compares them to DSP-oriented Riscy (40.7 kGE) in UMC 65 nm.
- Zero-riscy is ~2.2x smaller than Riscy and ~2x more energy efficient on mixed control/arithmetic; Micro-riscy is ~1.6x smaller than Zero-riscy with ~100 uW at 160 MHz and best on pure control.
- Always-on duty-cycle analysis shows leakage-dominated regimes where smaller cores beat faster DSP cores on total energy.

## Problem statement

IoT end-nodes face highly time-varying workloads (long idle, sporadic control, intermittent DSP bursts). A single core microarchitecture cannot optimally cover all regimes under milliwatt power and low area budgets.

## Motivation

Build an open RISC-V core family spanning DSP-heavy (Riscy), mixed arithmetic/control (Zero-riscy), and pure control (Micro-riscy) so heterogeneous IoT SoCs can match core choice to task class and duty cycle.

## Prior art

ARM Cortex-M0/M0+/M3/M4; Synopsys ARC EM; Minima Processor RVC32IMA; Rocket/BOOM (out of scope); Z-Scale; PULPino/Riscy; PicoRV32; mRISC; TI CC2650 and NXP LPC54100 heterogeneous MCUs; GAP-8 fabric controller pattern.

## Category of work

Primary: `circuit-design`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: Comparative microarchitecture and post-layout energy study of three open RISC-V IoT cores (Ibex lineage).

## Method / approach

**Riscy.** 4-stage RVC32IM + DSP extensions (HW loops, auto-inc LD/ST, bit-manip, MAC, fixed-point, packed SIMD, dot-product); cluster-oriented.

**Zero-riscy (Figs. 1-2).** 2-stage IF + IDE; 2R1W latch RF; shared adder for ALU/branch/AGU/div; multi-cycle mul/div/LD/ST/branch; minimal CSR; up to 32 IRQs; no forwarding.

**Micro-riscy.** Zero-riscy minus RVM (no HW mul/div) and RVE 16-register RF.

**Evaluation.** Each core integrated in PULPino (Fig. 4); Synopsys DC + Cadence Innovus UMC 65 nm; slow (10 ns) and fast (3 ns) netlists; post-layout PrimeTime power at 1.2 V and 0.8 V; workloads: 5x5 2D-convolution (16b), CoreMark, Runtime scheduler/driver stubs.

## Experimental setup

- Technology: UMC 65 nm; GE = 1.44 um2 NAND2.
- Slow-netlist: ~185 MHz @1.2 V / 55 MHz @0.8 V; fast-netlist: ~560 MHz @1.2 V / 160 MHz @0.8 V (typical).
- Switching activity from post-layout simulation; power via PrimeTime.
- Always-on experiment: 2D-conv at 0.8 V, 55 MHz slow-netlist with variable inter-event idle (Fig. 8).

## Results summary

- Area (Table I / Fig. 3): Riscy 40.7, Zero-riscy 18.9, Micro-riscy 11.6 kGE; RF dominates Zero/Micro area share.
- Performance (Table II): DSP 2D-conv cycles 1.0 / 6.1 / 53.4 vs Riscy; CoreMark 1.0 / 1.3 / 3.5; Runtime ~equal. CoreMark/MHz: Riscy 3.19, Zero 2.44, Micro 0.91 (vs Cortex-M0/M0+ ~2.33/2.46, M4 ~3.40).
- Power (Tables III-IV, Fig. 5): Zero/Micro ~2-3x lower dynamic density than Riscy; fast netlists ~14x leakage of slow; 0.8 V total power up to ~12x lower than 1.2 V at max speed.
- Energy: DSP -> Riscy best; mixed CoreMark -> Zero-riscy best (~1.9x / 2x better than Riscy/Micro); control Runtime -> Micro-riscy best (Zero/Riscy ~1.4x / 3.5x worse). Near-threshold 0.8 V ~0.3x energy of 1.2 V on average (Fig. 7).
- Always-on (Fig. 8): as idle grows, energy leadership shifts Riscy -> Zero-riscy -> Micro-riscy (leakage dominates).

## Contributions

- Present Zero-riscy and Micro-riscy microarchitectures targeting mixed and control IoT workloads.
- Quantitative area/power/performance/energy comparison vs Riscy across netlist constraints and voltages.
- Always-on duty-cycle analysis linking leakage and core sizing to event sparsity.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Shared-datapath 2-stage Zero-riscy removes forwarding while keeping RVM, hitting Cortex-M0-class CoreMark/MHz at ~18.9 kGE.
- Analysis: Explicit mapping of workload class to energy-optimal core (DSP/mixed/control) with measured ratios, not only area claims.
- Analysis: Always-on inter-event curves show when DSP cores lose to tiny cores despite active-phase superiority.

## Limitations and future work

- Post-layout PULPino instances, not full multi-core cluster silicon measurements for Zero/Micro in this paper.
- Only three micro-benchmarks; no OS/Linux or large application suite.
- Cortex-M area numbers partly estimated from public data (Table I footnote).
- Zero-riscy later evolved to Ibex; this paper is the original PATMOS comparison snapshot.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Prior RISC-V IoT cores rarely publish head-to-head energy across DSP/mixed/control plus always-on leakage regimes in one study.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Silicon of Zero/Micro, multi-core heterogeneous SoC with all three cores, and security/debug overhead not covered.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE registry: map Zero-riscy -> Ibex and cite this paper for area/energy baselines in core comparison tables.
- Analysis: Reproduce CoreMark energy ranking (Zero best) as a survey gate metric for MCU-class cores.
- Analysis: Extend always-on Fig. 8 methodology to Cheshire/Neo and Quentin duty-cycle scenarios.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Clear three-way energy ranking by workload class with post-layout evidence.
- Analysis: Direct Cortex-M area/CoreMark positioning aids survey readers.
- Analysis: Always-on leakage analysis is highly relevant to IoT sensing nodes.

### Cons

- Analysis: Simulation/P&R study rather than taped-out Zero/Micro silicon in this work.
- Analysis: Narrow kernel set; Runtime micro-benchmark is tiny (tens of cycles).
- Analysis: Toolchain GCC5.2 with Riscy extensions may bias DSP comparisons.

## Benchmarks and tables

Workloads: 5x5 2D-convolution (DSP), CoreMark (mixed), Runtime control stubs. Energy-optimal core: Riscy (DSP), Zero-riscy (mixed), Micro-riscy (control). Tables I-IV and Figs. 5/7/8 capture area, cycles/IPC, power, and always-on energy. Detailed tables follow Figures.

## Figures

### Figure 5: Power distribution of core units on CoreMark (slow-netlist @100 MHz, 1.2 V).

![Figure 5](./figures/figure_05.png)

*Page 6. Prefetch buffer dominates; Zero/Micro cut decoder/controller and multdiv power vs Riscy.*

### Figure 7: Near-threshold vs super-threshold energy by kernel.

![Figure 7](./figures/figure_07.png)

*Page 7. 0.8 V / 160 MHz vs 1.2 V / 560 MHz normalized energy; same core ranking by workload.*

### Figure 8: Always-on energy vs inter-event idle time.

![Figure 8](./figures/figure_08.png)

*Page 8. Leadership shifts from Riscy to Zero-riscy to Micro-riscy as idle grows.*

## Tables

### Table I: Area comparison vs ARM Cortex-M family.

| Core | Area [kGE] | Core | Area [kGE] |
|------|------------|------|------------|
| Riscy | 40.7 | Cortex-M4 / M3 | 53.0 / 37.9 |
| Zero-riscy / Micro-riscy | 18.9 / 11.6 | Cortex-M0 / M0+ | 13.3 / 12.5 |

*Page 3. Cortex-M0 from UMC 65 nm synthesis; M0+/M3/M4 estimated from public data.*

### Table II: Cycles, IPC, and code size (normalized to Riscy).

| Kernel | Riscy cycles/IPC/size | Zero-riscy | Micro-riscy |
|--------|----------------------|------------|-------------|
| 2D-Convolution | 1.0 (43.1K) / 0.82 / 1.0 | 6.1 / 0.52 / 1.0 | 53.4 / 0.66 / 1.0 |
| CoreMark | 1.0 (313.5K) / 0.79 / 1.0 | 1.3 / 0.67 / 1.1 | 3.5 / 0.67 / 1.3 |
| Runtime | 1.0 (37) / 0.76 / 1.0 | 1.0 / 0.68 / 1.1 | 1.0 (36) / 0.67 / 1.1 |

*Page 5. From paper Table II / tables/table_ii.csv.*

### Table III: Dynamic power density and leakage.

| Core | PDynD - PLkg @1.2 V | PDynD - PLkg @0.8 V |
|------|---------------------|---------------------|
| Slow Riscy | 5.07 - 1.91 | 1.40 - 0.22 |
| Slow Zero | 2.08 - 0.73 | 0.59 - 0.07 |
| Slow Micro | 1.88 - 0.45 | 0.52 - 0.04 |
| Fast Riscy | 6.70 - 24.90 | 2.10 - 2.96 |
| Fast Zero | 2.30 - 11.0 | 0.68 - 1.24 |
| Fast Micro | 2.03 - 6.25 | 0.60 - 0.70 |

*Page 6. PDynD in uW/MHz, leakage in uW.*

### Table IV: Total power at maximum speed.

| Core | Ptot @1.2 V | Ptot @0.8 V | Ratio |
|------|-------------|-------------|-------|
| Slow @185/55 MHz Riscy | 940 | 77 | 12.2 |
| Slow Zero | 386 | 33 | 11.7 |
| Slow Micro | 348 | 29 | 12.0 |
| Fast @560/160 MHz Riscy | 3777 | 339 | 11.1 |
| Fast Zero | 1299 | 110 | 11.8 |
| Fast Micro | 1143 | 97 | 11.8 |

*Page 6. Power in uW.*

## Reproducibility

| Artifact | Link / status |
|----------|----------------|
| Platform | PULPino (www.pulp-platform.org) |
| Cores | Zero-riscy / Micro-riscy announced open-source summer 2017; lineage continues as Ibex |
| Data | Post-layout UMC 65 nm results in paper; no public netlist dump |

## References

1. M. Gautschi et al., Near-threshold RISC-V with DSP (Riscy), IEEE TVLSI 2017. DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
2. RISC-V ISA manual. DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`

- Analysis: Shared-datapath 2-stage Zero-riscy removes forwarding while keeping RVM, hitting Cortex-M0-class CoreMark/MHz at ~18.9 kGE.
- Analysis: Explicit mapping of workload class to energy-optimal core (DSP/mixed/control) with measured ratios, not only area claims.
- Analysis: Always-on inter-event curves show when DSP cores lose to tiny cores despite active-phase superiority.
digestSections.limitations and future work:
- Post-layout PULPino instances, not full multi-core cluster silicon measurements for Zero/Micro in this paper.
- Only three micro-benchmarks; no OS/Linux or large application suite.
- Cortex-M area numbers partly estimated from public data (Table I footnote).
- Zero-riscy later evolved to Ibex; this paper is the original PATMOS comparison snapshot.
digestSections.research opportunity:
**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Prior RISC-V IoT cores rarely publish head-to-head energy across DSP/mixed/control plus always-on leakage regimes in one study.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Silicon of Zero/Micro, multi-core heterogeneous SoC with all three cores, and security/debug overhead not covered.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE registry: map Zero-riscy -> Ibex and cite this paper for area/energy baselines in core comparison tables.
- Analysis: Reproduce CoreMark energy ranking (Zero best) as a survey gate metric for MCU-class cores.
- Analysis: Extend always-on Fig. 8 methodology to Cheshire/Neo and Quentin duty-cycle scenarios.

### Pros

- Analysis: Clear three-way energy ranking by workload class with post-layout evidence.
- Analysis: Direct Cortex-M area/CoreMark positioning aids survey readers.
- Analysis: Always-on leakage analysis is highly relevant to IoT sensing nodes.

### Cons

- Analysis: Simulation/P&R study rather than taped-out Zero/Micro silicon in this work.
- Analysis: Narrow kernel set; Runtime micro-benchmark is tiny (tens of cycles).
- Analysis: Toolchain GCC5.2 with Riscy extensions may bias DSP comparisons.
digestSections.benchmarks and tables: Workloads: 5x5 2D-convolution (DSP), CoreMark (mixed), Runtime control stubs. Energy-optimal core: Riscy (DSP), Zero-riscy (mixed), Micro-riscy (control). # IOb-SoC

- **SCORE scripts:** `install_iob_soc.sh` / `generate_iob_soc.sh` / `run_iob_soc.sh` (README.md architectures table)

- **Verification:**
  - Upstream: `make pc-emul-run` PC emulation; board/sim make targets in generated build directory.
  - SCORE: multi-config generate (`USE_INTMEM`/`USE_EXTMEM`/`INIT_MEM` matrix) + Icarus/Verilator smoke → `datasets/iob-soc/<commit>/verification/`.

- **Primary paper:** none (Zenodo release tarball + product brief/presentation, not peer-reviewed venue paper)
- **Optional docs:** `papers/_incoming/iob-soc-zenodo-5791411-pb.pdf`, `iob-soc-zenodo-5791411-presentation.pdf`, extracted release `papers/_incoming/iob-soc-0.6/`
- **Limitations (from upstream, quoted):**
  - README: requires Py2HWSW / nix-shell for canonical `make setup` flow; pre-built release tarballs alternative.
  - Reference OS: Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS (README Operating Systems).
- **SCORE generate path:** `datasets/iob-soc/<commit>/rtl_designs/iob_soc_smoke/` (+ builds/logs/verification per config); commit pinned from `tools/iob-soc`

projects.fullMarkdown:
# FractalSync: Lightweight Scalable Global Synchronization of Massive Bulk Synchronous Parallel AI Accelerators

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Victor Isachi; Alessandro Nadalini; Riccardo Fiorani Gallotta; Angelo Garofalo; Francesco Conti; Davide Rossi |
| Affiliations | University of Bologna; University of Pavia |
| Venue | ACM CF 2025 |
| Venue type | conference |
| Year | 2025 |
| Paper DOI | [10.1145/3719276.3725203](https://doi.org/10.1145/3719276.3725203) |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.11668 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/MAGIA |
| Keywords | Barrier synchronization, BSP, MAGIA mesh, GenAI accelerator |
| Open access | ACM author version / arXiv |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- FractalSync is a hardware barrier synchronizer for Bulk Synchronous Parallel (BSP) AI accelerators, integrated in the open MAGIA mesh tile architecture.
- Up to 43× speedup vs software AMO barriers on 2×2 to 16×16 tile meshes; <0.01% area overhead; closes timing at MAGIA 1 GHz target.
- Each MAGIA tile: cv32e40x control core, RedMulE GeMM accelerator, iDMA, 1 MiB TCDM (32 banks), FractalSync unit.

## Problem statement

Massively parallel GenAI accelerators need fast global barriers; software atomic memory operations do not scale as tile counts grow.

## Motivation

BSP is the dominant parallel programming model for ML tiles; a lightweight hardware fractal barrier tree reduces synchronization cycles without significant area cost.

## Prior art

Software barriers/AMOs on shared memory; prior PULP cluster barriers; RedMulE, iDMA, MAGIA mesh architecture.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`, `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture MAGIA (interconnect/accelerator mesh).

## Method / approach

**MAGIA tile (Fig. 1).** 32×32 KiB TCDM banks; HCI single-cycle L1; OBI crossbar; RedMulE 24×8 semi-systolic GEMM; dual-channel iDMA; cv32e40x + Xif custom instructions for DMA/GEMM/sync.

**FractalSync.** Hierarchical hardware barrier network across mesh (FS nodes in Fig. 2); integrated as Xif-controlled synchronization IP replacing AMO spin barriers.

## Experimental setup

- RTL simulation / synthesis at 1 GHz target frequency.
- Mesh sizes 2×2 through 16×16 tiles.
- Compare FractalSync vs software AMO barrier baseline.

## Results summary

- Up to 43× synchronization speedup vs AMO baseline.
- Area overhead < 0.01%; meets 1 GHz timing.
- Scalability studied up to 16×16 PE mesh.

## Contributions

- FractalSync hardware barrier for BSP AI accelerators.
- Integration methodology in open MAGIA tiles with Xif dispatch.
- Scalability and area study on mesh sizes relevant to GenAI.

## Innovations

- Fractal barrier tree co-designed with MAGIA mesh NoC and TCDM banking for negligible area at 1 GHz.

## Limitations and future work

- 4-page CF brief; full silicon power/energy not central focus.
- MAGIA primary architecture paper is this FractalSync integration study — not a standalone MAGIA tapeout report.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Few open mesh AI accelerators document barrier hardware vs AMO at 256-tile scale.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: End-to-end LLM layer fusion benchmarks on MAGIA+FractalSync in SCORE flows remain open.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Pair digest with SCORE `magia` generate scripts for NoC/barrier RTL snapshots.
- Analysis: Compare FractalSync vs MemPool/Snitch cluster sync in survey tables.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Peer-reviewed CF DOI plus open MAGIA GitHub — strong Track A for MAGIA row.
- Analysis: Quantified 43× barrier speedup at negligible area.

### Cons

- Analysis: Focuses on synchronization subsystem, not full MAGIA silicon PPA.
- Analysis: Short conference format limits workload diversity.

## Benchmarks and tables

### Table 1: Performance of synchronization schemes

| Mesh config. | FSync (c) | FSync+P (c) | Naïve (c) | XY (c) | Best AMO speedup |
|--------------|----------:|------------:|----------:|-------:|-----------------:|
| Neighbor | 4 | 4 | 79 | 79 | 19× |
| 2×2 | 6 | 6 | 119 | 219 | 19× |
| 4×4 | 10 | 10 | 512 | 347 | 34× |
| 8×8 | 14 | 18 | 2488 | 614 | 34× |
| 16×16 | 18 | 34 | 13961 | 1462 | 43× |

*Page 3. Cycle counts (c) for FractalSync, FractalSync+Pipeline, naïve, and XY schemes; up to 43× vs best AMO on 16×16 mesh.*

## Figures

### Figure 1: MAGIA tile with FractalSync

![Figure 1](./figures/figure_01.png)

### Figure 2: FractalSync mesh placement and speedup

![Figure 2](./figures/figure_02.png)

## Reproducibility

| Artifact | Link / status |
|----------|----------------|
| MAGIA RTL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/MAGIA |
| Related IPs | RedMulE, iDMA, cv32e40x (cited) |

## References

1. T. Benz et al., iDMA modular DMA, IEEE TC 2024. DOI: [10.1109/TC.2023.3312019](https://doi.org/10.1109/TC.2023.3312019) -- `[resolved]`
2. V. Isachi et al., FractalSync, CF 2025. DOI: [10.1145/3719276.3725203](https://doi.org/10.1145/3719276.3725203) -- `[resolved]`

## Extraction notes

- Pass 0: arXiv:2506.11668v1 / CF 2025; 4 pages; manual clips Figs. 1–2.
- Pass 1: Digest from extracted_text.txt.

### Pass 2 audit log:

- Page 1: Abstract, intro, BSP motivation, FractalSync proposal, MAGIA overview start.
- Page 2: MAGIA tile architecture Fig. 1, TCDM/RedMulE/iDMA/Xif details.
- Page 3: FractalSync mesh Fig. 2, scalability experiments, speedup results.
- Page 4: Conclusion, references, ACM DOI block.

### Pass 3 accuracy audit:

- Verified: DOI 10.1145/3719276.3725203, 43× speedup, <0.01% area, 1 GHz, github.com/pulp-platform/MAGIA.
- Checked: two figure PNGs with ≥2 candidates.

### Pass 3: Figure selection

- Fig. 1: a_manual (MAGIA tile block).
- Fig. 2: a_manual (mesh + results panels).

### Pass 3: Table extraction

No numbered tables.

| Paper DOI | [10.1109/TC.2023.3307796](https://doi.org/10.1109/TC.2023.3307796) |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17742 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/mempool |
| Keywords | Manycore, RISC-V, shared L1, Snitch, 22FDX |
| Open access | arXiv preprint + IEEE |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- MemPool scales a shared-L1 cluster to 256 independently programmable Snitch RV32IMAXpulpimg cores with 1 MiB multi-banked L1 SPM (at most five-cycle access without conflicts).
- Hierarchical PE-to-L1 interconnect, cache-based instruction path, and distributed DMA keep stalls under 2% on kernels.
- 22 nm FDX: 600 MHz TT/0.80 V/25 C; up to 229 GOPS and 180 GOPS/W; open-source at pulp-platform/mempool.

## Problem statement

Shared-L1 clusters are believed not to scale beyond tens of PEs due to interconnect latency, instruction bandwidth, and wiring; multi-cluster and SIMT alternatives complicate programming or reduce flexibility.

## Motivation

Build an energy-efficient general-purpose manycore that keeps a single shared L1 programming model while scaling to hundreds of independent RISC-V cores.

## Prior art

GPU SMs (SIMT); multi-cluster designs (Manticore, ET-SoC-1); GAP9/Kalray/RC64-style clusters; Apple/Intel/Ampere cache-coherent CPUs; systolic arrays (Pixel Visual Core, TPU).

## Category of work

Primary: `circuit-design`  
Secondary: `system-architecture`, `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture MemPool.

## Method / approach

**Topology.** 64 tiles / 256 cores; banking factor 4 toward 1 MiB L1; hierarchical topologies (incl. TopH) with address scrambling vs full 256x1024 crossbar.

**Cores.** Snitch RV32 with Xpulpimg-style FUs; latency-tolerant outstanding memory ops.

**I-path.** Hierarchical shared instruction caches sized for aggregate IF bandwidth.

**DMA / system.** Distributed DMA backends; hierarchical AXI toward L2; up to 256 B/cycle streams.

**Software.** Multiple runtimes / abstraction levels; weak-scaling kernels and double-buffering.

## Experimental setup

- Tech: GF 22 nm FDX; TT/0.80 V/25 C; 600 MHz (~60 FO4).
- Post-layout / P&R MemPool group dieshots and area/power breakdowns.
- Kernels: matmul and related; speedup vs single-core; activity and energy breakdowns.

## Results summary

- L1 access within five cycles without conflicts; <2% execution stalls.
- Peak 229 GOPS; energy efficiency up to 180 GOPS/W.
- Hierarchical interconnect and hybrid addressing keep network cost manageable vs full crossbar.
- Instruction-cache and tile energy breakdowns quantify IF and SPM costs at scale.
- Open RTL release enables SCORE MemPool flows.

## Contributions

- Shared-L1 manycore scaled to 256 Snitch cores with productive programming model.
- Low-latency hierarchical interconnect + hybrid addressing analysis.
- Optimized instruction path and DMA for streaming.
- 22FDX PPA characterization and open-source release.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Shows shared-L1 need not stop at tens of cores if PE latency tolerance and hierarchical NoC are co-designed.
- Analysis: Separates IF scaling (cache hierarchy) from data SPM scaling as the key to independent PE execution at 256 cores.

## Limitations and future work

- Integer Snitch focus (FP via FU options); not a Linux host SoC by itself.
- Results are post-layout / simulated silicon story for 22FDX instance; system-level DRAM/HBM integration outside core paper scope.
- Fig. 1 and Fig. 9 not listed as unique figure captions in Pass 0 detector set.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Direct counterexample to "shared L1 does not scale" with open RTL.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Coherence with CVA6 hosts, chiplet/HBM packaging, and FP-heavy Spatz/Snitch-FPU mixes.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE table row pairing MemPool (256 shared L1) vs Occamy (multi-cluster Snitch) vs Spatz (vector PE cluster).
- Analysis: Stress hybrid addressing under irregular graph kernels beyond dense matmul.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Strong SCORE MemPool primary paper with open repo and clear PPA numbers.
- Analysis: Programming model stays flat shared L1.

### Cons

- Analysis: Kernel suite emphasizes regular parallel patterns.
- Analysis: Physical design still hierarchical; not a flat one-cycle L1.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# NEORV32 (Verilog + VHDL)

Shared Track B note for both SCORE generate variants (same upstream repo).

- **SCORE scripts:**
  - VHDL: `install_neorv32_vhdl.sh` / `generate_neorv32_vhdl.sh` / `run_neorv32_vhdl.sh`
  - Verilog: `install_neorv32_verilog.sh` / `generate_neorv32_verilog.sh` / `run_neorv32_verilog.sh`
  - (README.md architectures table)
- **Upstream:** https://github.com/stnolting/neorv32
- **License:** `tools/neorv32/LICENSE` — BSD 3-Clause
- **Category:** full_soc_platform
- **ISA / language:** RISC-V RV32 (configurable extensions); primary RTL in **platform-independent VHDL**. README: "customizable microcontroller-like system on chip (SoC)"; optional all-Verilog path via `rtl/verilog` auto-conversion. SCORE Verilog export uses GHDL synthesis (`tools/neorv32-verilog`, VHDL→Verilog wrapper).
- **Bus / memory:** README SoC connectivity: "32-bit external bus interface - Wishbone-compatible ([XBUS](https://stnolting.github.io/neorv32/#_processor_external_bus_interface_xbus)); bridge for AXI4-compatible interfaces"; optional tightly-coupled IMEM/DMEM, caches, SMC (PSRAM/flash XIP).
- **Verification:**
  - Upstream README CI: Processor check, Verilog conversion, RISC-V ACT (`neorv32-riscv-act`); quote: "Passes the official RISC-V Architectural Certification Tests (ACT)".
  - SCORE VHDL generate: optional GHDL import/sim (`--verify`); organizes CPU/SoC/peripheral/test RTL under `rtl_designs/`.
  - SCORE Verilog generate: optional Icarus compile of `neorv32_verilog_wrapper.v` (`--verify`).
- **FPGA / silicon:** README: "tested on AMD, Intel, Lattice, Microchip, Gowin and Cologne Chip FPGAs"; "taped out several times as an ASIC."
- **Software:** README software framework: Zephyr, FreeRTOS, MicroPython, Rust (Embassy), nommu-Linux; RISC-V GCC toolchain documented in User Guide.
- **Primary paper (architecture):** none — upstream datasheets/user guides remain authoritative for SoC architecture (`source_notes/neorv32.md`).
- **Supplementary paper (coprocessor integration):** Sainz-Estébanez et al., DCIS 2024, DOI [10.1109/DCIS62603.2024.10769177](https://doi.org/10.1109/DCIS62603.2024.10769177) — digest `neorv32-dcis-2024/analysis.md`. Characterizes XBUS, Stream, CFS, and CFU attachment modes (not a platform overview).
- **Limitations (from upstream, quoted):**
  - README: SoC modules are "entirely _optional_" and configured via generics.
  - Verilog SCORE path depends on GHDL ≥3.0 synthesis (`--out=verilog`); generate script fails fast on older GHDL.
- **SCORE generate path:**
  - VHDL: `datasets/neorv32-vhdl/<8-char-commit>/rtl_designs/` (categories: `neorv32_cpu`, `neorv32_soc`, `neorv32_peripherals`, `neorv32_tests`); logs `datasets/neorv32-vhdl/<commit>/logs/`
  - Verilog: `datasets/neorv32-verilog/<8-char-commit>/rtl_designs/neorv32_verilog/` (GHDL-converted `neorv32_verilog_wrapper.v` per config); logs under same commit folder

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Occamy: A 432-Core Dual-Chiplet Dual-HBM2E 768-DP-GFLOP/s RISC-V System for 8-to-64-bit Dense and Sparse Computing in 12nm FinFET

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Paul Scheffler; Thomas Benz; Viviane Potocnik; Tim Fischer; Luca Colagrande; Nils Wistoff; Yichao Zhang; Luca Bertaccini; Gianmarco Ottavi; Manuel Eggimann; Matheus Cavalcante; Gianna Paulin; Frank K. Gurkaynak; Davide Rossi; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich; University of Bologna; Axelera AI; Stanford University |
| Venue | arXiv preprint (IEEE copyrighted author manuscript; extends prior 2-page abstract arXiv:2406.15068) |
| Venue type | preprint |
| Year | 2025 |
| Volume / issue / pages | arXiv:2501.07330v1, 16 pages |
| Paper DOI | Not assigned on this preprint |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07330 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/occamy |
| Keywords | 2.5D integration, chiplet, interposer, RISC-V manycore, sparse acceleration, stencil, multi-precision |
| Open access | Yes (arXiv + permissive open-source RTL) |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Authors Scheffler and Benz contributed equally. Extends prior Occamy abstract [33] / arXiv:2406.15068.

## TL;DR

- Full Occamy paper: dual-chiplet 432-core RV32G manycore with dual 16 GiB HBM2E, digital D2D, sparsity-capable streaming units (SUs), and hierarchical DMA/interconnect in GF 12LP+ (73 mm2 chiplets) on 65 nm Hedwig interposer.
- Dense LA: up to 89% FPU util, 686 GFLOP/s, 39.8 GFLOP/s/W; stencils 83% / 571 GFLOP/s / 28.1 GFLOP/s/W; SpMM 42% / 307 GFLOP/s; SpMSpM 187 GCOMP/s; GPT-J FP16 up to 75% FPU / 490 tok/s; GCN up to 54%.
- Claims first open-source silicon-proven multi-chiplet RISC-V manycore; RTL at pulp-platform/occamy.

## Problem statement

ML and HPC increasingly mix dense and sparse memory-access computation, but CPUs/GPUs keep high FPU utilization on dense work while dropping below ~50% on stencils and often below ~10% on sparse LA; domain-specific sparse accelerators lack flexibility across sparsity patterns and precision.

## Motivation

Build a programmable, silicon-proven RISC-V manycore that sustains high utilization on both dense and general sparse/stencil workloads via ISA streaming extensions and a latency-tolerant hierarchical chiplet memory system, without locking to one sparsity regime.

## Prior art

Dense-oriented CPUs/GPUs; sparse ML accelerators (low precision / structured sparsity); sparse LA and tensor engines; CGRA and ISA-extension sparse proposals often not silicon-proven at scale; prior Occamy 2-page abstract [33]; PULP Snitch-class cores, FPnew, iDMA, and related interconnect work.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: Silicon-measured dual-chiplet open RISC-V sparse/dense manycore with full architecture, programming, and SoA comparison.

## Method / approach

**Hierarchy (Fig. 1).** Two 216-core chiplets on Hedwig passive interposer; each chiplet: RV64 Linux host, six groups of four nine-core clusters (8 workers + DMA control), 16 GiB 8-channel HBM2E, chiplet DMA, 512b/64b interconnects, digital D2D.

**Cluster.** 128 KiB 32-bank SPM, 8 KiB shared L1 I$, shared mul/div, barriers, perf counters; workers have 64-bit SIMD FPU (FP64/32/16/8 + alts, widening ops), FREP hardware loops, three SUs (Fig. 2): 4D affine streams, indirect indexed streams, index union/intersection for SpMSpM/graphs; DMA core 512-bit <=2D transfers at up to 64 GiB/s into SPM superbanks.

**Group/chiplet.** Full-bandwidth AXI4 group interconnect; latency-tolerant 512-bit data network + 64-bit control/sync; hosts on separate control network.

**D2D (Fig. 3 in paper).** Wide + narrow source-synchronous segments with fault-tolerant PHY disable; measured 1.6 pJ/b wide segment; RTL-sim 96% utilization at 16 kB transfers.

**Programming.** SU-programmed streams for dense GEMM, SpMM, SpMSpM, stencils (Fig. 4); double-buffered DMA tiling overlapping transfer and compute.

**Silicon (Figs. 5-8).** GF 12LP+ chiplets ~73 mm2; Hedwig 65 nm; bring-up board ATE + standalone; 1 GHz nominal compute; measurements at 25 C.

## Experimental setup

- ATE bring-up with Keysight supplies; JTAG/UART automation; cycle-accurate simulation for unobservable FLOP/comparison counts.
- Workloads: FP64 dense LA / GEMM, stencil suite, SpMM/SpMSpM on real sparse matrices [38], FP64-to-FP8 GEMM SIMD, GCN layer on citation graphs, full FP16 GPT-J (FlashAttention-2), D2D bandwidth/fault/latency study.
- Comparison Table I vs silicon CPUs/GPUs (x86, Arm, RISC-V) with node-normalized compute density metrics.

## Results summary

- Dense LA (SU): 89% FPU util, 686 GFLOP/s, 39.8 GFLOP/s/W; avg dense SU speedup 2.4x / energy 1.5x vs RV32G.
- Stencils: up to 3.9x vs optimized baseline; 83% util, 571 GFLOP/s, 28.1 GFLOP/s/W (j3d27pt); node-normalized density up to 11.1 DP-GFLOP/s/mm2 (1.7x / 1.2x SoA util/density claims).
- SpMM: up to 4.6x, 307 GFLOP/s, 16.0 GFLOP/s/W, 42% util; density 5.95 DP-GFLOP/s/mm2 (5.2x / 11x SoA claims).
- SpMSpM: up to 3.6x, 187 GCOMP/s, 17.4 GCOMP/s/W, 49% comparator util, 3.63 GCOMP/s/mm2.
- Precision scaling: FP8 EXP GEMM 4.1 QP-TFLOP/s, 263 QP-GFLOP/s/W; util drops 89%->66% FP64->FP8 EXP.
- GCN: avg 2.2x SU speedup; peak 54% util, 413 DP-GFLOP/s, 25.0 DP-GFLOP/s/W on citeseer.
- GPT-J FP16: up to 490 tok/s, 29.3 tok/s/W, 75% FPU util at seq 128; throughput falls with longer sequences (attention/softmax).
- D2D: bandwidth scales with enabled PHYs; 96% util @16 kB; host narrow SPM access 27 cycles; DMA wide 61 cycles; 1.6 pJ/b measured.

## Contributions

- Full architecture of dual-chiplet Occamy with SUs, hierarchical interconnect, HBM2E, and digital D2D.
- Programming model for dense/sparse/stencil via SUs + double-buffered DMA.
- Silicon implementation details (chiplet, Hedwig, board) and extended measurements beyond the 2-page abstract (dense LA, multi-precision, ML apps, D2D).
- Quantitative SoA CPU/GPU comparison with node-normalized densities (Table I).
- Open RTL under permissive license (github.com/pulp-platform/occamy).

## Innovations

- Analysis: General-purpose sparsity via cooperating SUs (affine + indirect + index intersect/union) covers CSR/CSC/CSF-class formats without fixed sparsity assumptions.
- Analysis: Hierarchical chiplet SPM + 512b DMA/iDMA fabric sustains high FPU issue rates under irregular access better than cache-centric GPUs on sparse LA.
- Analysis: First claimed open multi-chiplet RISC-V manycore in silicon with measured D2D energy and fault-tolerant link disable.

## Limitations and future work

- Preprint IEEE author manuscript; journal/conference final citation may differ.
- Host is RV64 Linux-capable but application results focus on accelerator clusters; full OS multi-tenant studies limited.
- Extremely sparse operands limited by SU setup cost and SPM indexing range.
- GPT-J eval is non-autoregressive; attention softmax becomes bottleneck at long sequences.
- Pass 0 caption parser missed `Fig. N:` style (0 figure captions in audit); figures clipped manually for survey-critical set.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Sparse accelerators usually specialize; Occamy shows silicon manycore flexibility across dense, stencil, SpMM, SpMSpM, GCN, and LLM tiles in one open design.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Public software stack maturity, multi-user Linux scheduling on host+clusters, and third-party reproducibility of Table I normalization methodology need follow-on artifacts.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE registry: promote Occamy deep-dive with dual-chiplet, HBM2E, SU, and D2D evidence columns from this full paper (supersede abstract-only metrics where they differ in detail).
- Analysis: Compare Cheshire/Neo host plug-in vs Occamy dual-chiplet host for DSA attachment survey dimension.
- Analysis: Reproduce AutoDMA-style tiling questions from HEROv2 against Occamy double-buffered DMA+SU programming.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Deepest Occamy primary source for the survey (architecture + silicon + ML apps + SoA table).
- Analysis: Open RTL claim with concrete GitHub pointer.
- Analysis: Strong sparse vs dense utilization contrast vs CPU/GPU baselines.

### Cons

- Analysis: Author manuscript; finalize venue/DOI when published.
- Analysis: Measurement scripts/board not packaged as a public benchmark suite in the PDF.
- Analysis: Fig. caption style breaks automated Pass 0 extraction.

## Benchmarks and tables

### Table I: Comparison of Occamy to SoA silicon CPUs and GPUs

![Table I](./tables/table_01.png)

*Page 12 (landscape). Package, die tech/area, DRAM, SRAM/SPM, frequency, peak FP64, stencil and sparse-dense utilization/efficiency/density vs competitors. Key Occamy claims used in Section VI: dense 89% util / 39.8 DP-GFLOP/s/W; stencil 83% / 11.1 DP-GFLOP/s/mm2 normalized; sparse-dense 42% / 5.95 DP-GFLOP/s/mm2 normalized.*

## Figures

### Figure 1: Hierarchical Occamy chiplet architecture (clusters, groups, HBM2E, D2D).

![Figure 1](./figures/figure_01.png)

*Page 2. Bottom-up hierarchy from cluster SPM/SUs through groups to dual-chiplet module.*

### Figure 2: Three cooperating sparsity-capable streaming units per worker core.

![Figure 2](./figures/figure_02.png)

*Page 3. 4D/indirect address generators, FIFOs, and index union/intersection path to FPU.*

### Figure 5: Hedwig interposer and carrier PCB design.

![Figure 5](./figures/figure_05.png)

*Page 6. Passive interposer packaging for dual chiplets and HBM stacks.*

### Figure 6: Hierarchical area breakdown of the Occamy system.

![Figure 6](./figures/figure_06.png)

*Page 6. Area split across HBM PHY/controller, groups, interconnect, host, D2D.*

### Figure 7: Annotated physical layouts of chiplet hierarchical components.

![Figure 7](./figures/figure_07.png)

*Page 7. Floorplans with block IO highlighted.*

### Figure 9: FP64 dense, stencil, SpMM, SpMSpM performance/efficiency/power with/without SUs.

![Figure 9](./figures/figure_09.png)

*Page 9. Primary silicon result panel for double-buffered workloads.*

## Reproducibility

| Artifact | Link / status |
|----------|----------------|
| RTL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/occamy (permissive open-source) |
| Silicon | GF 12LP+ dual chiplet + 65 nm Hedwig; bring-up board described |
| Prior abstract | arXiv:2406.15068 (2-page); this paper is the extended version |
| Data | Measurement methodology in Section V; matrix suite cites [38] |

## References

1. Prior Occamy abstract / Scheffler et al. related chiplet work. DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
2. L. Bertaccini et al., multi-format FPU / ARITH. DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
3. P. Scheffler et al., streaming units / TPDS. DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
4. T. Benz et al., modular DMA / TCOMP. DOI: [10.1109/TC.2023.3348158](https://doi.org/10.1109/TC.2023.3348158) -- `[resolved]`

projects.fullMarkdown:
# OpenPiton: An Open Source Hardware Platform For Your Research

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Jonathan Balkind, Michael McKeown, Yaosheng Fu, Tri Nguyen, Yanqi Zhou, Alexey Lavrov, Mohammad Shahrad, Adi Fuchs, Samuel Payne, Xiaohua Liang, Matthew Matl, David Wentzlaff |
| Affiliations | Princeton University (Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering); author footnotes note subsequent affiliations (NVIDIA, Baidu SVAIL, Microsoft, UC Berkeley) for work done at Princeton |
| Venue | Communications of the ACM |
| Venue type | journal |
| Year | 2019 |
| Volume / issue / pages | Vol. 62, No. 12, pp. 79-88 (approx; PDF footers mark pages 79-87 of CACM content) |
| Paper DOI | https://doi.org/10.1145/3366343 |
| arXiv | |
| URL | https://doi.org/10.1145/3366343 |
| Keywords | manycore, open-source hardware, SPARC v9, NoC, FPGA, ASIC tape-out |
| Open access | ACM Research Highlights; original ASPLOS 2016 paper; publication rights licensed to ACM |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Original conference version: "OpenPiton: An Open Source Manycore Research Framework," ASPLOS 2016, Atlanta, GA, April 2-6, 2016, ACM.

## TL;DR

- OpenPiton is an open-source, configurable, general-purpose multithreaded manycore framework built on a modified OpenSPARC T1 core plus a scratch-built P-Mesh uncore (caches, coherence, NoCs, chipset).
- Address space scales to 500 million cores (65,536 cores/chip x up to 8192 chips); default intra-chip 2D mesh of three NoCs.
- Validated by the 25-core Piton ASIC (IBM 32nm SOI, March 2015, 6mm x 6mm, 1GHz target) and FPGA prototypes including PicoPiton on a $160 Artix-7 at 29.5 MHz.
- Boots full-stack multiuser Debian Linux on Genesys2 at 87.5 MHz in under 4 minutes (about 1 minute to bash).
- Released at http://www.openpiton.org with Verilog RTL, FPGA scripts, process-agnostic synthesis/back-end scripts, and thousands of tests.

## Problem statement

Industry builds large manycore processors with deep institutional knowledge, but academic projects struggle to replicate that scale without high fabrication risk and incomplete software/tooling. The community needs open architecture frameworks for simulation, chip design, and software exploration that are extensible, scalable, and configurable, with mature verification and OS support. Prior open designs often leave integration to the user, lack push-button manycore scalability, or miss full-stack Linux and ASIC back-end enablement.

## Motivation

Multicore/manycore chips multiply points of failure in academic tape-outs. Reducing academic time-to-publication requires industry-standard HDLs, robust software stacks, and thorough test suites. A shared baseline that spans one core to hundreds of millions of cores addressability enables OS, compiler, security, CAD, and architecture research at realistic scale, including multi-chip shared memory.

## Prior art

Builds on OpenSPARC T1 (Oracle) for a mature 64-bit SPARC v9 core, ISA toolchain, and large test suite. Positions against other open processors surveyed in Table 2 (April 2018), including LEON3, OpenRISC, Rocket/BOOM, PULP cores, OpTiMSoC, BERI, Simply RISC S1, and GPGPU projects (Nyuzi, MIAOW). Related manycore context includes industry designs such as Tilera/TILE, Intel Teraflops/80-tile, and Larrabee-style fabrics. OpenPiton differentiates with scratch-built P-Mesh coherence spanning chips, PyHP-driven configurability, ASIC tape-out scripts, and Debian Linux on FPGA/ASIC chipset flows.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Open-source tiled manycore platform with P-Mesh NoC/coherence, FPGA/ASIC flows, and silicon-proven 25-core Piton prototype.

## Method / approach

**Platform architecture.** Tiled manycore: each tile has a modified OpenSPARC T1 core, L1.5, distributed L2 slice, FPU, CCX arbiter, MITTS traffic shaper, and three P-Mesh NoC routers. Intra-chip tiles connect by three NoCs (default 2D mesh). A chip bridge extends NoCs off-chip to chipset logic (DRAM, I/O, inter-chip routers). Coherence extends across chips for multi-chip shared memory (Figure 1 conceptual architecture; Figure 2 tile and chipset).

**Core defaults (Piton).** Threads reduced from 4 to 2; stream-processing unit removed; TLB default 16 entries (configurable 8/16/32/64); added configuration registers for in-core research hooks.

**Cache hierarchy (Figure 3).** Private write-through L1 I/D (defaults 16KB I / 8KB D); write-back L1.5 (default matches L1D; inclusive of L1D; instructions bypass L1.5 to L2); distributed shared write-back L2 (default 64KB/tile, 4-way, 64B lines) as point of coherence with directory (64 bits/entry default). Three NoCs prioritized NoC3 > NoC2 > NoC1 for deadlock freedom: NoC1 L1.5->L2 requests; NoC2 L2->L1.5/memory; NoC3 L1.5/memory->L2 responses. Packet format: 29 bits of core addressability (up to ~500M cores).

**Configurability.** PyHP (Python Hypertext Processor) preprocesses Verilog for mesh generation (up to 256x256 tiles/chip), cache sizing, and chipset XML-driven device attachment (DRAM, Ethernet, UART, SD/SDHC, VGA, PS/2, MIAOW GPU, etc.). Topologies: intra-chip 2D mesh/crossbar; inter-chip 2D/3D mesh, crossbar, butterfly.

**Validation flow.** Open-source plus commercial Verilog simulators; thousands of directed/random assembly and C tests; coverage reports; SLURM parallel regression; Jenkins CI; synthesis-safe checks.

## Experimental setup

- **Piton ASIC:** IBM 32nm SOI, March 2015; 25 tiles in 5x5 mesh; die 6mm x 6mm; target 1GHz; research features ExecD, CDR, MITTS per tile plus chip-level ORAM; characterized with OpenPiton chipset on FPGA.
- **FPGA:** Artix-7 (Nexys Video / Nexys 4 DDR PicoPiton), Kintex-7 (Genesys2), Virtex-7 (VC707); Zynq-7000 (ZC706) external port; multi-FPGA via FMC; serial P-Mesh links at 9 Gb/s (Figure 7).
- **Software:** Bare-metal over UART; full-stack multiuser Debian Linux from SD/SDHC; hypervisor port changes fewer than 10 instructions relative to OpenSPARC T1.
- **CAD:** Process-agnostic synthesis and back-end scripts derived from Piton tape-out flow (foundry PDK linked by user).

## Results summary

- PicoPiton on ~$160 Artix-7 at 29.5 MHz; Genesys2 Debian boot at 87.5 MHz under 4 minutes full, ~1 minute to bash (vs ~45 minutes for tethered OpenSPARC T1 MicroBlaze I/O).
- Test-suite coverage by module shown in Figure 4 (overall score 50.96% annotated on figure for default configuration).
- FPGA PicoPiton tile area breakdown in Figure 5 (core dominant; L2, L1.5, FPU, NoC routers, CCX, misc).
- Piton area (Figure 6 / text): Chip 35.97552 mm2; Tile 1.17459 mm2; Core 0.55205 mm2 (~47% of tile).
- Silicon power/energy characterization (cited McKeown et al. HPCA 2018) open-sourced with PCB designs at openpiton.org.
- External uses: CAD reliability workflow (Lerner et al.), hardware Trojan detection via performance counters on Debian/SPEC (Elnaggar et al.), ORAM NoC integration, student HTM/cache-policy/MIAOW/topology projects; DARPA POSH benchmark; industrial CAD vendor testing.

## Contributions

- Open release of OpenPiton: first open-source general-purpose multithreaded manycore framework with shared-memory scaling goals to 500 million cores.
- Scratch-built P-Mesh uncore: three NoCs, directory coherence spanning chips, chipset bridge/crossbar, and configurable topologies.
- End-to-end research stack: Verilog RTL, PyHP configurability, FPGA scripts, ASIC synthesis/back-end scripts, thousands of tests, Debian Linux.
- Silicon validation via 25-core Piton prototype and detailed area/power characterization data release.
- Demonstrated research and education use cases (ExecD, CDR, MITTS, ORAM, CAD, security, coursework).

## Innovations

- Analysis: Unifies an industry-hardened SPARC core with a fully redesigned scalable coherence/NoC fabric rather than only releasing a core or a small SoC.
- Analysis: Treats multi-chip shared memory as a first-class design target (chip bridge + inter-chip routers + off-chip coherence), uncommon among contemporaneous open cores.
- Analysis: PyHP-based Verilog generation for arbitrary rectangular meshes and XML chipset composition lowers integration friction for CAD-scale netlists and heterogeneous I/O (including GPU attachment).
- Analysis: Coherence Domain Restriction (CDR) framed as necessary for directory storage at million-core scale within this platform.

## Limitations and future work

- Taxonomy (Table 2) last checked April 2018; RISC-V ecosystem has since expanded beyond the paper's snapshot.
- SPARC v9 / OpenSPARC T1 base may be less attractive than RISC-V for new software ecosystems (later OpenPiton+Ariane work is outside this CACM article).
- Coverage figure shows modest overall score (~51%) for default configuration modules; not a claim of industrial verification completeness.
- Back-end scripts are process-agnostic shells; users must supply proprietary PDKs.
- Future roadmap in paper: more configurability, more FPGA vendors, AWS F1 cloud emulation, additional core types, and integration with other open hardware projects.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Open cores surveyed in Table 2 (April 2018) often ship a core or small SoC without multi-chip shared-memory coherence, process-agnostic back-end scripts, and a silicon-proven 25-core manycore story in one package; industry manycores (TILE, Teraflops) were closed.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Taxonomy is frozen at April 2018; SPARC-centric software path aged relative to RISC-V; coverage ~51% and FPGA MHz leave verification/performance gaps; Figure 1 conceptual multi-chip diagram is not in the capture set.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Port or compare P-Mesh multi-chip coherence against modern RISC-V NoC platforms (ESP, Chipyard, BlackParrot) on identical FPGA multi-board fabrics (Figure 7 serial P-Mesh setup).
- Analysis: Re-run Table 2-style taxonomy with 2024+ open SoCs (Basilisk, Celerity, Occamy, etc.) using the same columns to quantify what OpenPiton uniquely retains (back-end scripts, HW MT, Chip/25 tape-out).
- Analysis: Use OpenPiton's process-agnostic tape-out scripts as a stress workload for open EDA (OpenROAD/OpenLane) versus the commercial flow used for Piton.
- Analysis: Quantify CDR directory storage vs global directory at 1K-64K core simulated scales; publish open directory-overhead curves for SCORE-style manycore surveys (builds on Fu et al. MICRO 2015 / ref 8).
- Analysis: Reproduce Genesys2 Linux boot timing and area breakdowns (Figures 5-6) on current Vivado/tool versions as a regression baseline for platform health.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Rare combination of open RTL, multi-chip coherence story, FPGA Linux, and real ASIC tape-out with released characterization data.
- Analysis: Strong safety net for modifiers (thousands of tests, CI hooks, documented extension points via CCX/NoC/XML).
- Analysis: Explicit CAD-research enablement (large netlists, synthesis scripts) beyond architecture-only audiences.

### Cons

- Analysis: Aging SPARC software story relative to RISC-V-centric open SoC momentum (mitigated outside this paper by later ports).
- Analysis: Figure clips from CACM single-column capture are tall column regions; some embeds include surrounding body text (especially Fig. 2/4), so visual assets need careful reading against captions.
- Analysis: Table 2 is a 2018 snapshot and image-only extraction; several contemporaries lack NoC/back-end scripts, which can overstate uniqueness without updating the census.
- Analysis: Overall reported test coverage (~51%) and academic FPGA MHz leave a gap versus industrial bring-up expectations.
