digestSections.tl;dr:
- OpenPiton is an open-source, configurable, general-purpose multithreaded manycore framework built on a modified OpenSPARC T1 core plus a scratch-built P-Mesh uncore (caches, coherence, NoCs, chipset).
- Address space scales to 500 million cores (65,536 cores/chip x up to 8192 chips); default intra-chip 2D mesh of three NoCs.
- Validated by the 25-core Piton ASIC (IBM 32nm SOI, March 2015, 6mm x 6mm, 1GHz target) and FPGA prototypes including PicoPiton on a $160 Artix-7 at 29.5 MHz.
- Boots full-stack multiuser Debian Linux on Genesys2 at 87.5 MHz in under 4 minutes (about 1 minute to bash).
- Released at http://www.openpiton.org with Verilog RTL, FPGA scripts, process-agnostic synthesis/back-end scripts, and thousands of tests.
digestSections.problem statement: Industry builds large manycore processors with deep institutional knowledge, but academic projects struggle to replicate that scale without high fabrication risk and incomplete software/tooling. The community needs open architecture frameworks for simulation, chip design, and software exploration that are extensible, scalable, and configurable, with mature verification and OS support. Prior open designs often leave integration to the user, lack push-button manycore scalability, or miss full-stack Linux and ASIC back-end enablement.
digestSections.motivation: Multicore/manycore chips multiply points of failure in academic tape-outs. Reducing academic time-to-publication requires industry-standard HDLs, robust software stacks, and thorough test suites. A shared baseline that spans one core to hundreds of millions of cores addressability enables OS, compiler, security, CAD, and architecture research at realistic scale, including multi-chip shared memory.
digestSections.prior art: Builds on OpenSPARC T1 (Oracle) for a mature 64-bit SPARC v9 core, ISA toolchain, and large test suite. Positions against other open processors surveyed in Table 2 (April 2018), including LEON3, OpenRISC, Rocket/BOOM, PULP cores, OpTiMSoC, BERI, Simply RISC S1, and GPGPU projects (Nyuzi, MIAOW). Related manycore context includes industry designs such as Tilera/TILE, Intel Teraflops/80-tile, and Larrabee-style fabrics. OpenPiton differentiates with scratch-built P-Mesh coherence spanning chips, PyHP-driven configurability, ASIC tape-out scripts, and Debian Linux on FPGA/ASIC chipset flows.
digestSections.category of work:
Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Open-source tiled manycore platform with P-Mesh NoC/coherence, FPGA/ASIC flows, and silicon-proven 25-core Piton prototype.
digestSections.method / approach:
**Platform architecture.** Tiled manycore: each tile has a modified OpenSPARC T1 core, L1.5, distributed L2 slice, FPU, CCX arbiter, MITTS traffic shaper, and three P-Mesh NoC routers. Intra-chip tiles connect by three NoCs (default 2D mesh). A chip bridge extends NoCs off-chip to chipset logic (DRAM, I/O, inter-chip routers). Coherence extends across chips for multi-chip shared memory (Figure 1 conceptual architecture; Figure 2 tile and chipset).

**Core defaults (Piton).** Threads reduced from 4 to 2; stream-processing unit removed; TLB default 16 entries (configurable 8/16/32/64); added configuration registers for in-core research hooks.

**Cache hierarchy (Figure 3).** Private write-through L1 I/D (defaults 16KB I / 8KB D); write-back L1.5 (default matches L1D; inclusive of L1D; instructions bypass L1.5 to L2); distributed shared write-back L2 (default 64KB/tile, 4-way, 64B lines) as point of coherence with directory (64 bits/entry default). Three NoCs prioritized NoC3 > NoC2 > NoC1 for deadlock freedom: NoC1 L1.5->L2 requests; NoC2 L2->L1.5/memory; NoC3 L1.5/memory->L2 responses. Packet format: 29 bits of core addressability (up to ~500M cores).

**Configurability.** PyHP (Python Hypertext Processor) preprocesses Verilog for mesh generation (up to 256x256 tiles/chip), cache sizing, and chipset XML-driven device attachment (DRAM, Ethernet, UART, SD/SDHC, VGA, PS/2, MIAOW GPU, etc.). Topologies: intra-chip 2D mesh/crossbar; inter-chip 2D/3D mesh, crossbar, butterfly.

**Validation flow.** Open-source plus commercial Verilog simulators; thousands of directed/random assembly and C tests; coverage reports; SLURM parallel regression; Jenkins CI; synthesis-safe checks.
digestSections.experimental setup:
- **Piton ASIC:** IBM 32nm SOI, March 2015; 25 tiles in 5x5 mesh; die 6mm x 6mm; target 1GHz; research features ExecD, CDR, MITTS per tile plus chip-level ORAM; characterized with OpenPiton chipset on FPGA.
- **FPGA:** Artix-7 (Nexys Video / Nexys 4 DDR PicoPiton), Kintex-7 (Genesys2), Virtex-7 (VC707); Zynq-7000 (ZC706) external port; multi-FPGA via FMC; serial P-Mesh links at 9 Gb/s (Figure 7).
- **Software:** Bare-metal over UART; full-stack multiuser Debian Linux from SD/SDHC; hypervisor port changes fewer than 10 instructions relative to OpenSPARC T1.
- **CAD:** Process-agnostic synthesis and back-end scripts derived from Piton tape-out flow (foundry PDK linked by user).
digestSections.results summary:
- PicoPiton on ~$160 Artix-7 at 29.5 MHz; Genesys2 Debian boot at 87.5 MHz under 4 minutes full, ~1 minute to bash (vs ~45 minutes for tethered OpenSPARC T1 MicroBlaze I/O).
- Test-suite coverage by module shown in Figure 4 (overall score 50.96% annotated on figure for default configuration).
- FPGA PicoPiton tile area breakdown in Figure 5 (core dominant; L2, L1.5, FPU, NoC routers, CCX, misc).
- Piton area (Figure 6 / text): Chip 35.97552 mm2; Tile 1.17459 mm2; Core 0.55205 mm2 (~47% of tile).
- Silicon power/energy characterization (cited McKeown et al. HPCA 2018) open-sourced with PCB designs at openpiton.org.
- External uses: CAD reliability workflow (Lerner et al.), hardware Trojan detection via performance counters on Debian/SPEC (Elnaggar et al.), ORAM NoC integration, student HTM/cache-policy/MIAOW/topology projects; DARPA POSH benchmark; industrial CAD vendor testing.
digestSections.contributions:
- Open release of OpenPiton: first open-source general-purpose multithreaded manycore framework with shared-memory scaling goals to 500 million cores.
- Scratch-built P-Mesh uncore: three NoCs, directory coherence spanning chips, chipset bridge/crossbar, and configurable topologies.
- End-to-end research stack: Verilog RTL, PyHP configurability, FPGA scripts, ASIC synthesis/back-end scripts, thousands of tests, Debian Linux.
- Silicon validation via 25-core Piton prototype and detailed area/power characterization data release.
- Demonstrated research and education use cases (ExecD, CDR, MITTS, ORAM, CAD, security, coursework).
digestSections.innovations:
- Analysis: Unifies an industry-hardened SPARC core with a fully redesigned scalable coherence/NoC fabric rather than only releasing a core or a small SoC.
- Analysis: Treats multi-chip shared memory as a first-class design target (chip bridge + inter-chip routers + off-chip coherence), uncommon among contemporaneous open cores.
- Analysis: PyHP-based Verilog generation for arbitrary rectangular meshes and XML chipset composition lowers integration friction for CAD-scale netlists and heterogeneous I/O (including GPU attachment).
- Analysis: Coherence Domain Restriction (CDR) framed as necessary for directory storage at million-core scale within this platform.
digestSections.limitations and future work:
- Taxonomy (Table 2) last checked April 2018; RISC-V ecosystem has since expanded beyond the paper's snapshot.
- SPARC v9 / OpenSPARC T1 base may be less attractive than RISC-V for new software ecosystems (later OpenPiton+Ariane work is outside this CACM article).
- Coverage figure shows modest overall score (~51%) for default configuration modules; not a claim of industrial verification completeness.
- Back-end scripts are process-agnostic shells; users must supply proprietary PDKs.
- Future roadmap in paper: more configurability, more FPGA vendors, AWS F1 cloud emulation, additional core types, and integration with other open hardware projects.
digestSections.research opportunity:
**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Open cores surveyed in Table 2 (April 2018) often ship a core or small SoC without multi-chip shared-memory coherence, process-agnostic back-end scripts, and a silicon-proven 25-core manycore story in one package; industry manycores (TILE, Teraflops) were closed.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Taxonomy is frozen at April 2018; SPARC-centric software path aged relative to RISC-V; coverage ~51% and FPGA MHz leave verification/performance gaps; Figure 1 conceptual multi-chip diagram is not in the capture set.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Port or compare P-Mesh multi-chip coherence against modern RISC-V NoC platforms (ESP, Chipyard, BlackParrot) on identical FPGA multi-board fabrics (Figure 7 serial P-Mesh setup).
- Analysis: Re-run Table 2-style taxonomy with 2024+ open SoCs (Basilisk, Celerity, Occamy, etc.) using the same columns to quantify what OpenPiton uniquely retains (back-end scripts, HW MT, Chip/25 tape-out).
- Analysis: Use OpenPiton's process-agnostic tape-out scripts as a stress workload for open EDA (OpenROAD/OpenLane) versus the commercial flow used for Piton.
- Analysis: Quantify CDR directory storage vs global directory at 1K-64K core simulated scales; publish open directory-overhead curves for SCORE-style manycore surveys (builds on Fu et al. MICRO 2015 / ref 8).
- Analysis: Reproduce Genesys2 Linux boot timing and area breakdowns (Figures 5-6) on current Vivado/tool versions as a regression baseline for platform health.
digestSections.pros and cons:
### Pros

- Analysis: Rare combination of open RTL, multi-chip coherence story, FPGA Linux, and real ASIC tape-out with released characterization data.
- Analysis: Strong safety net for modifiers (thousands of tests, CI hooks, documented extension points via CCX/NoC/XML).
- Analysis: Explicit CAD-research enablement (large netlists, synthesis scripts) beyond architecture-only audiences.

### Cons

- Analysis: Aging SPARC software story relative to RISC-V-centric open SoC momentum (mitigated outside this paper by later ports).
- Analysis: Figure clips from CACM single-column capture are tall column regions; some embeds include surrounding body text (especially Fig. 2/4), so visual assets need careful reading against captions.
- Analysis: Table 2 is a 2018 snapshot and image-only extraction; several contemporaries lack NoC/back-end scripts, which can overstate uniqueness without updating the census.
- Analysis: Overall reported test coverage (~51%) and academic FPGA MHz leave a gap versus industrial bring-up expectations.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# A Lightweight High-Throughput Collective-Capable NoC for Large-Scale ML Accelerators

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Luca Colagrande; Lorenzo Leone; Chen Wu; Tim Fischer; Raphael Roth; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich |
| Venue | arXiv preprint (MLSys-style extended report) |
| Venue type | preprint |
| Year | 2026 |
| Paper DOI | not found |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26438 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/picobello |
| Keywords | Collective NoC, multicast, reduction, DCA, ML accelerator mesh |
| Open access | arXiv |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- Presents a collective-capable mesh NoC with hardware barrier, multicast, and in-network reduction (Direct Compute Access) for large ML accelerators.
- DCA adds 16.9% router area; 5.3× geomean multicast and 2.8× reduction speedups (1–32 KiB); up to 3.8× / 2.4× estimated GEMM performance vs unicast baseline; 1.17× energy savings.
- Co-designed for next-generation open ML accelerator platforms including Picobello/FlooNoC ecosystem.

## Problem statement

On-chip ML meshes need collective communication (barrier, multicast, reduction) but software or unicast NoCs leave communication on the critical path as PE counts scale.

## Motivation

Technology scaling enables thousand-PE dies where on-chip collectives resemble distributed systems; lightweight in-network support avoids memory-bound software reductions.

## Prior art

FlooNoC; NVIDIA/mesh GPU collectives; software multicast/reduction on scratchpad meshes; prior PULP manycore networks.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`, `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture Picobello (platform using collective NoC class).

## Method / approach

**Collective NoC.** Barrier, multicast, and reduction integrated in router fabric.

**Direct Compute Access (DCA).** Interconnect accesses PE compute resources for in-network reductions (+16.9% router area).

**Evaluation.** Compare vs unicast baseline on GEMM and collective microbenchmarks; placed-and-routed router implementations (Figs. 2–3).

## Experimental setup

- RTL simulation and place-and-route on representative router/mesh configs.
- Data sizes 1–32 KiB for multicast/reduction microbenchmarks.
- GEMM workload scaling on large meshes.

## Results summary

- Multicast: 5.3× geomean speedup; reduction: 2.8× geomean speedup.
- GEMM: up to 3.8× (multicast) and 2.4× (reduction) estimated performance vs unicast NoC; up to 1.17× energy savings.
- DCA router area overhead 16.9%.

## Contributions

- Collective-capable lightweight NoC design for ML accelerators.
- DCA paradigm for in-network reductions.
- Quantified speedups on collectives and estimated full-workload gains.

## Innovations

- DCA couples NoC flits to PE compute for high-throughput reductions with modest router area increase.

## Limitations and future work

- Long arXiv report — primary Picobello silicon PPA may be documented elsewhere.
- Some results simulation/estimation-based for full GEMM scaling.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Open collectives NoC RTL with P&R area breakdown rarely published for ML meshes.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: End-to-end Picobello tapeout metrics paired with this NoC in SCORE remain to be cross-linked.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Map digest to SCORE `picobello` generate outputs and FlooNoC dependencies.
- Analysis: Compare collective NoC vs MAGIA mesh sync (FractalSync) in survey interconnect section.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Strong quantitative collective speedups with open ETH/PULP authorship line.
- Analysis: Best available Track A evidence for Picobello-class interconnect until dedicated Picobello silicon paper.

### Cons

- Analysis: Preprint; platform naming emphasizes NoC layer over full Picobello SoC scope.
- Analysis: 20-page report — digest captures headline metrics only.

*Mid-report. Aggregated multicast/reduction speedup and GEMM scaling summary table — values captured in Results summary (5.3× multicast, 2.8× reduction geomean).*

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Energy-Efficient Near-Threshold Parallel Computing: The PULPv2 Cluster

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Davide Rossi; Antonio Pullini; Igor Loi; Michael Gautschi; Frank Kagan Gurkaynak; Adam Teman; Jeremy Constantin; Andreas Burg; Ivan Miro-Panades; Edith Beigne; Fabien Clermidy; Philippe Flatresse; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | University of Bologna; ETH Zurich; EPFL; CEA-LETI; STMicroelectronics |
| Venue | IEEE Micro (Cool Chips theme) |
| Venue type | journal |
| Year | 2017 |
| Volume / issue / pages | Vol. 37, No. 5, pp. 20-31 (September/October 2017) |
| Paper DOI | https://doi.org/10.1109/MM.2017.3711645 |
| arXiv | |
| URL | https://doi.org/10.1109/MM.2017.3711645 |
| Keywords | near-threshold computing, FD-SOI, body biasing, multicore cluster, TCDM, OpenRISC, IoT, ultra-low-power |
| Open access | IEEE Xplore (institutional); no arXiv copy identified |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Theme article: Cool Chips. Published by the IEEE Computer Society. ISSN 0272-1732.

## TL;DR

- Second-generation Parallel Ultra-Low-Power (PULPv2) SoC: 4-core OpenRISC cluster in 28 nm UTBB FD-SOI flip-well with aggressive forward body bias (FBB).
- Heterogeneous TCDM (SRAM + SCM), L1 MMUs, and reconfigurable pipeline stages (RPS) tune latency, banking, and active banks at runtime.
- Silicon: 193 MOPS/mW at 162 MOPS; up to 825 MHz with max FBB; design goal 1 GOPS within 10 mW met (0.66 V, 0.5 V FBB).
- Improves PULPv1 by 6.4x performance and 3.2x energy efficiency; outperforms cited ULP MCUs / wide-range DSPs by 1.3-7.6x in efficiency.
- SCORE note: historical silicon ancestor of the open `pulp_cluster` template (this chip uses OpenRISC; later PULP clusters moved to RISC-V).

## Problem statement

Near-sensor IoT workloads need GOPS-class flexible compute inside a few-mW envelope. Near-threshold (NT) operation improves energy efficiency but collapses single-core peak performance and worsens PVT sensitivity and SRAM reliability. Prior ULP MCUs reach roughly 100 MOPS/mW yet only tens of MOPS peak; wide voltage-range DSPs recover performance at the cost of efficiency. Parallel Ultra-Low-Power (PULP) must deliver both high efficiency and usable parallel performance across a wide voltage range while managing memory and variability bottlenecks.

## Motivation

IoT sensing (cameras, mic arrays, vital signs) needs programmable parallel compute, not fixed accelerators alone. PULP pairs tightly coupled multicore parallelism with body biasing as a second control knob versus pure VDD scaling. FD-SOI flip-well LVT devices plus FBB extend operation down to 0.32 V and recover frequency at NT. Architecture-level knobs (heterogeneous L1 memory, MMUs, RPS, fine-grained clock gating / BB regions) are needed so sequential phases and memory-bound phases do not destroy cluster efficiency.

## Prior art

Builds on PULPv1 (Rossi et al.) in conventional-well FD-SOI. Contrasts NT MCUs (Sleepwalker, REISC) and wide-range DSPs (HEXAGON, FRISBEE). Cites NT computing surveys, FD-SOI FBB techniques, SCM placement optimization, variation-tolerant shared-L1 clusters, and closed-loop BB compensation SoCs. Positions PULPv2 as a parallel NT platform rather than a single-core ULP MCU or high-clock VLIW DSP.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: Silicon-proven near-threshold multicore cluster SoC with memory/power-management microarchitecture; historical PULP cluster reference (OpenRISC ISA generation).

## Method / approach

**SoC organization (Fig. 1).** Two voltage/frequency domains: (1) tightly coupled 4-core cluster; (2) L2 memory + peripherals. Cluster crosses SoC AXI4 via DC FIFOs and level shifters; private FLL clock tree; fully clock-gateable.

**Cores.** Four-stage in-order OpenRISC cores (~30 KGE each), architectural clock gating on 98% of registers, private 1 Kbyte direct-mapped I$, no private D$ (shared TCDM instead). Toolchain: GCC 4.9 / LLVM 3.7; OpenMP 3.0 on bare-metal runtime.

**TCDM and interconnect.** Eight word-interleaved banks through a nonblocking interconnect; tightly coupled DMA for off-cluster L2/peripheral traffic over AXI4. Heterogeneous banks: 6T SRAM (BB on periphery) + fully body-biased SCM banks; I$ also SCM. Controlled SCM placement: 3.3x less active energy and 2.2x less leakage vs equivalent SRAM, 2.7x area (vs >4x naive SCM); cluster-level +38% efficiency vs all-SRAM TCDM.

**Reconfigurable pipeline stages (RPS).** Request/response pipeline blocks around SRAM paths address three voltage regions (above 0.7 V SRAM not limiting; 0.55-0.7 V degrading; below 0.55 V SRAM delay dominates). Up to +30% frequency (Fig. 3) at up to +2 cycles load/store latency; per-bank activation via peripheral registers.

**Selective FBB / PMU (Fig. 4).** Cluster partitioned into clock-gating and body-bias regions (cores, SCM, SRAM groups, interconnect). Fine-grained FBB limits leakage blow-up vs whole-cluster boost (example: 2 V FBB whole-cluster leakage x80 vs ~x32 if one core biased). Active/sleep sequencing: disable fetch, drain transactions, clock-gate, switch BB.

**L1 MMUs (Fig. 5).** Lightweight address remapping separates shared interleaved vs private contiguous regions; unused SRAM/SCM banks can power down. Improves TCDM contention and enables bank sleep for energy.

## Experimental setup

- Process: UTBB FD-SOI 28 nm flip-well, L=24 nm; cluster area 1.3 mm2; ~200K gates (Fig. 2).
- Memories: 8x32 Kbit SRAM TCDM; 16x4 Kbit SCM TCDM; 4x2x4 Kbit SCM I$; 64 Kbyte L2 high-density SRAM.
- Voltage / BB: VDD 0.32-1.15 V (SRAMs 0.45-1.15 V); BB 0-1.75 V.
- Frequency / power envelopes (Fig. 2): no BB 40.5-710 MHz / 0.56-85 mW; max FBB 63.5-825 MHz / 6.9-480 mW.
- Silicon measurements of frequency, energy efficiency, power vs VDD/FBB (Fig. 6); comparison vs ULP designs (Fig. 7, Table 1).
- Architectural benchmarks (Table 2): MatrixMul, Convolution, Sparse, DCT, SOR, LU, Dijkstra; single-core vs multicore; RPS on; MMU on. Nominal point for normalized metrics: 0.65 V, 0.5 V FBB, 250 MHz (RPS off) -> 1 GOPS @ 10 mW, 100 MOPS/mW multicore peak efficiency target.

## Results summary

- Peak energy efficiency: **193 MOPS/mW at 162 MOPS** (0.46 V, 0-V FBB); cluster power 840 uW at 40.5 MHz in that regime (text; Fig. 6).
- Within ~10 mW: ~100 MOPS/mW design goal; **1 GOPS at 0.66 V, 0.5 V FBB**.
- vs PULPv1: **6.4x performance**, **3.2x energy efficiency**.
- vs recent ULP MCUs / wide-range DSPs: energy-efficiency advantage **1.3x to 7.6x** (Fig. 7); Table 1 peak 3.3 GOPS, best power density 20.7 uW/MHz, max 825 MHz.
- Parallel kernels (MatrixMul, Convolution, Sparse, DCT, SOR): near-ideal speedups ~3.4-3.7x; MMU raises MatrixMul speedup to 3.92x and adds ~10-13% energy-efficiency.
- Pathological / sequential cases (LU, Dijkstra): limited or negative speedup; high I$ stalls / slave sleep; power management still improves single-core efficiency via clock gating unused cores.
- RPS: up to ~35% cycle increase on some kernels but VDD scaling can recover energy; MMU consistently helps efficiency on contended kernels.

## Contributions

- Present PULPv2, a second-generation NT parallel SoC in 28 nm FD-SOI flip-well with measured 193 MOPS/mW and 1 GOPS / 10 mW capability.
- Combine heterogeneous SCM/SRAM TCDM, RPS, L1 MMUs, and fine-grained FBB/clock-gating regions as runtime knobs for NT variability and application mix.
- Quantify silicon PPA and architectural IPC/stall/speedup/energy on representative signal-processing and irregular kernels.
- Show clear gains over PULPv1 and published ULP MCU / wide-range DSP points in the same Cool Chips comparison frame.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Treats FD-SOI FBB not only as a global turbo but as a selective boost for sequential bottlenecks inside a parallel cluster.
- Analysis: Heterogeneous TCDM + MMU remapping jointly attack SRAM Vmin and banking conflict / bank sleep, which are usually handled in isolation.
- Analysis: RPS makes SRAM timing a configurable pipeline depth rather than a hard Vmin floor, trading latency for frequency in the 0.55-0.7 V band.
- Analysis: Establishes the PULP "cluster as independent clock/power domain with TCDM + DMA" template later reused (and ISA-ported) across open PULP platforms.

## Limitations and future work

- ISA is OpenRISC; modern open `pulp_cluster` / SCORE row is RISC-V-centric -- this paper is the silicon/architecture ancestor, not bit-identical to today's RTL.
- Evaluation focuses on signal-processing / graph-ish kernels; no DNN end-to-end stacks (those appear in later PULP generations).
- Authors note future work on heterogeneous memory + deeper NT for the tightly coupled cluster (Conclusion).
- Commercial FD-SOI / ST fabrication; not an open-PDK tapeout.
- Table 2 footnotes define a specific nominal operating point; cross-paper comparison must keep that normalization in mind.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: ULP MCU papers maximize MOPS/mW at tiny absolute MOPS; DSP papers maximize GHz; few open multicore templates publish full NT silicon with bank-level memory/power knobs.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: OpenRISC-to-RISC-V migration impact on the same microarchitectural knobs is not measured here; later Conti et al. PULP survey covers evolution but not this chip's raw tables.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Use this digest as the primary silicon reference for SCORE **PULP cluster**, and map Fig. 1 blocks onto today's `pulp_cluster` RTL (cores, HCI/TCDM, DMA, PMU) for a continuity table in `PAPER.md`.
- Analysis: Reproduce Table 2 stall taxonomy (core / I$ / TCDM / slave sleep) as a checklist when characterizing later RISC-V PULP clusters (HERO, Carfield, Chimera).
- Analysis: Quantify how much of the 193 MOPS/mW result is process (FD-SOI FBB) vs architecture (SCM TCDM + MMU + RPS) by comparing against later bulk/FinFET PULP silicon at matched ISA.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Complete silicon story: micrograph, V/F/P envelopes, architectural counters, and peer comparison in one short IEEE Micro article.
- Runtime knobs (MMU, RPS, BB regions) are concrete and measurable, not only process tricks.
- Directly anchors the SCORE PULP cluster lineage with published NT efficiency numbers.

### Cons

- OpenRISC ISA limits drop-in comparison to current RISC-V SCORE builds without an ISA caveat.
- Cool Chips overview length constrains RTL/open-source release discussion (platform openness matured later).
- Some pathological parallelization cases show efficiency collapse -- cluster value is workload-dependent.

### Figure 1: Parallel Ultra-Low-Power version 2 (PULPv2) system-on-chip (SoC) architecture. The SoC is split into two separate voltage and frequency domains, with one including the tightly coupled multiprocessor cluster, and one containing the level-2 (L2) memory and the peripherals.

digestSections.tl;dr:
- Second-generation Parallel Ultra-Low-Power (PULPv2) SoC: 4-core OpenRISC cluster in 28 nm UTBB FD-SOI flip-well with aggressive forward body bias (FBB).
- Heterogeneous TCDM (SRAM + SCM), L1 MMUs, and reconfigurable pipeline stages (RPS) tune latency, banking, and active banks at runtime.
- Silicon: 193 MOPS/mW at 162 MOPS; up to 825 MHz with max FBB; design goal 1 GOPS within 10 mW met (0.66 V, 0.5 V FBB).
- Improves PULPv1 by 6.4x performance and 3.2x energy efficiency; outperforms cited ULP MCUs / wide-range DSPs by 1.3-7.6x in efficiency.
- SCORE note: historical silicon ancestor of the open `pulp_cluster` template (this chip uses OpenRISC; later PULP clusters moved to RISC-V).
digestSections.problem statement: Near-sensor IoT workloads need GOPS-class flexible compute inside a few-mW envelope. Near-threshold (NT) operation improves energy efficiency but collapses single-core peak performance and worsens PVT sensitivity and SRAM reliability. Prior ULP MCUs reach roughly 100 MOPS/mW yet only tens of MOPS peak; wide voltage-range DSPs recover performance at the cost of efficiency. Parallel Ultra-Low-Power (PULP) must deliver both high efficiency and usable parallel performance across a wide voltage range while managing memory and variability bottlenecks.
digestSections.motivation: IoT sensing (cameras, mic arrays, vital signs) needs programmable parallel compute, not fixed accelerators alone. PULP pairs tightly coupled multicore parallelism with body biasing as a second control knob versus pure VDD scaling. FD-SOI flip-well LVT devices plus FBB extend operation down to 0.32 V and recover frequency at NT. Architecture-level knobs (heterogeneous L1 memory, MMUs, RPS, fine-grained clock gating / BB regions) are needed so sequential phases and memory-bound phases do not destroy cluster efficiency.
digestSections.prior art: Builds on PULPv1 (Rossi et al.) in conventional-well FD-SOI. Contrasts NT MCUs (Sleepwalker, REISC) and wide-range DSPs (HEXAGON, FRISBEE). Cites NT computing surveys, FD-SOI FBB techniques, SCM placement optimization, variation-tolerant shared-L1 clusters, and closed-loop BB compensation SoCs. Positions PULPv2 as a parallel NT platform rather than a single-core ULP MCU or high-clock VLIW DSP.
digestSections.category of work:
Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: Silicon-proven near-threshold multicore cluster SoC with memory/power-management microarchitecture; historical PULP cluster reference (OpenRISC ISA generation).
digestSections.method / approach:
**SoC organization (Fig. 1).** Two voltage/frequency domains: (1) tightly coupled 4-core cluster; (2) L2 memory + peripherals. Cluster crosses SoC AXI4 via DC FIFOs and level shifters; private FLL clock tree; fully clock-gateable.

**Cores.** Four-stage in-order OpenRISC cores (~30 KGE each), architectural clock gating on 98% of registers, private 1 Kbyte direct-mapped I$, no private D$ (shared TCDM instead). Toolchain: GCC 4.9 / LLVM 3.7; OpenMP 3.0 on bare-metal runtime.

**TCDM and interconnect.** Eight word-interleaved banks through a nonblocking interconnect; tightly coupled DMA for off-cluster L2/peripheral traffic over AXI4. Heterogeneous banks: 6T SRAM (BB on periphery) + fully body-biased SCM banks; I$ also SCM. Controlled SCM placement: 3.3x less active energy and 2.2x less leakage vs equivalent SRAM, 2.7x area (vs >4x naive SCM); cluster-level +38% efficiency vs all-SRAM TCDM.

**Reconfigurable pipeline stages (RPS).** Request/response pipeline blocks around SRAM paths address three voltage regions (above 0.7 V SRAM not limiting; 0.55-0.7 V degrading; below 0.55 V SRAM delay dominates). Up to +30% frequency (Fig. 3) at up to +2 cycles load/store latency; per-bank activation via peripheral registers.

**Selective FBB / PMU (Fig. 4).** Cluster partitioned into clock-gating and body-bias regions (cores, SCM, SRAM groups, interconnect). Fine-grained FBB limits leakage blow-up vs whole-cluster boost (example: 2 V FBB whole-cluster leakage x80 vs ~x32 if one core biased). Active/sleep sequencing: disable fetch, drain transactions, clock-gate, switch BB.

**L1 MMUs (Fig. 5).** Lightweight address remapping separates shared interleaved vs private contiguous regions; unused SRAM/SCM banks can power down. Improves TCDM contention and enables bank sleep for energy.
digestSections.experimental setup:
- Process: UTBB FD-SOI 28 nm flip-well, L=24 nm; cluster area 1.3 mm2; ~200K gates (Fig. 2).
- Memories: 8x32 Kbit SRAM TCDM; 16x4 Kbit SCM TCDM; 4x2x4 Kbit SCM I$; 64 Kbyte L2 high-density SRAM.
- Voltage / BB: VDD 0.32-1.15 V (SRAMs 0.45-1.15 V); BB 0-1.75 V.
- Frequency / power envelopes (Fig. 2): no BB 40.5-710 MHz / 0.56-85 mW; max FBB 63.5-825 MHz / 6.9-480 mW.
- Silicon measurements of frequency, energy efficiency, power vs VDD/FBB (Fig. 6); comparison vs ULP designs (Fig. 7, Table 1).
- Architectural benchmarks (Table 2): MatrixMul, Convolution, Sparse, DCT, SOR, LU, Dijkstra; single-core vs multicore; RPS on; MMU on. Nominal point for normalized metrics: 0.65 V, 0.5 V FBB, 250 MHz (RPS off) -> 1 GOPS @ 10 mW, 100 MOPS/mW multicore peak efficiency target.
digestSections.results summary:
- Peak energy efficiency: **193 MOPS/mW at 162 MOPS** (0.46 V, 0-V FBB); cluster power 840 uW at 40.5 MHz in that regime (text; Fig. 6).
- Within ~10 mW: ~100 MOPS/mW design goal; **1 GOPS at 0.66 V, 0.5 V FBB**.
- vs PULPv1: **6.4x performance**, **3.2x energy efficiency**.
- vs recent ULP MCUs / wide-range DSPs: energy-efficiency advantage **1.3x to 7.6x** (Fig. 7); Table 1 peak 3.3 GOPS, best power density 20.7 uW/MHz, max 825 MHz.
- Parallel kernels (MatrixMul, Convolution, Sparse, DCT, SOR): near-ideal speedups ~3.4-3.7x; MMU raises MatrixMul speedup to 3.92x and adds ~10-13% energy-efficiency.
- Pathological / sequential cases (LU, Dijkstra): limited or negative speedup; high I$ stalls / slave sleep; power management still improves single-core efficiency via clock gating unused cores.
- RPS: up to ~35% cycle increase on some kernels but VDD scaling can recover energy; MMU consistently helps efficiency on contended kernels.
digestSections.contributions:
- Present PULPv2, a second-generation NT parallel SoC in 28 nm FD-SOI flip-well with measured 193 MOPS/mW and 1 GOPS / 10 mW capability.
- Combine heterogeneous SCM/SRAM TCDM, RPS, L1 MMUs, and fine-grained FBB/clock-gating regions as runtime knobs for NT variability and application mix.
- Quantify silicon PPA and architectural IPC/stall/speedup/energy on representative signal-processing and irregular kernels.
- Show clear gains over PULPv1 and published ULP MCU / wide-range DSP points in the same Cool Chips comparison frame.
digestSections.innovations:
- Analysis: Treats FD-SOI FBB not only as a global turbo but as a selective boost for sequential bottlenecks inside a parallel cluster.
- Analysis: Heterogeneous TCDM + MMU remapping jointly attack SRAM Vmin and banking conflict / bank sleep, which are usually handled in isolation.
- Analysis: RPS makes SRAM timing a configurable pipeline depth rather than a hard Vmin floor, trading latency for frequency in the 0.55-0.7 V band.
- Analysis: Establishes the PULP "cluster as independent clock/power domain with TCDM + DMA" template later reused (and ISA-ported) across open PULP platforms.
digestSections.limitations and future work:
- ISA is OpenRISC; modern open `pulp_cluster` / SCORE row is RISC-V-centric -- this paper is the silicon/architecture ancestor, not bit-identical to today's RTL.
- Evaluation focuses on signal-processing / graph-ish kernels; no DNN end-to-end stacks (those appear in later PULP generations).
- Authors note future work on heterogeneous memory + deeper NT for the tightly coupled cluster (Conclusion).
- Commercial FD-SOI / ST fabrication; not an open-PDK tapeout.
- Table 2 footnotes define a specific nominal operating point; cross-paper comparison must keep that normalization in mind.
digestSections.research opportunity:
**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: ULP MCU papers maximize MOPS/mW at tiny absolute MOPS; DSP papers maximize GHz; few open multicore templates publish full NT silicon with bank-level memory/power knobs.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: OpenRISC-to-RISC-V migration impact on the same microarchitectural knobs is not measured here; later Conti et al. PULP survey covers evolution but not this chip's raw tables.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Use this digest as the primary silicon reference for SCORE **PULP cluster**, and map Fig. 1 blocks onto today's `pulp_cluster` RTL (cores, HCI/TCDM, DMA, PMU) for a continuity table in `PAPER.md`.
- Analysis: Reproduce Table 2 stall taxonomy (core / I$ / TCDM / slave sleep) as a checklist when characterizing later RISC-V PULP clusters (HERO, Carfield, Chimera).
- Analysis: Quantify how much of the 193 MOPS/mW result is process (FD-SOI FBB) vs architecture (SCM TCDM + MMU + RPS) by comparing against later bulk/FinFET PULP silicon at matched ISA.
digestSections.pros and cons:
### Pros

- Complete silicon story: micrograph, V/F/P envelopes, architectural counters, and peer comparison in one short IEEE Micro article.
- Runtime knobs (MMU, RPS, BB regions) are concrete and measurable, not only process tricks.
- Directly anchors the SCORE PULP cluster lineage with published NT efficiency numbers.

### Cons

- OpenRISC ISA limits drop-in comparison to current RISC-V SCORE builds without an ISA caveat.
- Cool Chips overview length constrains RTL/open-source release discussion (platform openness matured later).
- Some pathological parallelization cases show efficiency collapse -- cluster value is workload-dependent.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Quentin: An Ultra-Low-Power PULPissimo SoC in 22nm FDX

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Pasquale Davide Schiavone; Davide Rossi; Antonio Pullini; Alfio Di Mauro; Francesco Conti; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich; University of Bologna |
| Venue | IEEE S3S 2018 |
| Venue type | conference |
| Year | 2018 |
| Volume / issue / pages | 3 pages |
| Paper DOI | [10.1109/S3S.2018.8640145](https://doi.org/10.1109/S3S.2018.8640145) |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/pulpissimo |
| Keywords | PULPissimo, IoT MCU, RISC-V, FD-SOI, forward body bias, open-source |
| Open access | IEEE Xplore; PULP IPs under SolderPad |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Funding: SNSF 162524 (MicroLearn), H2020 OPRECOMP 732631.

## TL;DR

- Quentin tapes out open-source PULPissimo in GF 22FDX with 520 kB heterogeneous L2 (504 kB SRAM + 16 kB SCM) and rich IoT peripherals.
- Peak 938 MHz at 0.8 V with 1.4 V forward body bias; best reported 433 MOPS/mW and 6 uW/MHz power density.
- SCM-only mode (SRAM gated) yields lowest power (0.95 mW at 0.5 V, 156 MHz) for 16 kB footprint workloads.

## Problem statement

IoT end-nodes need programmable ultra-low-power MCUs with wide voltage/performance range and efficient sensor I/O, enabled by FD-SOI body biasing but requiring architecture and memory design matched to the technology.

## Motivation

Demonstrate that open PULPissimo RTL in 22 nm FDX achieves state-of-the-art energy efficiency through near-threshold operation, heterogeneous SRAM/SCM memory, and autonomous uDMA I/O subsystem.

## Prior art

PULP platform [5], RISC-V ISA [6], RV32IMFC core [7], SCM cuts [8], uDMA [9], prior PULP silicon (GAP-8 [10], Mr.Wolf [11]), and efficient commercial MCUs [12], [13] compared in Fig. 7.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: Silicon-measured open-source IoT MCU SoC (processor + memory + peripherals).

## Method / approach

**Architecture (Fig. 1).** Single RV32IMFC 4-stage in-order core with PULP DSP extensions (HW loops, auto-increment loads/stores, bit manip, fixed-point/SIMD). 520 kB L2: four 114 kB interleaved banks (2x SCM + SRAM mix) plus two 32 kB private FC banks (one with 8 kB SCM register file with 3R2W ports). Peripherals: QSPI x2, I2C, 2x I2S, camera, UART, GPIO, JTAG, HyperBus; uDMA with dual 32b L2 ports (~1.6 Gbit/s aggregate at 57 MHz).

**Silicon (Fig. 2).** Floorplan 2.31 mm2 effective 1.22 mm2 (6154 kGE); chip partitioned in three designs; Quentin top-left region.

**Measurement.** 8x8 32-bit matrix multiply on Advantest hp93000; three setups: SRAM only, SCM with SRAM powered, SCM with SRAM gated; FBB sweeps to 1.4 V.

## Experimental setup

- GF 22FDX tapeout; frequencies/power with FBB up to 1.4 V body bias.
- Configurations: code/data on SRAM vs SCM; SRAM gating for ultra-low-power SCM-only mode.
- Benchmark: compiled 8x8 matrix multiply for power/frequency/efficiency sweeps.
- Comparison Fig. 7 vs GAP-8, Mr.Wolf fabric controllers, and literature efficient processors [12], [13].

## Results summary

- Max frequency: 570 MHz (SRAM) vs 670 MHz (SCM) at 0.8 V no BB; starts at 0.5 V (~148 MHz SRAM / 1156 MHz text typo in PDF likely 115 MHz).
- FBB: +60% frequency at 0.6 V; 938 MHz at 0.8 V with 1.4 V FBB (Fig. 4).
- Power: 0.95 mW at 0.5 V SCM-only (156 MHz) to 32.1 mW at 0.8 V + FBB (938 MHz); SRAM leakage +~2 mW when powered but unused (Fig. 5).
- Energy efficiency: SCM+gated best uW/MHz at all points; SCM+SRAM on beats SRAM-only above ~400 MHz (Figs 3, 6).
- System headline: up to 2400 MOPS equivalent RV32IMC; 433 MOPS/mW; 6 uW/MHz; tiny SCM apps up to 216 MOPS/mW.
- Fig. 7: highest energy efficiency and performance vs cited efficient processors in single-core MCU class.

## Contributions

- First 22 nm FDX implementation of open PULPissimo with heterogeneous L2 and uDMA-centric I/O.
- Silicon characterization of FBB impact on frequency, leakage, and energy across memory configurations.
- Evidence that open MCU architectures in advanced nodes match IoT PPA requirements.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Heterogeneous SRAM/SCM banking with 3R2W SCM register file enables 4x L2 bandwidth vs single-port without multi-port SRAM area penalty.
- Analysis: Separate SRAM power rails allow gating large memories while retaining 16 kB SCM always-on domain for ultra-low-power standby compute.
- Analysis: uDMA dedicated L2 ports decouple peripheral traffic from core memory bandwidth at IoT sensor aggregate rates.

## Limitations and future work

- Single-core PULPissimo only; no optional compute cluster on this chip.
- No on-chip power manager or state-retentive memory (vs Mr.Wolf); relies on external HyperBus extension.
- Short 3-page format limits workload diversity beyond matrix multiply and comparison figure.
- Typo/ambiguity in PDF frequency text at 0.5 V (148/1156 MHz) noted during audit.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Quentin closes open-hardware + advanced FD-SOI gap left by 65 nm GAP-8/Mr.Wolf with quantified FBB and SCM/SRAM tradeoffs.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Linux-capable host pairing (Cheshire/CVA6) + Quentin-class accelerator cluster integration and software stack not shown.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE registry link Quentin -> modern PULPissimo/Arnold lineage for silicon evidence column.
- Analysis: Reproduce SCM-vs-SRAM energy crossover (~400 MHz) as selection metric for TinyML always-on vs burst workloads.
- Analysis: Compare Quentin uW/MHz against Ibex/Zero-riscy cores on same ISA baseline in survey core-comparison tables.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Open-source end-to-end (PULPissimo) with silicon in 22 nm FDX.
- Analysis: Rich peripheral + uDMA story for IoT sensor hub survey dimension.
- Analysis: Body-bias and memory-gating measurements directly support FD-SOI discussion.

### Cons

- Analysis: No cluster accelerator; MCU-class not application-processor Linux SoC.
- Analysis: Limited benchmark set (matrix multiply primary).
- Analysis: External power manager dependency for SRAM gating.

## Benchmarks and tables

No numbered tables. Physical summary is embedded in Fig. 2; efficiency comparison in Fig. 7. Headline metrics: 520 kB L2 (504 SRAM + 16 SCM), up to 938 MHz with FBB, 0.95 mW @0.5 V SCM-gated, 433 MOPS/mW, 6 uW/MHz.

## Figures

### Figure 1: Quentin SoC architecture.

![Figure 1](./figures/figure_01.png)

*Page 1. RV32 core, heterogeneous L2, uDMA, and peripheral set.*

### Figure 2: Floorplan and physical results.

![Figure 2](./figures/figure_02.png)

*Page 2. Die photo and area summary table.*

### Figure 3: Maximum frequency vs supply (SRAM vs SCM, no body bias).

![Figure 3](./figures/figure_03.png)

*Page 2. fmax curves for SRAM and SCM placements.*

### Figure 4: Performance benefits from forward body bias.

![Figure 4](./figures/figure_04.png)

*Page 2. FBB boost larger at low voltage.*

### Figure 5: Leakage increase with forward body bias.

![Figure 5](./figures/figure_05.png)

*Page 3. FBB penalty stronger at lower supply voltages.*

### Figure 6: Quentin power density (uW/MHz).

![Figure 6](./figures/figure_06.png)

*Page 3. SCM-gated configuration is most energy efficient across points.*

### Figure 7: Comparison with state-of-the-art efficient processors.

![Figure 7](./figures/figure_07.png)

*Page 3. Quentin vs GAP-8, Mr.Wolf, and literature MCUs on efficiency/performance axes.*

## Reproducibility

| Artifact | Link / status |
|----------|----------------|
| RTL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/pulpissimo (SolderPad) |
| Silicon | GF 22FDX Quentin test chip; no public GDS |
| Software | PULP runtime referenced; not detailed in paper |

## References

1. D. Rossi et al., IEEE HCS 2015 (PULP). DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
2. A. Waterman et al., RISC-V manual, 2014. DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
3. M. Gautschi et al., IEEE TVLSI 2017 (Riscy core). DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
4. A. Teman et al., ASP-DAC 2015 (SCM). DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
5. A. Pullini et al., PATMOS 2017 (uDMA). DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
6. E. Flamand et al., ASAP 2018 (GAP-8). DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
7. A. Pullini et al., ESSCIRC 2018 (Mr.Wolf). DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
8. D. Bol et al., ISSCC 2012. DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`
9. N. Ickes et al., ESSCIRC 2011. DOI: not found -- `[unresolved]`

- Pass 0: `capture_figures.py` Figs 1,2,4,5,7; manual second candidates for Figs 4 and 7; Figs 3 and 6 present on die but omitted from digest figures; `audit_manifest.json` 3 pages, 6 figure captions.

- Page 1: Title, authors, abstract (2400 MOPS, 6 uW/MHz, 433 MOPS/mW), index terms, introduction (IoT, PULP, FDX FBB), Fig. 1 architecture, Section II Quentin SoC (core, 520 kB L2 layout, peripherals, uDMA bandwidth, JTAG debug).

# Open-Source Heterogeneous SoCs for AI: The PULP Platform Experience

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Francesco Conti; Angelo Garofalo; Davide Rossi; Giuseppe Tagliavini; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | University of Bologna (DEI, DISI); Integrated Systems Laboratory, ETH Zurich |
| Venue | Preprint submitted to IEEE Solid-State Circuits Magazine |
| Venue type | preprint |
| Year | 2024 |
| Volume / issue / pages | 8 pages |
| Paper DOI | Not assigned (preprint) |
| arXiv | arXiv:2412.20391v1 [cs.AR], 29 Dec 2024 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform |
| Keywords | Open-source hardware, heterogeneous SoC, AI acceleration, PULP |
| Open access | Yes (open hardware and software stacks) |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- Surveys how the PULP Platform uses open IP sharing to lower NRE and accelerate heterogeneous AI SoC design.
- Describes fractally heterogeneous clusters: RISC-V cores with Xpulp/Xpulpnn ISA extensions plus HWPE accelerators.
- Traces taped-out chips from Mia Wallace (2015) through Siracusa/Marsellus to Occamy, with efficiency comparisons to closed SoCs.
- Presents open deployment flows (DORY, Deeploy) with tiling, double-buffering, and constraint-programming buffer allocation.
- Argues open PDKs/EDA (e.g., Basilisk-scale flows) can further democratize tailored AI silicon.

## Problem statement

AI model complexity scales far faster than silicon efficiency, forcing rapid heterogeneous SoC iterations especially at the edge. Closed IP models inflate NRE on non-differentiating baseline blocks (processors, NoCs) and slow startups. PULP asks whether open hardware can compress design time while keeping competitive AI efficiency.

## Motivation

Epoch AI data show model parameters growing ~2x/year and training FLOPs ~4.2x/year vs ~1.3x/year hardware gains. Fabless teams need reusable open templates for processors, interconnect, accelerators, and software to focus budget on proprietary differentiating IP.

## Prior art

Commercial AI SoCs (Envision, Orlando, Metis, Esperanto, DIANA, etc.) set efficiency benchmarks. Academic many-core and TPU-style arrays exist, but few combine open RTL, HW/SW co-design, and a decade of silicon iterations. TVM and similar compilers assume cache hierarchies unlike PULP scratchpad-centric clusters.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`
Secondary: `survey`
Note: Experience article on open heterogeneous AI SoCs, ISA extensions, HWPEs, and deployment tooling.

## Method / approach

PULP clusters combine multi-banked L1 TCDM, 4-16 RISC-V cores, and HWPEs sharing the Heterogeneous Cluster Interconnect (HCI). ISA extensions (Xpulp, Xpulpnn, MPIC, Flex-V) accelerate dot-products and QNN ops; larger ops offload to HWPEs (HWCE, N-EUREKA, RedMulE) with standard controller/streamer/datapath templates.

Software uses hand-tuned kernels plus DORY (homogeneous clusters) or Deeploy (HWPE-aware) to fuse ONNX graphs, allocate multi-level scratchpads via constraint programming, and generate tiled C with DMA/HWPE synchronization.

## Experimental setup

- Silicon: PULP chips from 65 nm to 12 nm (Mia Wallace through Occamy).
- Metrics: GOPS/W or TOPS/W at peak-performance and peak-efficiency operating points; area vs performance; Transformer encoder case study on Siracusa (8 layers, dm=64, h=16, dff=256).
- Comparisons: Fig. 6 overlays PULP and third-party digital/analog AI SoCs.

## Results summary

Marsellus and Siracusa reach multi-TOPS/W class efficiency competitive with state-of-the-art digital designs; Diana (hybrid analog+digital with PULP technology) reports up to ~600 TOPS/W. Deeploy keeps data-transfer/marshaling overhead under 10% on a full Transformer encoder. Occamy demonstrates scalability to 432 Snitch cores but targets HPC rather than extreme-edge QNN efficiency.

## Contributions

- Open-model cost-sharing argument for SoC NRE reduction (Fig. 1).
- Template for heterogeneous PULP clusters, ISA extensions, and reusable HWPE integration.
- Retrospective of AI-oriented PULP silicon and competitive efficiency positioning.
- Open deployment methodology (tiling, double buffering, CP-based memory allocation) with DORY/Deeploy.

## Innovations

- Analysis: HWPE microarchitecture template decouples controller/streamer reuse (~30-60% RTL) from custom datapaths, including analog in-memory arrays.
- Analysis: Fractal heterogeneity -- multiple cluster flavors in one SoC -- as a modular open-design pattern.
- Analysis: Explicit split between hand-written local kernels and tool-generated global tiling orchestration.

## Limitations and future work

Higher-performance platforms remain mostly proprietary; Occamy trades AI efficiency for FP64/HPC features. Advanced IMC integration in PULP is still emerging. Open PDK+EDA ecosystem maturity (tapeout cost, tool QoR) remains a bottleneck despite recent Basilisk-class progress.

## Research opportunity

- Analysis: Co-design open host SoCs (Basilisk/Cheshire) with PULP AI clusters via open NoC/C2C links.
- Analysis: Extend Deeploy to LLM decoder memory-bound phases called out for NVM/at-memory approaches.
- Analysis: Benchmark HWPE template reuse vs closed vendor IP integration time on a fixed QNN graph set.
- Analysis: Port PULP deployment flows to RISC-V vector or upstream LLVM support to reduce hand-kernel burden.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Rare longitudinal evidence linking open IP strategy to multiple taped-out AI SoCs across nodes.
- Clear hardware/software co-design story with measurable deployment overhead (<10% marshaling).
- Competitive efficiency claims backed by broad Fig. 6 comparison including non-PULP designs using PULP IP.

### Cons

- Magazine-style breadth limits deep microarchitectural detail per chip.
- Some citation/index mismatches between figure callouts and reference list in the preprint PDF.
- Analysis: Software stack maturity varies by chip generation; not all combinations are turnkey for external teams.

## Benchmarks and tables

No numbered tables in this PDF.

Note: Experience article on open heterogeneous AI SoCs, ISA extensions, HWPEs, and deployment tooling.
digestSections.method / approach:
PULP clusters combine multi-banked L1 TCDM, 4-16 RISC-V cores, and HWPEs sharing the Heterogeneous Cluster Interconnect (HCI). ISA extensions (Xpulp, Xpulpnn, MPIC, Flex-V) accelerate dot-products and QNN ops; larger ops offload to HWPEs (HWCE, N-EUREKA, RedMulE) with standard controller/streamer/datapath templates.

Software uses hand-tuned kernels plus DORY (homogeneous clusters) or Deeploy (HWPE-aware) to fuse ONNX graphs, allocate multi-level scratchpads via constraint programming, and generate tiled C with DMA/HWPE synchronization.
digestSections.experimental setup:
- Silicon: PULP chips from 65 nm to 12 nm (Mia Wallace through Occamy).
- Metrics: GOPS/W or TOPS/W at peak-performance and peak-efficiency operating points; area vs performance; Transformer encoder case study on Siracusa (8 layers, dm=64, h=16, dff=256).
- Comparisons: Fig. 6 overlays PULP and third-party digital/analog AI SoCs.
digestSections.results summary: Marsellus and Siracusa reach multi-TOPS/W class efficiency competitive with state-of-the-art digital designs; Diana (hybrid analog+digital with PULP technology) reports up to ~600 TOPS/W. Deeploy keeps data-transfer/marshaling overhead under 10% on a full Transformer encoder. Occamy demonstrates scalability to 432 Snitch cores but targets HPC rather than extreme-edge QNN efficiency.
digestSections.contributions:
- Open-model cost-sharing argument for SoC NRE reduction (Fig. 1).
- Template for heterogeneous PULP clusters, ISA extensions, and reusable HWPE integration.
- Retrospective of AI-oriented PULP silicon and competitive efficiency positioning.
- Open deployment methodology (tiling, double buffering, CP-based memory allocation) with DORY/Deeploy.
digestSections.innovations:
- Analysis: HWPE microarchitecture template decouples controller/streamer reuse (~30-60% RTL) from custom datapaths, including analog in-memory arrays.
- Analysis: Fractal heterogeneity -- multiple cluster flavors in one SoC -- as a modular open-design pattern.
- Analysis: Explicit split between hand-written local kernels and tool-generated global tiling orchestration.
digestSections.limitations and future work: Higher-performance platforms remain mostly proprietary; Occamy trades AI efficiency for FP64/HPC features. Advanced IMC integration in PULP is still emerging. Open PDK+EDA ecosystem maturity (tapeout cost, tool QoR) remains a bottleneck despite recent Basilisk-class progress.
digestSections.research opportunity:
- Analysis: Co-design open host SoCs (Basilisk/Cheshire) with PULP AI clusters via open NoC/C2C links.
- Analysis: Extend Deeploy to LLM decoder memory-bound phases called out for NVM/at-memory approaches.
- Analysis: Benchmark HWPE template reuse vs closed vendor IP integration time on a fixed QNN graph set.
- Analysis: Port PULP deployment flows to RISC-V vector or upstream LLVM support to reduce hand-kernel burden.
digestSections.pros and cons:
### Pros

- Rare longitudinal evidence linking open IP strategy to multiple taped-out AI SoCs across nodes.
- Clear hardware/software co-design story with measurable deployment overhead (<10% marshaling).
- Competitive efficiency claims backed by broad Fig. 6 comparison including non-PULP designs using PULP IP.

### Cons

- Magazine-style breadth limits deep microarchitectural detail per chip.
- Some citation/index mismatches between figure callouts and reference list in the preprint PDF.
- Analysis: Software stack maturity varies by chip generation; not all combinations are turnkey for external teams.

# The Rocket Chip Generator

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Krste Asanovic, Rimas Avizienis, Jonathan Bachrach, Scott Beamer, David Biancolin, Christopher Celio, Henry Cook, Palmer Dabbelt, John Hauser, Adam Izraelevitz, Sagar Karandikar, Benjamin Keller, Donggyu Kim, John Koenig, Yunsup Lee, Eric Love, Martin Maas, Albert Magyar, Howard Mao, Miquel Moreto, Albert Ou, David Patterson, Brian Richards, Colin Schmidt, Stephen Twigg, Huy Vo, Andrew Waterman |
| Affiliations | Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, University of California, Berkeley |
| Venue | UC Berkeley EECS Technical Report |
| Venue type | technical report |
| Year | 2016 |
| Volume / issue / pages | UCB/EECS-2016-17 |
| Paper DOI | |
| arXiv | |
| URL | https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2016/EECS-2016-17.html |
| Keywords | Rocket Chip, Chisel, RISC-V, SoC generator, TileLink, BOOM, RoCC, open source |
| Open access | BSD-licensed generator on GitHub (https://github.com/chipsalliance/rocket-chip) |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- Rocket Chip is an open-source, highly parameterized Chisel SoC generator that emits synthesizable RTL for RISC-V systems ranging from embedded microcontrollers to multi-core servers.
- The generator composes plug-and-play libraries for Rocket (in-order), BOOM (out-of-order), Z-scale (AHB-Lite embedded), caches, TileLink coherence, RoCC coprocessors, and AMBA peripherals.
- Custom accelerators attach via RoCC instructions, coherent TileLink ports, or independent cores; eleven Berkeley tapeouts (Raven, EOS, SWERVE families) had booted Linux by report time.
- Supporting infrastructure includes FPGA Zynq deployment (25-100 MHz), GroundTest memory stressors, RISC-V Torture random ISA testing, and Axe memory-model checking.

## Problem statement

Systems-on-chip need integration and customization to improve efficiency, but hand-crafted RTL scales poorly as designs grow heterogeneous. Rocket Chip addresses the gap by providing a stable, open, generator-based platform that produces many SoC instances from one parameterized source, rather than a single fixed chip.

## Motivation

Continued efficiency gains push toward specialized SoCs, yet design cost must remain tractable for research and industry. A free RISC-V ISA plus Chisel generator methodology removes licensing friction and enables reusable cores, caches, and interconnects that have already produced working silicon prototypes.

## Prior art

Builds on the RISC-V ISA and Chisel HDL. Contrasts with single fixed open cores by offering a composable generator ecosystem. Cites AXI, OpenSoC, RapidIO, Hwacha, Berkeley HardFloat, and prior Berkeley RISC-V test chips. Positions BOOM as an education/research/industry baseline OoO RISC-V core reusing Rocket front-end and FPU blocks.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Open-source parameterized SoC generator framework (cores, coherence, peripherals) with silicon validation narrative.

## Method / approach

**Generator composition.** Rocket Chip is a Chisel library of parameterized generators with standardized interfaces: core (Rocket in-order, BOOM OoO, optional FPU and branch predictors), caches/TLBs, RoCC coprocessor template, coherent tile template, TileLink networks, and AMBA (AXI/AHB/APB) peripherals including Z-scale.

**Heterogeneity and accelerators.** Three integration paths: (1) RoCC tightly coupled coprocessors sharing cache/PTW and optionally TileLink; (2) MMIO accelerators on TileLink; (3) fully independent cores.

**TileLink.** Protocol framework separating coherence transactions, cache controllers, and physical networks; supports directories, snooping, DMA/non-cacheable agents, and converters to AXI4/AHB-Lite/APB.

**Cores in brief.** Rocket: 5-stage in-order RV64G-class core with BTB/BHT/RAS, optional M/A/F/D, Chisel FPUs, machine/supervisor/user modes. BOOM: RV64G OoO superscalar generator reusing Rocket blocks (~10k LoC Chisel). Z-scale: RV32IM 3-stage core for AHB-Lite embedded use (not cache-coherent with Rocket tiles).

**Verification and bring-up.** GroundTest tile-socket memory traffic generators; RISC-V Torture random interleaved instruction streams vs Spike golden model; Axe trace checking for memory consistency. FPGA flow for Xilinx Zynq-7000 (ZC706, ZedBoard) at 25-100 MHz with prebuilt or custom bitstreams.

## Experimental setup

Retrospective report (April 2016) cataloging generator capabilities and eleven UC Berkeley tapeouts: four Raven (STMicro 28 nm FD-SOI), six EOS (IBM 45 nm SOI), one SWERVE (TSMC 28 nm). Examples include Raven vector processors with on-chip DC-DC and adaptive clocking; EOS dual-core vector with monolithic photonic links. No new benchmark tables in this report.

## Results summary

- Demonstrates a modular open-source SoC generator stable enough for repeated silicon success (11 tapeouts, Linux-capable prototypes).
- Documents plug-and-play composition of heterogeneous tiles (Rocket vs BOOM), RoCC accelerators (SHA3, Hwacha cited), and configurable memory hierarchies.
- Provides infrastructure for fast FPGA simulation, directed/random core test, and memory-system validation.
- Positions TileLink as an extensible coherence framework decoupling protocol, controllers, and networks.

## Contributions

- Present Rocket Chip as an open-source, parameterized RISC-V SoC generator emitting synthesizable RTL.
- Catalog generator libraries: Rocket, BOOM, Z-scale, caches, RoCC, tiles, TileLink, peripherals.
- Describe three accelerator integration mechanisms and heterogeneous multi-tile composition.
- Summarize verification/FPGA infrastructure (GroundTest, Torture, Axe, Zynq flow).
- Document Berkeley silicon prototype lineage through April 2016.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Treats SoC design as a generator-composition problem with diplomacy-style plug-and-play interfaces rather than a monolithic RTL handoff.
- Analysis: TileLink orthogonalizes coherence protocol, controllers, and networks, enabling interchangeable policies and physical implementations.
- Analysis: RoCC provides a reusable coprocessor attachment model with cache/PTW sharing and coherent high-bandwidth TileLink egress (driven by Hwacha).
- Analysis: BOOM achieves a compact OoO generator by reusing Rocket repository components, lowering the cost of research/education OoO RISC-V cores.

## Limitations and future work

- April 2016 snapshot; privileged RISC-V spec still draft; generator features evolved substantially afterward (later Chipyard ecosystem).
- Technical report with no quantitative QoR tables comparing generator variants or flows.
- Z-scale is not a drop-in coherent replacement for Rocket/BOOM application cores.
- Analog/AMS, advanced PD automation, and cloud-scale verification are out of scope.
- Figure captions use inline "Figure N:" text not parsed by `audit_manifest.json`; artwork not auto-extracted.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Pre-2016 open RISC-V efforts offered cores or tutorials, but lacked a unified generator for coherent multi-tile SoCs, coprocessor sockets, and repeatable silicon lineage.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Quantitative generator QoR (area/timing across configs), cross-node PD portability, and AMS integration remain for downstream frameworks (Chipyard, Hammer).

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Reproduce Figure 2-class heterogeneous Rocket/BOOM/RoCC configs in SCORE `datasets/rocket-chip/` and measure elaboration time, gate count, and Torture pass rate vs config complexity.
- Analysis: Compare TileLink coherence generator outputs vs BlackParrot BedRock on identical tile counts for SCORE interconnect surveys.
- Analysis: Track config-parameter sensitivity (cache sizes, tile count) against silent misconfiguration bugs noted in later Chipyard retrospective.
- Analysis: Extend RoCC template metrics (area, interface width) for SHA3/Gemmini attachment studies in SCORE accelerator corpus.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Foundational open generator whose TileLink/RoCC abstractions underpin much of the academic/industrial RISC-V SoC stack.
- Analysis: Eleven tapeouts provide rare evidence that generator output reached working Linux-capable silicon across multiple processes.
- Analysis: Explicit verification stack (Torture, GroundTest, Axe) beyond block-level reuse.
- Analysis: Heterogeneous tile composition (Rocket + BOOM + accelerators) in one framework was ahead of many 2016 open SoC efforts.

### Cons

- Analysis: Report is descriptive/catalog-style with minimal quantitative benchmarking.
- Analysis: Z-scale and Rocket/BOOM coexist without unified coherent embedding for the smallest core class.
- Analysis: Figure artwork not captured automatically; inline figure numbering missed by caption parser.
- Analysis: Heavily superseded in practice by Chipyard/FIRRTL multi-flow integration for modern agile teams.

## Benchmarks and tables

No numbered tables in the PDF (`table_caption_count=0` in `audit_manifest.json`).

## Figures

`audit_manifest.json` reports `figure_caption_count=0` (inline "Figure N:" labels without parser-friendly caption blocks). The PDF contains four figures described here for completeness:

- **Figure 1 (page 5):** Example Rocket Chip instance with two tiles, 4-bank L2, AXI DRAM/IO, BOOM tile with RoCC accelerator and Rocket tile with different L1 parameters.
- **Figure 2 (page 4):** Generator sub-component map (Core, Cache, RoCC, Tile, TileLink, Peripherals).
- **Figure 3 (page 6):** Z-scale 3-stage pipeline (PC Gen, IF, IDE, EX, MEM, WB, I/D buses, MUL).
- **Figure 4 (page 10):** Berkeley tapeout timeline 2011-2016 (Raven, EOS, SWERVE families).

No `./figures/figure_*.png` embeds (no entries in `figures_manifest.json`).

digestSections.tl;dr:
- Rocket Chip is an open-source, highly parameterized Chisel SoC generator that emits synthesizable RTL for RISC-V systems ranging from embedded microcontrollers to multi-core servers.
- The generator composes plug-and-play libraries for Rocket (in-order), BOOM (out-of-order), Z-scale (AHB-Lite embedded), caches, TileLink coherence, RoCC coprocessors, and AMBA peripherals.
- Custom accelerators attach via RoCC instructions, coherent TileLink ports, or independent cores; eleven Berkeley tapeouts (Raven, EOS, SWERVE families) had booted Linux by report time.
- Supporting infrastructure includes FPGA Zynq deployment (25-100 MHz), GroundTest memory stressors, RISC-V Torture random ISA testing, and Axe memory-model checking.
digestSections.problem statement: Systems-on-chip need integration and customization to improve efficiency, but hand-crafted RTL scales poorly as designs grow heterogeneous. Rocket Chip addresses the gap by providing a stable, open, generator-based platform that produces many SoC instances from one parameterized source, rather than a single fixed chip.
digestSections.motivation: Continued efficiency gains push toward specialized SoCs, yet design cost must remain tractable for research and industry. A free RISC-V ISA plus Chisel generator methodology removes licensing friction and enables reusable cores, caches, and interconnects that have already produced working silicon prototypes.
digestSections.prior art: Builds on the RISC-V ISA and Chisel HDL. Contrasts with single fixed open cores by offering a composable generator ecosystem. Cites AXI, OpenSoC, RapidIO, Hwacha, Berkeley HardFloat, and prior Berkeley RISC-V test chips. Positions BOOM as an education/research/industry baseline OoO RISC-V core reusing Rocket front-end and FPU blocks.
digestSections.category of work:
Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Open-source parameterized SoC generator framework (cores, coherence, peripherals) with silicon validation narrative.
digestSections.method / approach:
**Generator composition.** Rocket Chip is a Chisel library of parameterized generators with standardized interfaces: core (Rocket in-order, BOOM OoO, optional FPU and branch predictors), caches/TLBs, RoCC coprocessor template, coherent tile template, TileLink networks, and AMBA (AXI/AHB/APB) peripherals including Z-scale.

**Heterogeneity and accelerators.** Three integration paths: (1) RoCC tightly coupled coprocessors sharing cache/PTW and optionally TileLink; (2) MMIO accelerators on TileLink; (3) fully independent cores.

**TileLink.** Protocol framework separating coherence transactions, cache controllers, and physical networks; supports directories, snooping, DMA/non-cacheable agents, and converters to AXI4/AHB-Lite/APB.

**Cores in brief.** Rocket: 5-stage in-order RV64G-class core with BTB/BHT/RAS, optional M/A/F/D, Chisel FPUs, machine/supervisor/user modes. BOOM: RV64G OoO superscalar generator reusing Rocket blocks (~10k LoC Chisel). Z-scale: RV32IM 3-stage core for AHB-Lite embedded use (not cache-coherent with Rocket tiles).

**Verification and bring-up.** GroundTest tile-socket memory traffic generators; RISC-V Torture random interleaved instruction streams vs Spike golden model; Axe trace checking for memory consistency. FPGA flow for Xilinx Zynq-7000 (ZC706, ZedBoard) at 25-100 MHz with prebuilt or custom bitstreams.
digestSections.experimental setup: Retrospective report (April 2016) cataloging generator capabilities and eleven UC Berkeley tapeouts: four Raven (STMicro 28 nm FD-SOI), six EOS (IBM 45 nm SOI), one SWERVE (TSMC 28 nm). Examples include Raven vector processors with on-chip DC-DC and adaptive clocking; EOS dual-core vector with monolithic photonic links. No new benchmark tables in this report.
digestSections.results summary:
- Demonstrates a modular open-source SoC generator stable enough for repeated silicon success (11 tapeouts, Linux-capable prototypes).
- Documents plug-and-play composition of heterogeneous tiles (Rocket vs BOOM), RoCC accelerators (SHA3, Hwacha cited), and configurable memory hierarchies.
- Provides infrastructure for fast FPGA simulation, directed/random core test, and memory-system validation.
- Positions TileLink as an extensible coherence framework decoupling protocol, controllers, and networks.
digestSections.contributions:
- Present Rocket Chip as an open-source, parameterized RISC-V SoC generator emitting synthesizable RTL.
- Catalog generator libraries: Rocket, BOOM, Z-scale, caches, RoCC, tiles, TileLink, peripherals.
- Describe three accelerator integration mechanisms and heterogeneous multi-tile composition.
- Summarize verification/FPGA infrastructure (GroundTest, Torture, Axe, Zynq flow).
- Document Berkeley silicon prototype lineage through April 2016.
digestSections.innovations:
- Analysis: Treats SoC design as a generator-composition problem with diplomacy-style plug-and-play interfaces rather than a monolithic RTL handoff.
- Analysis: TileLink orthogonalizes coherence protocol, controllers, and networks, enabling interchangeable policies and physical implementations.
- Analysis: RoCC provides a reusable coprocessor attachment model with cache/PTW sharing and coherent high-bandwidth TileLink egress (driven by Hwacha).
- Analysis: BOOM achieves a compact OoO generator by reusing Rocket repository components, lowering the cost of research/education OoO RISC-V cores.
digestSections.limitations and future work:
- April 2016 snapshot; privileged RISC-V spec still draft; generator features evolved substantially afterward (later Chipyard ecosystem).
- Technical report with no quantitative QoR tables comparing generator variants or flows.
- Z-scale is not a drop-in coherent replacement for Rocket/BOOM application cores.
- Analog/AMS, advanced PD automation, and cloud-scale verification are out of scope.
- Figure captions use inline "Figure N:" text not parsed by `audit_manifest.json`; artwork not auto-extracted.
digestSections.research opportunity:
**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Pre-2016 open RISC-V efforts offered cores or tutorials, but lacked a unified generator for coherent multi-tile SoCs, coprocessor sockets, and repeatable silicon lineage.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Quantitative generator QoR (area/timing across configs), cross-node PD portability, and AMS integration remain for downstream frameworks (Chipyard, Hammer).

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Reproduce Figure 2-class heterogeneous Rocket/BOOM/RoCC configs in SCORE `datasets/rocket-chip/` and measure elaboration time, gate count, and Torture pass rate vs config complexity.
- Analysis: Compare TileLink coherence generator outputs vs BlackParrot BedRock on identical tile counts for SCORE interconnect surveys.
- Analysis: Track config-parameter sensitivity (cache sizes, tile count) against silent misconfiguration bugs noted in later Chipyard retrospective.
- Analysis: Extend RoCC template metrics (area, interface width) for SHA3/Gemmini attachment studies in SCORE accelerator corpus.
digestSections.pros and cons:
### Pros

- Analysis: Foundational open generator whose TileLink/RoCC abstractions underpin much of the academic/industrial RISC-V SoC stack.
- Analysis: Eleven tapeouts provide rare evidence that generator output reached working Linux-capable silicon across multiple processes.
- Analysis: Explicit verification stack (Torture, GroundTest, Axe) beyond block-level reuse.
- Analysis: Heterogeneous tile composition (Rocket + BOOM + accelerators) in one framework was ahead of many 2016 open SoC efforts.

### Cons

- Analysis: Report is descriptive/catalog-style with minimal quantitative benchmarking.
- Analysis: Z-scale and Rocket/BOOM coexist without unified coherent embedding for the smallest core class.
- Analysis: Figure artwork not captured automatically; inline figure numbering missed by caption parser.
- Analysis: Heavily superseded in practice by Chipyard/FIRRTL multi-flow integration for modern agile teams.

## TL;DR

- Presents a RISC-V Efficient Trace (E-Trace) compliant tracing system with trace encoder (TE), TIP on CVA6, and AXI4 encapsulator exporting packets over Ethernet.
- Integrated into Shaheen host domain (CVA6 nano-UAV platform): 9.2% FPGA resource overhead on CVA6 subsystem (VCU118) with no critical-path frequency impact.
- Average 95.1% compression vs full-opcode instruction tracing across platform regression tests (Table 1).

## Problem statement

Profiling and debug of multi-core and event-driven edge software need non-intrusive, fine-grained execution visibility; standardized RISC-V instruction branch tracing (E-Trace) must be implemented efficiently on real platforms.

## Motivation

Prior profiling is intrusive or coarse; E-Trace defines block-based PC delta packets — this work delivers a hardware TE + host integration on a modern CVA6 edge SoC and quantifies area/compression trade-offs.

## Prior art

Causal profiling (Coz, SOSP 2015); RISC-V E-Trace specification v1.1; Shaheen heterogeneous SoC (Valente et al., IEEE TCAS-I 2024).

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture rv_tracer.

## Method / approach

**Trace encoder (Fig. 1a).** Modules: te_filter, te_priority, te_packet_emitter; te_reg (APB config), te_branch_map (31-bit branch map), te_resync_counter; supports multi-issue retirement via replicated block inputs.

**Integration (Fig. 1b).** CVA6 extended with Trace Interface Port (TIP); TE connects to AXI4 encapsulator → crossbar → Ethernet; placed in Shaheen host domain alongside LLC, peripherals, L2 TCDM.

**Decoder.** Software trace decoder on host reconstructs execution from packets + binary (development ongoing per conclusion).

## Experimental setup

- Target: Xilinx VCU118 FPGA emulation of Shaheen CVA6 subsystem + tracing system.
- Benchmarks: platform-specific tests (dhrystone, fp16 matmul, CAN, timer, LLC tests, etc.).
- Metrics: LUT/FF overhead vs CVA6 subsystem; compression rate per test.

## Results summary

- Area: TE 3.5%, TIP 3.2%, Encapsulator AXI 2.5% → 9.2% of CVA6 subsystem (CVA6 core alone ~10% relative overhead stated).
- Compression: 85.2%–99.8% per test; average 95.1% (Table 1).
- No critical-path impact on operating frequency.

## Contributions

- E-Trace compliant TE design with multi-retire support and branch-map backpressure.
- End-to-end integration on CVA6/Shaheen with Ethernet export path.
- FPGA evaluation of area overhead and compression on real firmware tests.

## Innovations

- Elastic FIFO-based encapsulator enabling trace export through existing AXI fabric without stalling core retirement (configurable FIFO depth vs packet loss trade-off).

## Limitations and future work

- 2-page summit brief; trace decoder not yet released; comprehensive benchmarks and extra TE features listed as future work.
- Evaluation on single CVA6 host domain / one FPGA board.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Few open E-Trace implementations publish end-to-end FPGA overhead on application-class RISC-V hosts.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Multi-core E-Trace, TD open release, and SCORE `rv_tracer` integration with CVA6/Carfield hosts need follow-on.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Compare rv_tracer compression vs logic-analyzer baselines on SCORE CVA6/Cheshire snapshots.
- Analysis: Formal verification of TE packet completeness under FIFO sizing sweeps.

### Pros

- Analysis: Standards-aligned (E-Trace) with quantified 95.1% compression and modest 9.2% area overhead.
- Analysis: Direct SCORE architecture link via `rv_tracer` repo and CVA6 ecosystem.

### Cons

- Analysis: Brief format; decoder and open-source drop still pending at publication time.
- Analysis: Shaheen-specific integration — generalization to other SCORE platforms not demonstrated.
