# SentryCore: A RISC-V Co-Processor System for Safe, Real-Time Control Applications

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Michael Rogenmoser; Alessandro Ottaviano; Thomas Benz; Robert Balas; Matteo Perotti; Angelo Garofalo; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich (Integrated Systems Laboratory); University of Bologna (DEI) |
| Venue | RISC-V Summit Europe 2024 (Munich); arXiv preprint |
| Venue type | conference + preprint |
| Year | 2024 |
| Paper DOI | not found |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06546 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/safety_island |
| Keywords | Safety-critical co-processor, triple-core lockstep, RISC-V, real-time control, AXI4 |
| Open access | arXiv + open-source RTL |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Corresponding: michaero@iis.ee.ethz.ch. Funding: HORIZON CHIPS-JU TRISTAN (101095947).

## TL;DR

- SentryCore is an open-source 32-bit RISC-V mega-IP for safety-critical, real-time co-processing in mixed-criticality SoCs, exposed via AXI4.
- Three CV32RT cores in triple-core lockstep with ECC-protected I/D memories; CLIC + fastirq yields 6-cycle interrupt latency and <110-cycle context switch.
- Intel16 implementation: 0.42 mm² macro, 500 MHz, 128 KiB ECC memory, ~50–70 mW estimated; supports FreeRTOS, ThreadX, and RTIC.

## Problem statement

Mixed-criticality edge systems must run high-performance non-critical workloads alongside dependable, bounded-latency control tasks, but vendor-neutral open RISC-V co-processor IPs with both reliability and predictability are missing.

## Motivation

Physical isolation with dedicated co-processors is the state-of-the-art freedom-from-interference approach; SentryCore targets the compact control domain with lockstep cores, ECC, and RTOS-ready interrupt architecture instead of closed automotive MCUs.

## Prior art

Burns & Davis mixed-criticality survey; ST Stellar and Renesas automotive SoCs; CV32RT fast interrupt work; hybrid modular redundancy for space clusters; OBI interconnect; iDMA real-time engine (IEEE TC 2024).

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`, `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture Safety Island (upstream `safety_island`).

## Method / approach

**Architecture (Fig. 1).** TCLS group of three CV32RT cores with FPU; OBI crossbar to ECC instruction/data memories with scrubbers; CLIC, PCRs, timer, boot ROM, JTAG debug; manager/subordinate AXI4 ports; iDMA with real-time scheduled 3D transfers on peripheral bus.

**Reliability.** Majority voting on lockstep outputs; software recovery saves correct state and resynchronizes within ~600 cycles after mismatch.

**Software.** FreeRTOS, ASIL-D ThreadX, Rust RTIC supported for safety-critical domains.

## Experimental setup

- Technology: Intel 16 nm (Intel16).
- Macro floorplan with 20 µm core spacing for single-event mitigation (Fig. 2).
- Gate-level power estimate; RTOS interrupt latency compared to Arm Cortex-M4 reference from prior CV32RT work.

## Results summary

- Context switching below 110 clock cycles; interrupt latency as low as 6 cycles.
- 0.42 mm² macro at 500 MHz with 128 KiB ECC-protected memory.
- Preliminary power 50–70 mW.
- Open mega-IP integrable into larger MCS via AXI4.

## Contributions

- Vendor-neutral dependable RISC-V co-processor mega-IP for MCS integration.
- TCLS + ECC memory + CLIC/fastirq for predictable real-time control.
- iDMA real-time engine for autonomous periodic sensor data movement.
- Intel16 silicon characterization and multi-RTOS software support.

## Innovations

- Combines lockstep dependability, sub-110-cycle context switch, and AXI4 plug-in co-processor packaging in one open IP aimed at automotive/robotics/avionics/space.

## Limitations and future work

- Interconnect reliability deferred to external watchdog (future work).
- 2-page summit brief — limited benchmark detail vs full journal paper.
- ETH institutional report DOI (10.3929/ethz-b-000673440) is separate documentation, not this digest primary.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Closed automotive MCUs (ST Stellar, Renesas R-Car) lack vendor-neutral open RTL with published TCLS + ECC co-processor packaging.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Full-system ISO 26262 evidence, interconnect ECC, and integration with SCORE Carfield/Cheshire MCS hosts remain open.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Pair Safety Island source note with SentryCore digest for SCORE `safety-island` vs `carfield` MCS partitioning studies.
- Analysis: Benchmark RTIC vs FreeRTOS context-switch bounds on FPGA emulation of the open mega-IP.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Strong SCORE Track A evidence for dependable real-time RISC-V co-processor with silicon metrics.
- Analysis: AXI4 plug-in model fits heterogeneous open SoC surveys.

### Cons

- Analysis: Short summit format; limited workload benchmarks.
- Analysis: Watchdog-dependent interconnect safety story incomplete.

## Benchmarks and tables

No numbered tables in PDF (`table_caption_count: 0`). Latency and area metrics appear inline in text and Fig. 2 floorplan.

## Figures

### Figure 1: SentryCore architecture

![Figure 1](./figures/figure_01.png)

### Figure 2: SentryCore floorplan in Intel16

![Figure 2](./figures/figure_02.png)

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Snitch: A tiny Pseudo Dual-Issue Processor for Area and Energy Efficient Execution of Floating-Point Intensive Workloads

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Florian Zaruba; Fabian Schuiki; Torsten Hoefler; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich (IIS + SPCL) |
| Venue | IEEE Transactions on Computers |
| Venue type | journal |
| Year | 2021 |
| Volume / issue / pages | Vol. 70, No. 11 |
| Paper DOI | [10.1109/TC.2020.3027900](https://doi.org/10.1109/TC.2020.3027900) |
| arXiv | — (ETH author PDF used) |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/snitch_cluster |
| Keywords | RISC-V, Snitch, SSR, FREP, energy efficiency, 22 nm |
| Open access | Author PDF |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- Snitch is a ~10 kGE RV32 integer control core paired with a DP FPU; SSR and FREP ISA extensions make the pair effectively dual-issue (+3.2% area) by eliding loads/stores and sequencing FP micro-loops.
- More flexible than a contemporary vector lane at ~2x energy efficiency; octa-core 22 nm cluster: >6x multi-core speedup and 3.5x energy-efficiency gain on parallel microkernels.
- Foundational SCORE Snitch-cluster paper used across Occamy, MemPool (integer Snitch), and related PULP accelerators.

## Problem statement

FP-heavy workloads waste most energy on control/memory overhead around a few pJ of useful FPU work; accelerators are inflexible; OoO cores are too costly.

## Motivation

Maximize FPU utilization with a tiny control core and minimal ISA extensions instead of wide OoO or rigid vector lanes.

## Prior art

Ariane energy breakdown; vector lanes; prior SSR work; BOOM OoO; classic DSP VLIW.

## Category of work

Primary: `circuit-design`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE Snitch cluster.

## Method / approach

**Snitch CC.** Tiny integer core + FPU subsystem; Hive shares mul/div and I$; Cluster of M Hives with TCDM.

**SSR.** Map memory streams to FP register reads/writes; elide explicit loads/stores.

**FREP.** Micro-loop buffer sequences FP ops, decoupling integer pipeline for other work / dual-issue effect.

## Experimental setup

- 22 nm FDX octa-core cluster PPA.
- Microkernels (matmul, FFT, etc.); single- vs multi-core speedups; area/power hierarchies.
- Comparison vs Ara vector and compute-equivalent baselines.

## Results summary

- SSR+FREP: effective dual-issue at +3.2% incremental cost; ~2x energy efficiency vs comparable vector lane flexibility claim.
- Octa-core: >6x multi-core speedup; 3.5x energy-efficiency gain on parallel microkernels.
- Hierarchical area: Snitch CC ~188 kGE class; cluster ~3.3 MGE class (paper figures).
- High FPU utilization on dense kernels (Tables 1-2).

## Contributions

- Snitch tiny core + SSR/FREP extensions.
- Cluster template and 22 nm evaluation.
- Comparison vs vector-lane style execution.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Moves stream and repeat control into tiny ISA hooks rather than widening the integer pipeline.
- Analysis: Separates integer control energy from FPU datapath as the primary efficiency lever.

## Limitations and future work

- Custom SSR/FREP (not standard RVV); later Spatz/Ara target standard vectors.
- Pass 0 missed Fig. 2 and Fig. 8 captions in unique set.
- Integer-only Snitch variants (MemPool) omit FPU story.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Open tiny-core+FPU recipe that spawned MemPool/Occamy ecosystems.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Hypervisor/Linux host coupling and multi-cluster NoCs treated in later Occamy/Cheshire papers.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE lineage table Snitch -> MemPool / Occamy / Spatz.
- Analysis: Quantify SSR vs RVV programmer-model trade-offs for survey text.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Definitive Snitch primary for SCORE.
- Analysis: Clear energy narrative from Ariane-style breakdown to SSR/FREP.

### Cons

- Analysis: ISA extensions are PULP-specific.
- Analysis: Microkernel suite, not full apps.

# A Push-button Idea to GDS-II SoC Design Flow

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Habiba Gamal; Amr Gouhar; Mohamed Shalan |
| Affiliations | American University in Cairo; eFabless Corporation |
| Venue | WOSET (Workshop on Open-Source EDA) |
| Venue type | workshop |
| Year | 2020 |
| Paper DOI | not found |
| arXiv | none |
| URL | https://github.com/habibagamal/SoC_Automation |
| Keywords | SoCGen, JSON, OpenLANE, AHB, APB, GDS-II, SKY130 |
| Open access | workshop paper + open-source SoCGen |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- SoCGen automates Verilog RTL generation from JSON SoC descriptions (AHB/APB masters, peripherals, pads) and integrates with OpenLANE for SKY130 GDS-II.
- Demonstrated SoC: ARM Cortex-M0 + flash/SRAM/GPIO + APB subsystem (I2C/SPI/timer/PWM); self-checking testbench; verified with M0/M3/N5 masters.
- ~121K-cell core hardened in <14 h; 3 mm × 3 mm die; DRC/LVS clean layout (Fig. 5).

## Problem statement

SoC RTL-to-GDS flows are lengthy and error-prone when done manually; IoT/deep-embedded designs repeat similar IP compositions and bus wiring.

## Motivation

JSON-driven generation plus open IP library and OpenLANE hardening enables push-button iteration for students and designers (SCORE SoC Automation teaching flow).

## Prior art

GEN AMBA bus skeletons; OpenLANE/OpenROAD flow; Arm Cortex-M SoC design texts; manual OpenLANE Basilisk-style flows.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: SCORE architecture SoC Automation (`habibagamal/SoC_Automation`).

## Method / approach

**JSON input.** Components, connections, addressing, pad mapping, testbench specs.

**Bus generation.** AHB masters (incl. multi-bus masters), APB subsystems, AHB-APB bridges, arbiters/multiplexers (GEN AMBA-derived).

**IP library.** UART, timer, PWM, watchdog, SPI/I2C, GPIO, QSPI flash, SRAM controllers; generic peripherals via auto wrappers; VIP hooks.

**Hierarchy.** Board (testbench) → SoC chip → SoC core → AHB/APB trees (Fig. 1).

**OpenLANE integration (Sec. III).** Harden macros → flatten soft IPs → core hardening → chip with pad frame; SKY130 default PDK.

## Experimental setup

- Example SoC Fig. 4: single AHB master, flash/SRAM/GPIO, APB peripherals, board-level VIP connections.
- Verification: dummy master register sweep or real M0/M3/N5 masters; hierarchical testbenches.
- Physical: OpenLANE on SKY130 HD library.

## Results summary

- Verilog + self-checking testbench generated in seconds (button press).
- GDS-II for Fig. 4 SoC core (Cortex-M0) in <14 hours; ~121K cells; 3×3 mm²; DRC/LVS clean (Fig. 5).

## Contributions

- End-to-end JSON→Verilog→OpenLANE methodology for IoT-class SoCs.
- Extensible IP/masters/pads libraries with teaching-oriented automation.
- Open-source SoCGen release.

## Innovations

- Combines bus-centric SoC assembly (beyond GEN AMBA skeletons) with push-button verification and documented OpenLANE hardening path.

## Limitations and future work

- OpenLANE integration not fully automated at publication time (manual OpenLANE invocation).
- AXI/Wishbone support and early PPA estimators listed as future work.
- Workshop paper — not full journal evaluation.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Few teaching flows document JSON→GDS with open masters library on SKY130.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Full CI integration with SCORE `generate_soc_automation.sh` and RISC-V master support remain open.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Compare SoCGen JSON schema vs Chipyard/LiteX generator models in SCORE survey.
- Analysis: Automate OpenLANE config emission in SCORE datasets.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Direct Track A evidence for SCORE SoC Automation row (open GitHub + GDS result).
- Analysis: Pedagogical push-button story with measurable hardening outcome.

### Cons

- Analysis: WOSET workshop venue; limited architecture diversity (AHB/APB only).
- Analysis: Cortex-M masters, not RISC-V-native.

- Demonstrated SoC: ARM Cortex-M0 + flash/SRAM/GPIO + APB subsystem (I2C/SPI/timer/PWM); self-checking testbench; verified with M0/M3/N5 masters.
- ~121K-cell core hardened in <14 h; 3 mm × 3 mm die; DRC/LVS clean layout (Fig. 5).
digestSections.problem statement: SoC RTL-to-GDS flows are lengthy and error-prone when done manually; IoT/deep-embedded designs repeat similar IP compositions and bus wiring.
digestSections.motivation: JSON-driven generation plus open IP library and OpenLANE hardening enables push-button iteration for students and designers (SCORE SoC Automation teaching flow).
digestSections.prior art: GEN AMBA bus skeletons; OpenLANE/OpenROAD flow; Arm Cortex-M SoC design texts; manual OpenLANE Basilisk-style flows.
digestSections.category of work:
Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: SCORE architecture SoC Automation (`habibagamal/SoC_Automation`).
digestSections.method / approach:
**JSON input.** Components, connections, addressing, pad mapping, testbench specs.

**Bus generation.** AHB masters (incl. multi-bus masters), APB subsystems, AHB-APB bridges, arbiters/multiplexers (GEN AMBA-derived).

**IP library.** UART, timer, PWM, watchdog, SPI/I2C, GPIO, QSPI flash, SRAM controllers; generic peripherals via auto wrappers; VIP hooks.

**Hierarchy.** Board (testbench) → SoC chip → SoC core → AHB/APB trees (Fig. 1).

**OpenLANE integration (Sec. III).** Harden macros → flatten soft IPs → core hardening → chip with pad frame; SKY130 default PDK.
digestSections.experimental setup:
- Example SoC Fig. 4: single AHB master, flash/SRAM/GPIO, APB peripherals, board-level VIP connections.
- Verification: dummy master register sweep or real M0/M3/N5 masters; hierarchical testbenches.
- Physical: OpenLANE on SKY130 HD library.
digestSections.results summary:
- Verilog + self-checking testbench generated in seconds (button press).
- GDS-II for Fig. 4 SoC core (Cortex-M0) in <14 hours; ~121K cells; 3×3 mm²; DRC/LVS clean (Fig. 5).
digestSections.contributions:
- End-to-end JSON→Verilog→OpenLANE methodology for IoT-class SoCs.
- Extensible IP/masters/pads libraries with teaching-oriented automation.
- Open-source SoCGen release.
digestSections.innovations: - Combines bus-centric SoC assembly (beyond GEN AMBA skeletons) with push-button verification and documented OpenLANE hardening path.
digestSections.limitations and future work:
- OpenLANE integration not fully automated at publication time (manual OpenLANE invocation).
- AXI/Wishbone support and early PPA estimators listed as future work.
- Workshop paper — not full journal evaluation.

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Few teaching flows document JSON→GDS with open masters library on SKY130.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Full CI integration with SCORE `generate_soc_automation.sh` and RISC-V master support remain open.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Compare SoCGen JSON schema vs Chipyard/LiteX generator models in SCORE survey.
- Analysis: Automate OpenLANE config emission in SCORE datasets.

- Analysis: Direct Track A evidence for SCORE SoC Automation row (open GitHub + GDS result).
- Analysis: Pedagogical push-button story with measurable hardening outcome.

### Cons

- Analysis: WOSET workshop venue; limited architecture diversity (AHB/APB only).
- Analysis: Cortex-M masters, not RISC-V-native.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Spatz: Clustering Compact RISC-V-Based Vector Units to Maximize Computing Efficiency

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Matteo Perotti; Samuel Riedel; Matheus Cavalcante; Luca Benini |
| Affiliations | ETH Zurich; University of Bologna (Benini) |
| Venue | IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems (preprint twin) |
| Venue type | journal preprint |
| Year | 2025 (TCAD); arXiv 2023 |
| Volume / issue / pages | IEEE TCAD DOI 10.1109/TCAD.2025.3528349 |
| Paper DOI | [10.1109/TCAD.2025.3528349](https://doi.org/10.1109/TCAD.2025.3528349) |
| arXiv | https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10137 |
| URL | https://github.com/pulp-platform/spatz |
| Keywords | RISC-V vector, Zve64d, shared L1, Spatz, 12LPP |
| Open access | arXiv |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- Spatz is a compact 64-bit FP-capable RISC-V vector PE (Zve64d) with only a 2 KiB latch-based VRF, clustered on a shared L1 SCM.
- GF 12LPP eight-FPU cluster: ~7.7 FMA/cycle, 15.7 GFLOPSDP, 95.7 GFLOPSDP/W at 1 GHz TT/0.80 V; balanced 2D kernel reaches 99.3 GFLOPSDP/W and 171 GFLOPSDP/W/mm2.
- At equi-area, Spatz cluster is ~30% more energy-efficient than a Snitch/SSR-style scalar FP cluster with the same FPU count.

## Problem statement

Large VRFs and scalar FP control cores waste energy on instruction/data movement; need compact vector PEs that keep FPU utilization high in a shared-L1 cluster.

## Motivation

Show that small VRF vector units, when clustered on SCM, beat wide VRF or SSR-scalar designs on energy and area efficiency.

## Prior art

Snitch+SSR FP clusters; Ara/Ara2 long-vector units; Vitruvius+; classical Cray-style VRF-heavy vectors.

## Category of work

Primary: `circuit-design`  
Secondary: `measurement-characterization`  
Note: SCORE architecture Spatz.

## Method / approach

**PE.** Spatz vector unit controlled by lightweight core; Zve64d; 2 KiB latch VRF; F FPUs per PE.

**Cluster.** Shared multi-banked L1 SCM; energy model for banking vs FPU count; dual Spatz PE examples.

**Physical.** GF 12LPP P&R of Spatz-based CC / cluster; compare to SSR-based Snitch cluster at equi-area.

## Experimental setup

- 12LPP TT/0.80 V/25 C, 1 GHz headline numbers.
- Matmul 256x256 DP; 7x7 2D kernel; FPU util vs ideal bound.
- Area/power post-implementation breakdowns.

## Results summary

- Matmul: FPU util 3.4% below ideal; 7.7 FMA/cycle; 15.7 GFLOPSDP; 95.7 GFLOPSDP/W; >55% power in FPUs.
- Balanced 2D: 95.0% FPU util; 15.2 GFLOPSDP; 99.3 GFLOPSDP/W; 171 GFLOPSDP/W/mm2.
- +30% energy efficiency vs equi-area SSR/Snitch FP cluster.
- Open-source Spatz RTL.

## Contributions

- Compact Spatz vector PE + shared-L1 cluster template.
- Energy/area optimality analysis for small VRF.
- 12LPP implementation and comparison vs Snitch SSR cluster.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Reframes VRF size as an energy knob: tiny latch VRF can still hit near-peak FPU util in a cluster.
- Analysis: Equi-area comparison isolates vector PE vs SSR-scalar control overhead.

## Limitations and future work

- Zve64d embedded vector subset (not full V app-class).
- Cluster-scale study; host SoC / DRAM hierarchy lightly treated.
- Table I sensitivity caption present; Table IV SoA comparison needs careful manual read.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Positions Spatz between Snitch SSR and Ara long-vector as the compact-cluster vector style.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Multi-cluster Spatz meshes (MAGIA/Picobello-class) and RVV 1.0 app features.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: SCORE triad Ara / Spatz / AraXL for three RVV scaling styles.
- Analysis: Revisit banking factor recommendations under sparse ML kernels.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Clear SCORE Spatz primary with open RTL and strong efficiency metrics.
- Analysis: Direct comparison to Snitch SSR strengthens registry narrative.

### Cons

- Analysis: Results focus on dense FP kernels.
- Analysis: 2 KiB VRF limits very long-vector reuse vs AraXL.

projects.fullMarkdown:
# PicoRV32

- **SCORE scripts:** `install_picorv32.sh` / `generate_picorv32.sh` / — (no `run_*.sh`; README.md architectures table)
- **Upstream:** https://github.com/YosysHQ/picorv32
- **License:** ISC (README: "PicoRV32 is free and open hardware licensed under the [ISC license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISC_license)")
- **Category:** processor_core
- **ISA / language:** Verilog (`picorv32.v`); RISC-V RV32E/I/M/C configurable. README: "implements the RISC-V RV32IMC Instruction Set" with optional RV32E and interrupt controller.
- **Bus / memory:** Native valid-ready memory interface; optional `picorv32_axi` (AXI4-Lite master) or `picorv32_wb` (Wishbone master). README: "The core exists in three variations: `picorv32`, `picorv32_axi` and `picorv32_wb`."
- **Verification:**
  - Upstream: GitHub Actions CI badge on README; Makefile targets `make test`, `make test_ez` (Icarus Verilog testbenches); `tests/` from riscv-tests.
  - SCORE: Verilator lint on `picorv32.v` and optional PicoSoC (`picosoc/*.v`) → `datasets/picorv32/<commit>/verification/`.
- **FPGA / silicon:** README evaluation on Xilinx 7-Series (LUT/fmax tables); intended "auxiliary processor in FPGA designs and ASICs."
- **Software:** RISC-V GNU toolchain; README documents RV32I[M][C] toolchain build and newlib linking (`firmware/riscv.ld`).
- **Primary paper:** none
- **Limitations (from upstream, quoted):**
  - README performance note: "This core is optimized for size and f<sub>max</sub>, not performance."
  - README on RV32E: "The RV32E ISA spec requires a hardware trap for when code tries to access this registers. This is not implemented in PicoRV32."
  - README IRQ: "The IRQ handling features in PicoRV32 do not follow the RISC-V Privileged ISA specification."
- **SCORE generate path:** `datasets/picorv32/<commit>/` (RTL snapshot via `score_simple_snapshot_rtl`); summary `picorv32_summary.txt`; logs `datasets/picorv32/<commit>/logs/`

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Security Verification of the OpenTitan Hardware Root of Trust

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Andres Meza, Francesco Restuccia, Jason Oberg, Dominic Rizzo, Ryan Kastner |
| Affiliations | University of California San Diego (Meza, Restuccia, Kastner); Cycuity (Oberg); OpenTitan (Rizzo) |
| Venue | IEEE Security & Privacy Magazine |
| Venue type | journal |
| Year | 2023 |
| Volume / issue / pages | Vol. 21, No. 3, May/June 2023, pp. 27-36 |
| Paper DOI | https://doi.org/10.1109/MSEC.2023.3251954 |
| arXiv | |
| URL | https://doi.org/10.1109/MSEC.2023.3251954 |
| Keywords | OpenTitan, root of trust, OTP controller, information flow tracking, IFT, Radix, hardware security verification, PRESENT cipher, declassification |
| Open access | Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 |
| Theme | Impact of Emerging Hardware on Security and Privacy |
| Date of current version | 20 April 2023 |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

## TL;DR

- Case study of security verification for OpenTitan's OTP memory controller using Cycuity Radix information-flow tracking (IFT).
- Asset under test: RndCnstKey, the random constant key for OTP scrambling with a PRESENT-based lightweight cipher.
- Initial noninterference-style property fails; refined property with declassification of fully encrypted ready outputs still finds intermediate-round leakage on data_o when ready_o==0.
- One-line RTL fix zeros data_o unless valid_q; patch accepted by OpenTitan and a new CWE proposed for intermediate cryptographic state leakage.

## Problem statement

Commercial-grade open-source silicon roots of trust such as OpenTitan combine complex RTL, cryptographic datapaths, and access-control logic. Security properties that only check final encrypted outputs can miss unintended information flows of secret assets through intermediate cryptographic state on module ports. This paper asks how to systematically verify that a critical OTP scrambling key does not leak through the OTP controller, and what RTL defects IFT can expose beyond functional tests.

## Motivation

OpenTitan is used as a platform identity module / U2F / TPM-like hardware RoT with Ibex (RV32IMCB), AES/KMAC/HMAC, and ROM/FLASH/SRAM/OTP plus controllers. OTP stores secrets with scrambling, locking, and integrity checks. A silent leak of RndCnstKey (or related intermediate state) on controller outputs undermines confidentiality assumptions even when ciphertext looks correct. Magazine-style case study demonstrates industrial IFT tooling (Radix) on a real open-source RoT block.

## Prior art

Classical noninterference [1], hyperproperties [2], and hardware information-flow tracking surveys [3] frame confidentiality as absence of illegal flows. Automating hardware security property generation [4] and classic security-policy models [5] inform property design. Downgrading / declassification policies [6] justify ignoring fully encrypted outputs under explicit conditions. MITRE CWE [7] catalogs weakness classes; the authors argue intermediate crypto-state leakage needs a dedicated entry.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Security-verification case study of OpenTitan OTP controller RTL using commercial IFT monitors in simulation.

## Method / approach

Six-step process centered on asset RndCnstKey:

1. Identify security-critical assets in the OTP controller / scrambler (RndCnstKey for PRESENT-based scrambling).
2. State information-flow security properties (RndCnstKey must not appear on OTP controller outputs).
3. Encode properties as Radix security rules; combine with RTL to generate IFT security monitors.
4. Insert monitors into existing semiconductor simulation (or emulation) and run functional / security traces.
5. Diagnose failing traces (waveform labels, hierarchical flow graphs) and refine properties with declassification when encrypted data is legitimately released (e.g., data_o when ready_o==1).
6. Propose and verify RTL remediation; upstream patch and CWE submission.

Radix workflow (Figure 3): rules + RTL -> security monitors -> simulation/emulation.

## Experimental setup

Design under test: OpenTitan OTP memory controller with scrambling datapath (PRESENT block cipher style). Tooling: Cycuity Radix IFT monitors in RTL simulation. Visual diagnostics: functional vs IFT-enhanced waveforms (Figures 2, 4, 6, 7) and hierarchical information-flow path graphs (Figure 5). No separate public benchmark suite or timing/area campaign; evidence is property fail/pass traces before and after the RTL change.

## Results summary

1. Initial property (RndCnstKey must not flow to OTP controller outputs) fails because encrypted data paths still carry labeled information that must be declassified when ready_o==1 on data_o (and related unlock-token paths such as test_unlock_token).
2. After refining the property to ignore/declassify fully encrypted data_o when ready, the main output leak is fixed in the analysis sense, but intermediate encryption rounds still leak via data_o when ready_o==0; input material can also be exposed on data_o.
3. Fix: `assign data_o = (valid_q)? data_state_q : 0;` instead of always driving data_state_q onto data_o, so intermediate cryptographic state is not continuously observable.
4. Patch accepted by OpenTitan; assessed low risk under their threat model; authors submit a new CWE to MITRE for intermediate cryptographic state leakage.

Figures 4-5 show pre-fix leakage to test_unlock_token and via data_o; Figure 6 shows refined property without unlock-token red labels but residual data_o leakage; Figure 7 shows post-fix clean data_o.

## Contributions

- State-of-the-art OpenTitan security verification case study for the OTP controller.
- Demonstration of commercial IFT (Radix) for hardware root-of-trust confidentiality properties with explicit declassification.
- Uncover OTP scrambler weakness (intermediate state on data_o), accepted RTL patch, and proposed CWE for intermediate cryptographic state leakage.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Shows that declassification of "ready" ciphertext is necessary but insufficient if ports still mirror intermediate round state when not ready.
- Analysis: Couples waveform-level IFT labels with hierarchical flow graphs to explain unlock-token and data_o leaks in one OTP controller instance.
- Analysis: Bridges magazine narrative and actionable upstream OpenTitan remediation plus CWE taxonomy impact.

## Limitations and future work

Single-block focus (OTP controller / scrambler) rather than full-chip OpenTitan IFT. Relies on commercial Radix tooling (not fully open reproduction of monitors). Threat-model judgment that the bug is low risk is project-specific; other deployments may differ. CWE acceptance status depends on MITRE process after submission. Broader automation of property generation [4] is cited but not fully re-evaluated here.

## Research opportunity

- Analysis: Replicate the RndCnstKey properties with open-source hardware IFT (e.g., academic gate/RTL IFT) on the same OpenTitan OTP RTL commit for tool-independent confirmation.
- Analysis: Extend the six-step Radix workflow to other OpenTitan secret assets (lifecycle tokens, flash scrambling keys, CSR fields) with a shared declassification policy library.
- Analysis: Build regression tests that assert data_o is zero whenever ready_o==0 / valid_q==0 across PRESENT and related lightweight cipher modules.
- Analysis: Formalize intermediate-crypto-state leakage as a reusable property template for SoC security CI alongside functional UVM tests.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Concrete, reproducible defect (one assignment) with before/after IFT evidence that practitioners can map to RTL.
- Analysis: Clear treatment of declassification vs residual intermediate-state leakage - a common pitfall in crypto datapath verification.
- Analysis: Direct impact path (OpenTitan patch + CWE) beyond academic-only findings.

### Cons

- Analysis: Commercial tool dependence limits open reproduction of the exact monitor generation flow.
- Analysis: No quantitative coverage metrics (property set size, false-positive rates, sim runtime) for scaling claims.
- Analysis: Magazine length leaves limited RTL listings and commit hashes for exact bisect of the patched revision.

digestSections.tl;dr:
- Case study of security verification for OpenTitan's OTP memory controller using Cycuity Radix information-flow tracking (IFT).
- Asset under test: RndCnstKey, the random constant key for OTP scrambling with a PRESENT-based lightweight cipher.
- Initial noninterference-style property fails; refined property with declassification of fully encrypted ready outputs still finds intermediate-round leakage on data_o when ready_o==0.
- One-line RTL fix zeros data_o unless valid_q; patch accepted by OpenTitan and a new CWE proposed for intermediate cryptographic state leakage.
digestSections.problem statement: Commercial-grade open-source silicon roots of trust such as OpenTitan combine complex RTL, cryptographic datapaths, and access-control logic. Security properties that only check final encrypted outputs can miss unintended information flows of secret assets through intermediate cryptographic state on module ports. This paper asks how to systematically verify that a critical OTP scrambling key does not leak through the OTP controller, and what RTL defects IFT can expose beyond functional tests.
digestSections.motivation: OpenTitan is used as a platform identity module / U2F / TPM-like hardware RoT with Ibex (RV32IMCB), AES/KMAC/HMAC, and ROM/FLASH/SRAM/OTP plus controllers. OTP stores secrets with scrambling, locking, and integrity checks. A silent leak of RndCnstKey (or related intermediate state) on controller outputs undermines confidentiality assumptions even when ciphertext looks correct. Magazine-style case study demonstrates industrial IFT tooling (Radix) on a real open-source RoT block.
digestSections.prior art: Classical noninterference [1], hyperproperties [2], and hardware information-flow tracking surveys [3] frame confidentiality as absence of illegal flows. Automating hardware security property generation [4] and classic security-policy models [5] inform property design. Downgrading / declassification policies [6] justify ignoring fully encrypted outputs under explicit conditions. MITRE CWE [7] catalogs weakness classes; the authors argue intermediate crypto-state leakage needs a dedicated entry.

digestSections.method / approach:
Six-step process centered on asset RndCnstKey:

1. Identify security-critical assets in the OTP controller / scrambler (RndCnstKey for PRESENT-based scrambling).
2. State information-flow security properties (RndCnstKey must not appear on OTP controller outputs).
3. Encode properties as Radix security rules; combine with RTL to generate IFT security monitors.
4. Insert monitors into existing semiconductor simulation (or emulation) and run functional / security traces.
5. Diagnose failing traces (waveform labels, hierarchical flow graphs) and refine properties with declassification when encrypted data is legitimately released (e.g., data_o when ready_o==1).
6. Propose and verify RTL remediation; upstream patch and CWE submission.

Radix workflow (Figure 3): rules + RTL -> security monitors -> simulation/emulation.

Visual diagnostics: functional vs IFT-enhanced waveforms (Figures 2, 4, 6, 7) and hierarchical information-flow path graphs (Figure 5). No separate public benchmark suite or timing/area campaign; evidence is property fail/pass traces before and after the RTL change.

## TL;DR

- BlackParrot targets a community-driven, Linux-capable, cache-coherent RV64G multicore in standard SystemVerilog for accelerator-host SoCs.
- Development follows Be Tiny, Be Modular, Be Friendly plus four adoption metrics: quality, virality, functionality, and efficiency.
- Architecture: heterogeneous 2-D mesh tiles, BedRock race-free directory coherence (VI/MSI/MESI), three specialized NoCs, decoupled front/back/memory ends.
- Silicon-validated in GlobalFoundries 12-nm; post-tapeout refactor claimed 50% tile area and 50% wire-length reduction.
- Cosimulation with Dromajo, RISC-V/BEEBS/Spec/CoreMark regressions, and UW OpenROAD Free45 flow in progress.

## Problem statement

RISC-V has a strong open ISA and software stack, but lacks a globally maintained open-source Linux-capable SoC implementation that industrial designers can trust, extend, and integrate with agile accelerators. Prior generator-centric efforts (Rocket Chip, BOOM) evolved with centralized stewardship and languages (Chisel) that raise onboarding friction for some teams. BlackParrot aims to be the default open RV64 multicore fabric for accelerator SoCs, optimizing PPA and complexity while treating software-engineering principles (narrow interfaces, modularity, verification coverage) as first-class design metrics.

## Motivation

Post-Dennard scaling pushes specialized accelerators paired with efficient host cores. Open RISC-V cores exist, yet a cohesive, silicon-proven, SystemVerilog multicore with coherent accelerator attachment remains a gap. UW/BU bootstrap the effort with DARPA support but seek community stewardship comparable to RISC-V ISA maintenance. Success requires not only ISA compliance and Linux boot but adoption-friendly out-of-box experience, inclusive collaboration culture, and ASIC validation to catch physical-design limits invisible in RTL-only studies.

## Prior art

Contrasts Rocket Chip [4], BOOM [5], and commercial SiFive U54 (closed reference in Fig. 2). Builds on BaseJump STL [8], Berkeley HardFloat [6], Verilator [7], and Dromajo cosimulation [1]. Positions against bus-centric SoCs (AXI/AHB complexity) and organically evolved centralized generator stacks. OpenROAD / UW Free45 flow [2],[3] cited for democratized physical validation. Ariane/Zaruba application-class core [10] appears as benchmark peer in Fig. 2 snapshot.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Open Linux-capable RV64 multicore generator/platform for accelerator-host SoCs with coherence, NoC tiling, and agile verification methodology.

## Method / approach

**Design philosophy.** Four success metrics (quality, virality, functionality, efficiency) and manifesto rules: Be Tiny (minimal RTL, emulate non-critical spec features), Be Modular (latency-insensitive narrow interfaces), Be Friendly (approachable community and design).

**ISA and OS support.** RV64G (I/M/A/F/D), machine/supervisor/user, SV39 virtual memory, Linux-capable with CLINT/PLIC-style interrupt distribution per tile.

**BedRock coherence.** Distributed directory protocol via local cache engines (LCEs) and programmable cache coherence engines (CCEs) over a coherent NoC. Supports VI, MSI, MESI. Race-free property: coherence state transitions occur at CCEs, not LCEs, reducing protocol complexity. CCE variants: microprogrammed (default, firmware-updatable), fixed-function, minimal uncached (I/O/accelerators).

**Tiled SoC microarchitecture.** Heterogeneous 2-D mesh with one router per network per tile; wormhole, dimension-ordered, credit-based flow control. Tile classes: Core (processor + directory shard + L2 slice), L2 extension (scale-out cache), Coherent accelerator (LCE + backing cache; attach options from D$ reuse to custom LCE), Streaming/I/O (no local cache/directory; GPUs, NICs, peripherals). Bus adapters (AXI, WishBone) at boundaries rather than internal coupling.

**Decoupled core.** Three Ends: Front (speculative in-order fetch/issue queue; TLB misses/exceptions to back end), Back (execution, architectural state, branch resolution metadata to front), Memory (BedRock LCE/CCE). Thin struct-based latency-insensitive FIFO interfaces; back end nonstalling after issue, flush/replay on cache misses handled via BedRock.

**Three NoC classes.** BedRock (coherent, request/command/response channels), DRAM (0.5-D to memory controllers), I/O (1-D peripheral transduction).

**Verification and agile process.** System-level program execution (RISC-V tests, BEEBS, Spec, CoreMark); hybrid Dromajo checkpoint cosimulation; coverage metrics tracked daily. VLSI class (35 students, 3 weeks) demonstrated feature extensions (pipeline latency, cache banking, branch predictors). Tapeout collateral and OpenROAD Free45 push planned.

## Experimental setup

- Silicon: GlobalFoundries 12-nm FinFET quad-core tapeout (July 2019); chip running in lab; ongoing 12-nm and 40-nm tapeouts.
- Performance snapshot: CoreMark/MHz comparison vs open and SiFive U54 closed core (Fig. 2; living-project snapshot).
- Physical metrics: post-GF12 tapeout refactor claimed 50% tile area and 50% total wire-length reduction (Fig. 4).
- Simulation: Synopsys VCS primary; Verilator supported. Cosimulation with Dromajo checkpoints.
- Educational validation: UW VLSI course project outcomes as complexity/virality proxy.

## Results summary

- Presents a modular, SystemVerilog, BSD-licensed RV64G multicore validated in GF12 ASIC, booting Linux with coherent caches and accelerator attachment paths.
- Introduces BedRock race-free programmable directory coherence and tiled NoC-centric integration model tuned for hierarchical ASIC flows.
- Documents agile/process evidence: student extensions, Dromajo cosim, coverage-driven verification, and planned open PD via Free45.
- Positions BlackParrot as Pareto-oriented host fabric for accelerator SoCs vs centralized Chisel generator stacks.
- Quantitative PPA claims are snapshot CoreMark comparisons and post-silicon area/wire reductions; no full Spec/Energy published in this overview article.

## Contributions

- Introduce BlackParrot as an open, Linux-capable, cache-coherent RV64 multicore aimed at global community stewardship for accelerator SoCs.
- Articulate software-engineering-of-hardware methodology: intentional interfaces, modular three-End core, hierarchical design docs, and verification coverage as adoption metrics.
- Present BedRock distributed directory coherence with race-free CCE-centric transitions and microprogrammable CCE option.
- Describe heterogeneous tiled mesh SoC with Core, L2 extension, coherent accelerator, and streaming/I/O tiles plus BedRock/DRAM/I/O NoCs.
- Report GF12 silicon validation, Dromajo cosimulation flow, and educational out-of-box complexity evaluation.
- Release codebase on GitHub under BSD-3 license with tapeout reference directories.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Treats race-free coherence (transitions only at CCEs) as a complexity reduction lever for verifiable directory protocols in open multicores.
- Analysis: Combines software-Linux-style modularity (latency-insensitive Ends, BaseJump STL) with explicit rejection of generator knob explosion (Be Tiny emulation for non-critical spec features).
- Analysis: Shifts accelerator integration from ad-hoc buses to tiered LCE attachment options within a coherent mesh rather than bolt-on non-coherent DMA-only models.
- Analysis: Microprogrammed CCE firmware updates enable post-silicon coherence/security experimentation uncommon in fixed open cores.
- Analysis: Positions SystemVerilog + minimal dependencies as virality strategy vs Chisel/BlueSpec generator ecosystems.

## Limitations and future work

- Overview article: limited published benchmark breadth (CoreMark snapshot; Spec/energy not deeply quantified here).
- Commercial EDA (VCS) still primary; open Verilator support is goal but not sole flow.
- OpenROAD Free45 integration in progress, not complete turnkey at paper time.
- Fig. 2 comparison is time snapshot of moving open-source projects; SiFive U54 is closed reference.
- Coherence protocols listed (VI/MSI/MESI) but security side-channel and formal verification completeness not claimed solved.
- Community virality/friendliness goals are qualitative; long-term stewardship success not yet demonstrated.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Rocket/BOOM and commercial cores provide Linux RV64 options, but few combine SystemVerilog readability, race-free programmable coherence, heterogeneous tile mesh for accelerators, and silicon-proven agile verification narrative in one stewarded platform.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: Quantitative multi-accelerator SoC studies (Gemmini/NVDLA-class attach), OpenROAD QoR on BlackParrot configs, and head-to-head full-system FireSim comparisons vs Chipyard/Rocket hosts remain open. Fig. 4 area gains lack public PPA tables.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Integrate BlackParrot coherent accelerator tile with Gemmini or other RoCC/MMIO accelerators; measure BedRock traffic vs Chipyard TileLink baselines on identical DNN workloads.
- Analysis: Reproduce GF12 quad-core config through UW Free45 and compare turnaround vs commercial PD for SCORE registry evidence.
- Analysis: Stress-test microprogrammed CCE with security/coherence protocol variants using Dromajo checkpoint cosim as regression harness.
- Analysis: Extend student-modifiability study to measure interface stability metrics (PR merge time vs Rocket Chip) for agile-SoC survey rubric.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: Clear design manifesto (Tiny/Modular/Friendly) maps directly to integrator decisions for accelerator-host SoCs.
- Analysis: SystemVerilog + BaseJump STL lowers barrier for industry RTL engineers vs generator DSLs.
- Analysis: BedRock race-free coherence and tile taxonomy give structured coherent accelerator attachment paths.
- Analysis: Silicon validation (GF12) and Dromajo cosim address trust gaps common in RTL-only open cores.
- Analysis: Educational 3-week project evidence supports modularity/onboarding claims.

### Cons

- Analysis: Performance evidence in paper is mostly CoreMark/MHz snapshot; limited published power/area tables vs BOOM/Ariane.
- Analysis: Manual full-page figure clips needed because auto capture found captions but no artwork bboxes.
- Analysis: Fig. 4 (die photo/PR) referenced in text but absent from audit_manifest figure list.
- Analysis: Dependence on commercial sim for primary development may limit reproducibility for some labs.
- Analysis: Community stewardship ambition not yet proven relative to Berkeley-centric generator ecosystems.

## Benchmarks and tables

No numbered tables in this article. Performance comparisons appear graphically in Figure 2 (CoreMark/MHz vs open RV64 Linux-capable cores and SiFive U54 reference).

# VeeR EL2

- **SCORE scripts:** `install_veer_el2.sh` / `generate_veer_el2.sh` / — (no `run_*.sh`; README.md architectures table)
- **Upstream:** https://github.com/chipsalliance/Cores-VeeR-EL2
- **License:** Apache-2.0 (README: "governed by Apache-2.0 (LICENSE)")
- **Category:** processor_core
- **ISA / language:** SystemVerilog EL2 RISC-V core RTL under `design/` (fetch/decode/EXU/LSU/debug blocks per README directory structure).

- **Verification:**
  - Upstream: Verilator model build documented in README; `testbench/` with assembly/hex tests; Python 3.10+ verification env; Verible lint/format.
  - SCORE: snapshot + lint per `generate_veer_el2.sh` → `datasets/veer-el2/<commit>/verification/`.

- **Software:** RISC-V GCC ≥8.3 required (README Dependencies); hello-world Verilator run prints "Hello World from VeeR EL2".
- **Primary paper:** none
- **Optional docs:** `papers/_incoming/tech-brief-western-digital-risc-v.pdf` (WD RISC-V tech brief — vendor overview, not EL2-specific peer paper)
- **Limitations (from upstream, quoted):**
  - README testbench described as "(Very) simple testbench."
  - Verilator ≥5 required; optional `espresso` for decode table generation when modifying ISA.
- **SCORE generate path:** `datasets/veer-el2/<commit>/` (RTL snapshot); logs under commit folder

projects.fullMarkdown:
# Chipyard: Integrated Design, Simulation, and Implementation Framework for Custom SoCs

## Bibliographic information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Authors | Alon Amid, David Biancolin, Abraham Gonzalez, Daniel Grubb, Sagar Karandikar, Harrison Liew, Albert Magyar, Howard Mao, Albert Ou, Nathan Pemberton, Paul Rigge, Colin Schmidt, John Wright, Jerry Zhao, Yakun Sophia Shao, Krste Asanovic, Borivoje Nikolic |
| Affiliations | University of California, Berkeley |
| Venue | IEEE Micro |
| Venue type | journal |
| Year | 2020 |
| Volume / issue / pages | Vol. 40, No. 4, pp. 10-21 (July/August 2020) |
| Paper DOI | https://doi.org/10.1109/MM.2020.2996616 |
| arXiv | |
| URL | https://doi.org/10.1109/MM.2020.2996616 |
| Keywords | agile hardware, open-source SoC, RISC-V, Rocket Chip, FIRRTL, FireSim, Hammer, FireMarshal |
| Open access | Author PDF; framework at https://github.com/ucb-bar/chipyard/ |

**PDF:** [paper.pdf](./paper.pdf)

Theme article: Agile and Open-Source Hardware. Date of publication 22 May 2020; date of current version 30 June 2020.

## TL;DR

- Specialization raises SoC complexity; agile generator flows help, but integrating and validating heterogeneous SoCs remains hard.
- Chipyard unifies the Rocket Chip generator ecosystem with FIRRTL transforms for multi-stage flows, Verilator/commercial RTL sim, FireSim cloud FPGA-accelerated simulation, Hammer VLSI (tool/PDK plug-ins including ASAP7), and FireMarshal workload management.
- Composable open IP includes BOOM, Ariane, Hwacha, DSP/ML/crypto accelerators, memory, and peripherals, with Diplomacy/TileLink and Verilog blackbox support.
- Motivated by Berkeley RISC-V test chips across IBM 45nm SOI, ST 28nm FD-SOI, TSMC 28nm, TSMC 16nm FFC, and Intel 22nm FFL, including a late-config bug that halved cache capacity.
- Positions against OpenPiton-style tile manycores and frameworks with more rigid subsystems / proprietary IP.

## Problem statement

Continued efficiency gains require specialized hardware, but custom silicon raises design cost. Agile generator methodologies reduce that cost for relatively homogeneous processor chips, yet building complex heterogeneous SoCs exposes integration and validation gaps: misconfiguration under rich parameterization, weak full-system coverage for interfaces/CDCs/third-party IP/power, and process-portability friction when physical design scripts do not track generator parameters. Chipyard targets a unified open-source framework so independently developed generators and tools can compose complete SoCs with consistent design intent across design, simulation, and implementation.

## Motivation

Technology scaling slowdowns push domain-specific architectures (a "new golden age" of architecture), escalating development costs for differentiated systems. Berkeley's series of Rocket Chip-based RISC-V test chips grew from modest cores to multi-core designs with accelerators and full analog subsystems (SerDes, ADCs, PLLs). Verification shifted from block-level reuse toward system-integration validation. Small agile teams struggle to parallelize architecture, RTL, physical design, verification, and validation while retaining institutional memory of good CAD practices across process nodes.

## Prior art

Builds on Rocket Chip / Chisel / Diplomacy / TileLink and prior Berkeley agile RISC-V chips. Related open frameworks emphasize tile-granularity manycore customization (e.g., OpenPiton) or more rigid subsystems and proprietary IP (contrasted in-text with ESP-like and CHIPKIT-style frameworks). FIRRTL compiler work enables reusable transforms; FireSim provides cloud FPGA-accelerated simulation; Hammer provides reusable physical design plug-ins; OpenROAD and ASAP7 are cited as open digital-flow / PDK progress. Analog generator efforts such as BAG are discussed as future integration targets rather than solved in this paper.

## Category of work

Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Integrated open SoC generator framework spanning RTL composition, multi-flow simulation/emulation, and portable VLSI implementation.

## Method / approach

**Unified SoC framework.** Chipyard fronts on the Rocket Chip SoC generator: Chisel-based parameterized generators, Diplomacy parameter negotiation, and TileLink interconnect. A unified top-level generator builds heterogeneous systems from parameterized configurations. Non-Chisel IP (e.g., Verilog) enters via Chisel wrappers / blackboxes or Verilog-to-FIRRTL paths.

**IP corpus.** Beyond Rocket, generators include BOOM, Ariane, Hwacha, DSP modules, domain-specific accelerators (ML and cryptography), memory systems, and peripherals. Fine-grained intracore parameterization lets Rocket variants serve as Linux-capable application cores (e.g., RV64GC with FPU and virtual memory) or smaller controllers (e.g., RV64IMAC with reduced predictors/caches and no VM). Accelerators attach as RoCC tightly coupled units or MMIO periphery blocks.

**FIRRTL multi-flow transforms.** Front-end RTL elaborates to FIRRTL. Custom transforms emit collateral for concurrent flows from one shared source: software RTL simulation, FPGA-accelerated simulation, and back-end physical design (different memory/I/O abstractions, FPGA interfaces, cosimulation clock gating, etc.).

**Software RTL simulation.** Makefile wrappers build Verilator and proprietary commercial simulator executables for tethered designs with emulated peripherals (host loads programs); un-tethered boot-ROM SoCs are also supported.

**FireSim FPGA-accelerated simulation.** FireSim on AWS EC2 models timing of the DUT and I/Os/peripherals for deterministic full-system evaluation (unlike FPGA prototyping). Integrated as a Chipyard library consuming Chipyard configs and FIRRTL (Golden Gate compiler), including external Verilog where needed.

**Hammer VLSI flow.** Modular physical design with vendor-specific process-technology and EDA-tool plug-ins implementing abstracted APIs (Tcl, clocks, power, macros, straps). Supports hierarchical PD; FIRRTL grouping/flattening can retarget logical vs physical hierarchy. ASAP7 open predictive PDK plug-in included after a short port; aims to share descriptions across predictive kits and advanced nodes.

**FireMarshal workloads.** Version-controlled software workload descriptions generate images for Spike/QEMU, RTL sim, and FireSim without per-target rewrites. Provides Linux templates/kernels/drivers plus versioned standard and custom RISC-V toolchains for nonstandard extensions.

**Concurrent agile use model.** Multiple team members iterate custom features through modeling, simulation, integration, FireSim validation, and physical design with continuous integration via configured workloads.

## Experimental setup

- Retrospective silicon context: Berkeley Rocket Chip-based RISC-V test chips since ~2012 across IBM 45nm SOI, ST 28nm FD-SOI, TSMC 28nm, TSMC 16nm FFC, Intel 22nm FFL.
- Framework evaluation is primarily methodological: composition of generators, multi-flow FIRRTL transforms, Verilator/commercial sim, FireSim cloud FPGA simulation, Hammer with ASAP7 plug-in, FireMarshal software targeting.
- Example configurations in Figure 2: (b) single Rocket + educational SHA3 RoCC accelerator; (c) heterogeneous mix (RV32 Rocket control, RV64 Rocket app, RV64GC BOOM 3-wide OoO) with per-core accelerators, peripherals, L2, simulated block device and DRAM.
- Funding acknowledgments: DARPA CRAFT HR0011-16-C0052; ARPA-E DE-AR0000849; ADEPT Lab sponsors; prototype fabrication donations from Intel, STMicroelectronics, TSMC.

## Results summary

- Demonstrates an integrated open framework that keeps design intent consistent across RTL generation, software/FPGA simulation, and portable VLSI implementation.
- Documents real agile-process failure modes motivating continuous full-system validation (e.g., late configuration change that inadvertently halved cache capacity).
- Shows FireSim integration for accessible high-performance full-system simulation on public-cloud FPGAs, and Hammer ASAP7 plug-in as evidence that process/tool plug-ins can be added quickly for academic prototyping.
- Positions Chipyard as more fine-grained and generator-centric than tile-only manycores or rigid/proprietary subsystem frameworks.
- Future-looking claims (not silicon results of this paper): BAG-like AMS generator integration and progress toward fully open custom SoC stacks via OpenROAD-class digital flows.

## Contributions

- Present Chipyard as an integrated SoC design, simulation, and implementation environment for specialized compute systems.
- Provide configurable, composable, open-source, generator-based IP usable across hardware development stages while maintaining integration consistency.
- Integrate FIRRTL transforms so one shared source RTL/config drives multiple concurrent flows (RTL sim, FireSim, Hammer).
- Integrate FireSim cloud FPGA-accelerated simulation and FireMarshal shared software workload management for continuous validation.
- Include Hammer modular VLSI with tool/PDK plug-ins (including ASAP7) for portable physical design.
- Articulate lessons from Berkeley's multi-node RISC-V test-chip series on agile SoC integration/validation challenges.

## Innovations

- Analysis: Treats multi-stage flow consistency (sim/emulation/ASIC) as a first-class framework problem solved via shared FIRRTL transforms rather than ad-hoc per-flow scripts.
- Analysis: Combines fine-grained generator customization (Diplomacy/TileLink, RoCC vs MMIO attachment, heterogeneous Rocket/BOOM roles) with cloud FPGA-accelerated full-system timing simulation and portable PD plug-ins in one open stack.
- Analysis: FireMarshal's single workload description across Spike/QEMU/RTL/FireSim reduces software-hardware co-validation friction typical of agile SoC teams.
- Analysis: Hierarchical Hammer + FIRRTL hierarchy retargeting addresses agile PD task distribution that prior generator papers often left as process-specific scripts.

## Limitations and future work

- Analog/mixed-signal and manufacturing interfaces still lack mature open integration models; BAG-style AMS generators are proposed as future Chipyard integration, not delivered here.
- Submicron digital PD remains coupled to NDA PDKs and commercial EDA; Hammer plug-ins mitigate but do not eliminate proprietary stacks (OpenROAD cited as encouraging progress).
- Paper is a framework/overview article: limited quantitative head-to-head benchmarks vs OpenPiton/ESP/CHIPKIT.
- Agile small-team challenges (effort parallelization, institutional memory of CAD practices) are mitigated by tooling but not claimed solved.
- Continuous validation depends on team discipline and workload coverage; parameterization can still misconfigure systems if validation is incomplete.

## Research opportunity

**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Prior Rocket Chip / agile RISC-V generator work [2],[3] and manycore frameworks [8],[9] advanced reusable RTL, but left multi-flow consistency, cloud full-system timing simulation, portable PD plug-ins, and shared software workloads as separately maintained stacks.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: AMS integration, fully open PD for advanced nodes, and quantitative cross-framework productivity/QoR comparisons remain open; ASAP7 is predictive, not a tapeout PDK substitute for leading-edge silicon.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Reproduce Figure 2(c)-class heterogeneous configs through Verilator, FireSim, and Hammer ASAP7 as a SCORE regression suite measuring turnaround time and config-bug catch rate (motivated by the halved-cache incident).
- Analysis: Compare Chipyard RoCC/MMIO accelerator attachment effort vs ESP NoC sockets / OpenPiton CCX on the same accelerator RTL (SHA3, Gemmini [11], NVDLA [12]).
- Analysis: Extend Hammer plug-in matrix with open PDKs beyond ASAP7 and measure how much FIRRTL hierarchy retargeting reduces PD script churn when generator parameters change.
- Analysis: Co-design FireMarshal Linux workloads with ML accelerators (Gemmini) to quantify software reuse across Spike vs FireSim for SCORE-style SoC platform surveys.
- Analysis: Prototype BAG-to-Chipyard behavioral-model hooks for SerDes/ADC/PLL blocks cited in the Berkeley chip retrospective, targeting digital-analog interface validation gaps called out in the Open-Source SoC Development section.

## Pros and cons

### Pros

- Analysis: End-to-end open stack from generators through cloud FPGA-accelerated simulation and portable VLSI is unusually complete for 2020 academic SoC frameworks.
- Analysis: Diplomacy/TileLink plus fine-grained Rocket parameterization supports heterogeneous roles (app vs controller cores) without swapping entirely different cores.
- Analysis: Concrete silicon retrospective across five process nodes grounds the integration/validation claims beyond a pure tooling pitch.
- Analysis: FireSim+FireMarshal lowers the barrier for small teams to get deterministic full-system software/hardware co-validation.

### Cons

- Analysis: Overview paper lacks quantitative comparison tables (runtime, area QoR, bring-up time) versus OpenPiton/ESP, so adoption arguments are qualitative.
- Analysis: Commercial EDA/PDK dependence remains for real tapeouts; ASAP7 enables flow prototyping but not drop-in advanced-node manufacturing.
- Analysis: capture_figures found captions but no clean artwork clips; figure embeds are full-page renders and include surrounding body text.
- Analysis: Parameterization power that enables agility still admits silent misconfiguration unless continuous full-system validation is enforced.

## Benchmarks and tables

No numbered tables in the PDF (`table_caption_count=0` in `audit_manifest.json`).

## Figures

### Figure 1: Increasing complexity of custom RISC-V SoC test chips built at Berkeley using the Rocket Chip SoC generator since 2012.

![Figure 1](./figures/figure_01.png)

*Page 3. Interpretation: Timeline/complexity growth of Berkeley Rocket Chip-based RISC-V test chips motivating Chipyard's integration and validation focus.*

### Figure 2: SoC customization in Chipyard using the Rocket Chip generator configuration system. (a) A typical Chipyard SoC can include multiple heterogeneous application cores, as well as multiple configurations of BOOM or Rocket cores that can serve various purposes within the SoC, such as a controller unit. Customization can be performed across various levels of the SoC, including Rocket Custom Coprocessor (RoCC) accelerators, MMIO accelerators, and peripherals. (b) An example configuration of a simple design, consisting of a single Rocket in-order processor core and a custom educational SHA3 tightly integrated accelerator. (c) An example configuration of a more complex SoC, consisting of a multiple cores of various capabilities (RV32 Rocket in-order control core, RV64 Rocket in-order application core, RV64GC BOOM 3-wide out-of-order application core), custom accelerators attached to each core, a standard set of peripherals, and a deeper memory hierarchy with an L2 cache. This example also includes a simulated block device and simulated backing DRAM memory.

![Figure 2](./figures/figure_02.png)

*Page 5. Interpretation: Configuration hierarchy from SoC-level heterogeneous cores down to RoCC/MMIO accelerators, with simple SHA3 and complex multi-core examples.*

### Figure 3: Multiple disparate design flows supported by the Chipyard framework through generators and transformations. A series of FIRRTL transformations consumes generators with a custom configuration, and outputs appropriate Verilog and associated collateral for different design stage platforms.

![Figure 3](./figures/figure_03.png)

*Page 6. Interpretation: Shared generator/config source fans out via FIRRTL transforms to simulation, FPGA-accelerated simulation, and VLSI implementation flows.*

### Figure 4: Shared software development in Chipyard using FireMarshal. Designers can use the standard RISC-V software toolchains, or custom software toolchains. While the core application logic and libraries are consistent with the SoC design, kernel and driver configuration may change based on the target platforms or tethered systems. FireMarshal automates workload generation to enable targeting multiple platforms using a single description.

![Figure 4](./figures/figure_04.png)

*Page 8. Interpretation: FireMarshal maps one workload description onto Spike/QEMU, RTL simulation, and FireSim with standard or custom RISC-V toolchains.*

## Reproducibility

|----------|----------------|
| Code | https://github.com/ucb-bar/chipyard/ |
| Data | Not reported (framework paper) |
| Supplement | FireSim, Hammer, FireMarshal integrated in Chipyard ecosystem; ASAP7 Hammer plug-in in core Hammer repository |

Theme article: Agile and Open-Source Hardware. Date of publication 22 May 2020; date of current version 30 June 2020.
digestSections.tl;dr:
- Specialization raises SoC complexity; agile generator flows help, but integrating and validating heterogeneous SoCs remains hard.
- Chipyard unifies the Rocket Chip generator ecosystem with FIRRTL transforms for multi-stage flows, Verilator/commercial RTL sim, FireSim cloud FPGA-accelerated simulation, Hammer VLSI (tool/PDK plug-ins including ASAP7), and FireMarshal workload management.
- Composable open IP includes BOOM, Ariane, Hwacha, DSP/ML/crypto accelerators, memory, and peripherals, with Diplomacy/TileLink and Verilog blackbox support.
- Motivated by Berkeley RISC-V test chips across IBM 45nm SOI, ST 28nm FD-SOI, TSMC 28nm, TSMC 16nm FFC, and Intel 22nm FFL, including a late-config bug that halved cache capacity.
- Positions against OpenPiton-style tile manycores and frameworks with more rigid subsystems / proprietary IP.
digestSections.problem statement: Continued efficiency gains require specialized hardware, but custom silicon raises design cost. Agile generator methodologies reduce that cost for relatively homogeneous processor chips, yet building complex heterogeneous SoCs exposes integration and validation gaps: misconfiguration under rich parameterization, weak full-system coverage for interfaces/CDCs/third-party IP/power, and process-portability friction when physical design scripts do not track generator parameters. Chipyard targets a unified open-source framework so independently developed generators and tools can compose complete SoCs with consistent design intent across design, simulation, and implementation.
digestSections.motivation: Technology scaling slowdowns push domain-specific architectures (a "new golden age" of architecture), escalating development costs for differentiated systems. Berkeley's series of Rocket Chip-based RISC-V test chips grew from modest cores to multi-core designs with accelerators and full analog subsystems (SerDes, ADCs, PLLs). Verification shifted from block-level reuse toward system-integration validation. Small agile teams struggle to parallelize architecture, RTL, physical design, verification, and validation while retaining institutional memory of good CAD practices across process nodes.
digestSections.prior art: Builds on Rocket Chip / Chisel / Diplomacy / TileLink and prior Berkeley agile RISC-V chips. Related open frameworks emphasize tile-granularity manycore customization (e.g., OpenPiton) or more rigid subsystems and proprietary IP (contrasted in-text with ESP-like and CHIPKIT-style frameworks). FIRRTL compiler work enables reusable transforms; FireSim provides cloud FPGA-accelerated simulation; Hammer provides reusable physical design plug-ins; OpenROAD and ASAP7 are cited as open digital-flow / PDK progress. Analog generator efforts such as BAG are discussed as future integration targets rather than solved in this paper.
digestSections.category of work:
Primary: `system-architecture`  
Secondary: `circuit-design`  
Note: Integrated open SoC generator framework spanning RTL composition, multi-flow simulation/emulation, and portable VLSI implementation.
digestSections.method / approach:
**Unified SoC framework.** Chipyard fronts on the Rocket Chip SoC generator: Chisel-based parameterized generators, Diplomacy parameter negotiation, and TileLink interconnect. A unified top-level generator builds heterogeneous systems from parameterized configurations. Non-Chisel IP (e.g., Verilog) enters via Chisel wrappers / blackboxes or Verilog-to-FIRRTL paths.

**IP corpus.** Beyond Rocket, generators include BOOM, Ariane, Hwacha, DSP modules, domain-specific accelerators (ML and cryptography), memory systems, and peripherals. Fine-grained intracore parameterization lets Rocket variants serve as Linux-capable application cores (e.g., RV64GC with FPU and virtual memory) or smaller controllers (e.g., RV64IMAC with reduced predictors/caches and no VM). Accelerators attach as RoCC tightly coupled units or MMIO periphery blocks.

**FIRRTL multi-flow transforms.** Front-end RTL elaborates to FIRRTL. Custom transforms emit collateral for concurrent flows from one shared source: software RTL simulation, FPGA-accelerated simulation, and back-end physical design (different memory/I/O abstractions, FPGA interfaces, cosimulation clock gating, etc.).

**Software RTL simulation.** Makefile wrappers build Verilator and proprietary commercial simulator executables for tethered designs with emulated peripherals (host loads programs); un-tethered boot-ROM SoCs are also supported.

**FireSim FPGA-accelerated simulation.** FireSim on AWS EC2 models timing of the DUT and I/Os/peripherals for deterministic full-system evaluation (unlike FPGA prototyping). Integrated as a Chipyard library consuming Chipyard configs and FIRRTL (Golden Gate compiler), including external Verilog where needed.

**Hammer VLSI flow.** Modular physical design with vendor-specific process-technology and EDA-tool plug-ins implementing abstracted APIs (Tcl, clocks, power, macros, straps). Supports hierarchical PD; FIRRTL grouping/flattening can retarget logical vs physical hierarchy. ASAP7 open predictive PDK plug-in included after a short port; aims to share descriptions across predictive kits and advanced nodes.

**FireMarshal workloads.** Version-controlled software workload descriptions generate images for Spike/QEMU, RTL sim, and FireSim without per-target rewrites. Provides Linux templates/kernels/drivers plus versioned standard and custom RISC-V toolchains for nonstandard extensions.

**Concurrent agile use model.** Multiple team members iterate custom features through modeling, simulation, integration, FireSim validation, and physical design with continuous integration via configured workloads.
digestSections.experimental setup:
- Retrospective silicon context: Berkeley Rocket Chip-based RISC-V test chips since ~2012 across IBM 45nm SOI, ST 28nm FD-SOI, TSMC 28nm, TSMC 16nm FFC, Intel 22nm FFL.
- Framework evaluation is primarily methodological: composition of generators, multi-flow FIRRTL transforms, Verilator/commercial sim, FireSim cloud FPGA simulation, Hammer with ASAP7 plug-in, FireMarshal software targeting.
- Example configurations in Figure 2: (b) single Rocket + educational SHA3 RoCC accelerator; (c) heterogeneous mix (RV32 Rocket control, RV64 Rocket app, RV64GC BOOM 3-wide OoO) with per-core accelerators, peripherals, L2, simulated block device and DRAM.
- Funding acknowledgments: DARPA CRAFT HR0011-16-C0052; ARPA-E DE-AR0000849; ADEPT Lab sponsors; prototype fabrication donations from Intel, STMicroelectronics, TSMC.
digestSections.results summary:
- Demonstrates an integrated open framework that keeps design intent consistent across RTL generation, software/FPGA simulation, and portable VLSI implementation.
- Documents real agile-process failure modes motivating continuous full-system validation (e.g., late configuration change that inadvertently halved cache capacity).
- Shows FireSim integration for accessible high-performance full-system simulation on public-cloud FPGAs, and Hammer ASAP7 plug-in as evidence that process/tool plug-ins can be added quickly for academic prototyping.
- Positions Chipyard as more fine-grained and generator-centric than tile-only manycores or rigid/proprietary subsystem frameworks.
- Future-looking claims (not silicon results of this paper): BAG-like AMS generator integration and progress toward fully open custom SoC stacks via OpenROAD-class digital flows.
digestSections.contributions:
- Present Chipyard as an integrated SoC design, simulation, and implementation environment for specialized compute systems.
- Provide configurable, composable, open-source, generator-based IP usable across hardware development stages while maintaining integration consistency.
- Integrate FIRRTL transforms so one shared source RTL/config drives multiple concurrent flows (RTL sim, FireSim, Hammer).
- Integrate FireSim cloud FPGA-accelerated simulation and FireMarshal shared software workload management for continuous validation.
- Include Hammer modular VLSI with tool/PDK plug-ins (including ASAP7) for portable physical design.
- Articulate lessons from Berkeley's multi-node RISC-V test-chip series on agile SoC integration/validation challenges.
digestSections.innovations:
- Analysis: Treats multi-stage flow consistency (sim/emulation/ASIC) as a first-class framework problem solved via shared FIRRTL transforms rather than ad-hoc per-flow scripts.
- Analysis: Combines fine-grained generator customization (Diplomacy/TileLink, RoCC vs MMIO attachment, heterogeneous Rocket/BOOM roles) with cloud FPGA-accelerated full-system timing simulation and portable PD plug-ins in one open stack.
- Analysis: FireMarshal's single workload description across Spike/QEMU/RTL/FireSim reduces software-hardware co-validation friction typical of agile SoC teams.
- Analysis: Hierarchical Hammer + FIRRTL hierarchy retargeting addresses agile PD task distribution that prior generator papers often left as process-specific scripts.
digestSections.limitations and future work:
- Analog/mixed-signal and manufacturing interfaces still lack mature open integration models; BAG-style AMS generators are proposed as future Chipyard integration, not delivered here.
- Submicron digital PD remains coupled to NDA PDKs and commercial EDA; Hammer plug-ins mitigate but do not eliminate proprietary stacks (OpenROAD cited as encouraging progress).
- Paper is a framework/overview article: limited quantitative head-to-head benchmarks vs OpenPiton/ESP/CHIPKIT.
- Agile small-team challenges (effort parallelization, institutional memory of CAD practices) are mitigated by tooling but not claimed solved.
- Continuous validation depends on team discipline and workload coverage; parameterization can still misconfigure systems if validation is incomplete.
digestSections.research opportunity:
**Gap from prior art.** Analysis: Prior Rocket Chip / agile RISC-V generator work [2],[3] and manycore frameworks [8],[9] advanced reusable RTL, but left multi-flow consistency, cloud full-system timing simulation, portable PD plug-ins, and shared software workloads as separately maintained stacks.

**Gap from this paper.** Analysis: AMS integration, fully open PD for advanced nodes, and quantitative cross-framework productivity/QoR comparisons remain open; ASAP7 is predictive, not a tapeout PDK substitute for leading-edge silicon.

**Concrete opportunities.**

- Analysis: Reproduce Figure 2(c)-class heterogeneous configs through Verilator, FireSim, and Hammer ASAP7 as a SCORE regression suite measuring turnaround time and config-bug catch rate (motivated by the halved-cache incident).
- Analysis: Compare Chipyard RoCC/MMIO accelerator attachment effort vs ESP NoC sockets / OpenPiton CCX on the same accelerator RTL (SHA3, Gemmini [11], NVDLA [12]).
- Analysis: Extend Hammer plug-in matrix with open PDKs beyond ASAP7 and measure how much FIRRTL hierarchy retargeting reduces PD script churn when generator parameters change.
- Analysis: Co-design FireMarshal Linux workloads with ML accelerators (Gemmini) to quantify software reuse across Spike vs FireSim for SCORE-style SoC platform surveys.
- Analysis: Prototype BAG-to-Chipyard behavioral-model hooks for SerDes/ADC/PLL blocks cited in the Berkeley chip retrospective, targeting digital-analog interface validation gaps called out in the Open-Source SoC Development section.
digestSections.pros and cons:
### Pros

- Analysis: End-to-end open stack from generators through cloud FPGA-accelerated simulation and portable VLSI is unusually complete for 2020 academic SoC frameworks.
- Analysis: Diplomacy/TileLink plus fine-grained Rocket parameterization supports heterogeneous roles (app vs controller cores) without swapping entirely different cores.
- Analysis: Concrete silicon retrospective across five process nodes grounds the integration/validation claims beyond a pure tooling pitch.
- Analysis: FireSim+FireMarshal lowers the barrier for small teams to get deterministic full-system software/hardware co-validation.

### Cons

- Analysis: Overview paper lacks quantitative comparison tables (runtime, area QoR, bring-up time) versus OpenPiton/ESP, so adoption arguments are qualitative.
- Analysis: Commercial EDA/PDK dependence remains for real tapeouts; ASAP7 enables flow prototyping but not drop-in advanced-node manufacturing.
- Analysis: capture_figures found captions but no clean artwork clips; figure embeds are full-page renders and include surrounding body text.
- Analysis: Parameterization power that enables agility still admits silent misconfiguration unless continuous full-system validation is enforced.

digestSections.figures:
### Figure 1: Increasing complexity of custom RISC-V SoC test chips built at Berkeley using the Rocket Chip SoC generator since 2012.

![Figure 1](./figures/figure_01.png)

*Page 3. Interpretation: Timeline/complexity growth of Berkeley Rocket Chip-based RISC-V test chips motivating Chipyard's integration and validation focus.*

### Figure 2: SoC customization in Chipyard using the Rocket Chip generator configuration system. (a) A typical Chipyard SoC can include multiple heterogeneous application cores, as well as multiple configurations of BOOM or Rocket cores that can serve various purposes within the SoC, such as a controller unit. Customization can be performed across various levels of the SoC, including Rocket Custom Coprocessor (RoCC) accelerators, MMIO accelerators, and peripherals. (b) An example configuration of a simple design, consisting of a single Rocket in-order processor core and a custom educational SHA3 tightly integrated accelerator. (c) An example configuration of a more complex SoC, consisting of a multiple cores of various capabilities (RV32 Rocket in-order control core, RV64 Rocket in-order application core, RV64GC BOOM 3-wide out-of-order application core), custom accelerators attached to each core, a standard set of peripherals, and a deeper memory hierarchy with an L2 cache. This example also includes a simulated block device and simulated backing DRAM memory.

![Figure 2](./figures/figure_02.png)

*Page 5. Interpretation: Configuration hierarchy from SoC-level heterogeneous cores down to RoCC/MMIO accelerators, with simple SHA3 and complex multi-core examples.*

### Figure 3: Multiple disparate design flows supported by the Chipyard framework through generators and transformations. A series of FIRRTL transformations consumes generators with a custom configuration, and outputs appropriate Verilog and associated collateral for different design stage platforms.

![Figure 3](./figures/figure_03.png)

*Page 6. Interpretation: Shared generator/config source fans out via FIRRTL transforms to simulation, FPGA-accelerated simulation, and VLSI implementation flows.*

### Figure 4: Shared software development in Chipyard using FireMarshal. Designers can use the standard RISC-V software toolchains, or custom software toolchains. While the core application logic and libraries are consistent with the SoC design, kernel and driver configuration may change based on the target platforms or tethered systems. FireMarshal automates workload generation to enable targeting multiple platforms using a single description.

![Figure 4](./figures/figure_04.png)

*Page 8. Interpretation: FireMarshal maps one workload description onto Spike/QEMU, RTL simulation, and FireSim with standard or custom RISC-V toolchains.*
